<a href="articles_maths/product-and-form-conventions.html">Product and Form Conventions</a>
<!-- the twelve products and their names: the four general products, their symmetric and antisymmetric parts, the three-letter code read letter by letter, and the reduced biquaternion space where four of the twelve collapse; the form as the scalar part of a product, the generic form and norm, the four brackets and their letters $P$, $N$, $H$, $K$, the table of the four, and the names in each layer. the norms are in the next article. -->

<a href="articles_maths/norm-and-unitary-conventions.html">Norm and Unitary Conventions</a>
<!-- the four algebraic norms read with one argument, the qualified regular and degenerate, and the six layer tables with the form, the algebraic norm, the realified signature and the role of each bracket; the unitary convention layer by layer, with the unit circle, the unit hyperbola, the two dual lines and the groups of invertibles; the letters $U$ and $u$ inside and outside the layers. -->

<a href="articles_maths/special-element-and-peirce-conventions.html">Special Element and Peirce Conventions</a>
<!-- the root, the idempotent and the nilpotent as glyphs and not as new objects, with their case rule, coordinates and subscripts; the general Peirce convention and its biquaternion reading, the four levels, the Peirce components, the multiplication rule and the canonical frame of the standard pair; the spin as the maximal weight of a carrier of the rotor group $S^3=\mathrm{Spin}(3)$, the unit quaternions, isomorphic to $SU(2)$ whose image is the standard display, the elementary spinor and the Dirac spinor, with the two carriers $S_\pm(\vec u)$ and the chirality letters of the two parts. -->

<a href="articles_maths/frame-and-metric-conventions.html">Frame and Metric Conventions</a>
<!-- the two spacetime frames of the mathematical corpus, and the rule that a frame is declared before it is used; the $\mathbb{B}$ frame, the general frame of the biquaternion universe, read in its own coordinate, with the Euclidean form $(1,1,1,1)$, and the material $\mathbb{B}_{\Phi}$ frame, a particular case kept for reading familiar equations, with metric $(1,-1,-1,-1)$, the substitution $Q_t=ix_0$ and the table of the two; the metric each coordinate frame carries, the plain weight $\varepsilon$ and the Clifford metric, and the coincidence each frame makes; the Clifford map $\mathsf{K}$ from the four directions into $M_4(\mathbb{C})$, not a basis, with the base change $\Lambda_{\mathbb{B}\to\mathbb{B}_{\Phi}}=\mathrm{diag}(1,-i,-i,-i)$ and the metric read from it; the gamma index low and the frame in brackets; eight rules; the same Dirac operator squared in both frames. conventions only. -->

<a href="articles_maths/matrix-representations-conventions.html">Matrix Representations Conventions</a>
<!-- the two matrix models: the $2\times2$ isomorphism and its four forced images, the trace and the determinant; the $4\times4$ regular representation, the left and right copies, the canonical Peirce frame, the gamma set, the Clifford structure of the frame operators, the comparison map and the gamma arrays in both frames. -->

<a href="articles_maths/operator-and-calculus-conventions.html">Operator and Calculus Conventions</a>
<!-- the operator that is its element, the named operators, the two-sided operator, the dagger, the array rule and the Fock exception; the derivative marks, the unhalved coordinate derivative, the gradient and the d'Alembertian; the plain, quaternionic, Hermitian and Krein products read on the gradient. -->

<a href="articles_maths/operator-family-conventions.html">Operator Family Conventions</a>
<!-- the vocabulary of the operator families, and nothing else: the four letters $L$, $R$, $LR$, $\Theta$; the two slots and the argument, the index of a basis operator, the slot label which is the chirality and the chirality operator of a frame; the four sets $\operatorname{End}_L$, $\operatorname{End}_R$, $\operatorname{End}_{LR}$, $\operatorname{End}_{LR\ast}$ and the four matrix letters $\mathsf M_{4L}$, $\mathsf M_{4R}$, $\mathsf M_{4LR}$, $\mathsf M_{4LR\ast}$; what the names do not assert; the units of the algebra $e_t,\vec e_x,\vec e_y,\vec e_z$ and the matrix units $E_{ij}$; the bracket $[F]_{\mathcal{B}}$ and the Peirce change $C_{\Pi}$; the four strata $\Sigma_{11}$, $\Sigma_{10}$, $\Sigma_{01}$, $\Sigma_{00}$ and the two halves $\mathbb{B}_{\Psi}$, $\mathbb{B}_{\Phi}$; the words rank, length and dimension; the closed ray of the identity; and the four adjoint signs ${}^{\approx}$, ${}^{N}$, ${}^{\ast}$, ${}^{\natural\ast}$ with the dagger excluded. Names no dimension, no closure, no inclusion and no theorem. conventions only. -->

<a href="articles_maths/index-and-notation-conventions.html">Index and Notation Conventions</a>
<!-- the superscripts $\mathrm{fop}$ and $\mathrm{opp}$; the upper and low marks, with the prime, the bar and the underline that are not indices; the caret that carries no label; the label rules, the count against the role label and the admitted forms; the subscript rules; the word *interval*, the refusal of $\iota$ in Part VI and the parameter $h_{\mathrm{def}}$; the LaTeX and typesetting rules; the index of the corpus tokens. -->

<a href="articles_maths/reserved-letters-conventions.html">Reserved Letters Conventions</a>
<!-- the last of the ten conventions articles, and a summary: the eight glyphs that carry one role each and are spent once, the angle $\theta$ real with the $i$ of a rotation in the exponential and the imaginary angle written $i\theta$ at the point of use, the scale $\varrho$, the wave number $\nu=k/2\pi=1/\lambda$, the wavelength $\lambda=1/\nu$, the eigenvalue $\eta$, the scalar imaginary $i$ with the dotless index $\imath$, the two sectors $\Phi$ and $\Psi$ uppercase, and the element families $Q$, $Ζ$ and $\Pi$ reserved for the generic element, the roots and the potents; the fallback $\digamma$ for every other scalar, with the subscript that names its sense. conventions only. -->

## PART I : ALGEBRA

## Foundations of Algebra

### Theory

<a href="articles_maths/sets-functions-and-relations.html">Sets, Functions and Relations</a>
<!-- sets and the membership relation; subsets, the power set and the algebra of subsets; ordered pairs and the Cartesian product; relations and their properties; equivalence relations, partitions and quotients; order relations, partial and total; functions as a special kind of relation, injective, surjective and bijective maps, composition and inverse; families and indexed sets; the algebra of subsets as the first example of a Boolean algebra, forward-referenced to Part VI. -->

<a href="articles_maths/logic-and-proof.html">Logic and Proof</a>
<!-- propositional logic: the connectives, truth tables and tautologies; the laws of the algebra of propositions and their identity with the algebra of subsets, forward-referenced to the Boolean algebras of Part VI; predicate logic: variables, quantifiers, free and bound occurrences; the rules of inference and the structure of a formal proof; direct, contrapositive and contradiction arguments; induction and recursion as proof principles; consistency and completeness in outline; the notational conventions used throughout this corpus. -->

<a href="articles_maths/order-theory-and-lattices.html">Order Theory and Lattices</a>
<!-- partial orders, total orders and well-orders; lattices, complete, distributive and modular lattices; Galois connections; the Knaster–Tarski theorem; the lattice of subsets, forward-referenced to the Boolean algebras of Part VI. -->

<a href="articles_maths/mereology-and-collective-set-theory.html">Mereology and Collective Set Theory</a>
<!-- the whole as primitive and the parts as the divisions of the whole, against the element-first construction of Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory; the division relation and its postulates, a pre-order that is not antisymmetric, with the divisibility of $\mathbb{Z}$ as the standard model and the passage to $\mathbb{N}$ as the antisymmetrisation; the observation that the postulates constrain the relation and not the quotient, so a unit-quotient rule is a physical hypothesis rather than a theorem; the quotient by mutual division; parthood and the two definitions of a proper part, which agree exactly when the relation is antisymmetric; mutual parts; overlap and disjointness; the strong and the weak supplementation principle, the non-part and the disjoint forms of the first, and the two-element order that separates them, together with the recovery of the classical implication under the second definition of a proper part when antisymmetry fails; extensionality as a postulate independent of antisymmetry under the first definition and equivalent to it under the second; the correspondence of classical mereology with a Boolean algebra without a least element, forward-referenced to Part VI. -->

<a href="articles_maths/cardinality-and-the-axiom-of-choice.html">Cardinality and the Axiom of Choice</a>
<!-- finite and infinite sets; equipotence and cardinality; countable and uncountable sets, the countability of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ and of $\mathbb{Z}$, the uncountability of the power set of $\mathbb{N}$; Cantor's theorem and the cardinality of the power set; the continuum hypothesis; the axiom of choice, Zorn's lemma and the well-ordering theorem, and their equivalence; the uses of Zorn's lemma in this corpus: maximal ideals, bases of a vector space, algebraic closure, maximal filters; cardinal arithmetic. -->

<a href="articles_maths/set-theoretic-foundations.html">Set-Theoretic Foundations</a>
<!-- the Zermelo–Fraenkel axioms and the axiom of choice; ordinals and cardinals; transfinite induction and recursion; the cumulative hierarchy; the independence of the continuum hypothesis; large cardinals in outline. -->

<a href="articles_maths/formal-logic-and-computability.html">Formal Logic and Computability</a>
<!-- first-order logic, formal systems and derivations; soundness and completeness; compactness and the Löwenheim–Skolem theorem; Turing machines and recursive functions; decidability and undecidability; Gödel's incompleteness theorems; the halting problem. -->

<a href="articles_maths/model-theory.html">Model Theory</a>
<!-- structures and languages; satisfaction and elementary equivalence; compactness; quantifier elimination; ultraproducts; the model theory of algebraically closed, real-closed and valued fields. -->

<a href="articles_maths/proof-theory-and-type-theory.html">Proof Theory and Type Theory</a>
<!-- natural deduction and the sequent calculus; cut elimination; normalisation; intuitionistic logic; the Curry–Howard correspondence; the lambda calculus; the categorical reading of proofs. -->

<a href="articles_maths/universal-properties-and-categories.html">Universal Properties and Categories</a>
<!-- objects and morphisms; the categories of sets, of groups, of rings and of modules over a fixed ring; functors, natural transformations and equivalence of categories; initial and terminal objects; universal properties and universal objects, with existence and uniqueness formulated as a single statement; products, coproducts, free objects, quotients and localisations as universal constructions; the universal properties this corpus relies on: the free group, the tensor product, the symmetric and exterior algebras, the fraction field, the completion; adjunction in outline. -->

### * Theory

<a href="articles_maths/involutive-groups.html">Involutive Groups</a>
<!-- an involutive group, that is a group with an involution, an anti-automorphism of order two; the notion presupposes no commutativity, and unlike a ring a group always carries one, the inversion, which is the canonical isomorphism with the opposite group, so the informative object is the set of involutions, in bijection with the involutive automorphisms through $\sigma \mapsto \sigma\iota$ and with the split extensions by $C_2$, while an anti-automorphism is an automorphism exactly when the group is abelian. The general structure: the fixed set $A^\sigma$, a subgroup exactly when its elements commute pairwise, and the inverted set $I(\sigma) = G^{\sigma\iota}$, which always is one; the conjugate products $g\sigma(g)$ and $\sigma(g)g$, which are only conjugate and need not be fixed; real, strongly real and ambivalent elements, with $S_n$ and $D_n$ ambivalent and strongly real, $Q_8$ ambivalent with only $\pm 1$ as products of two elements of order two, and $A_4$ not ambivalent; $\sigma$-stable subgroups and the induced involution on a quotient, with the image of the fixed set possibly strict; products, the swap with fixed set the diagonal, and the graph of an anti-isomorphism as the fixed set of a twisted involution; the semidirect product by an involutive automorphism, the split and non-split extensions, with the dihedral and dicyclic examples and the groups of order $2p$; and the involutions read off a presentation, the inversion and the word reversal in a free group, the Coxeter inversion together with the diagram automorphisms, and the inversion and reversal automorphisms of the braid groups, which are torsion-free and have no elements of order two. **An additional structure on the group, not a rung of any chain; it stands in the Theory list immediately after *Group Cohomology*, the last article it draws on, and before *The Classification of Finite Simple Groups*, so that every article it uses precedes it and the classification still closes the category.** The geometry of the spaces built from a fixed subgroup is Part IV, and the representation-theoretic treatment of the real elements is later still. -->

<a href="articles_maths/involutions-and-the-fixed-point-subgroup.html">Involutions and the Fixed-Point Subgroup</a>
<!-- the fixed-point set of an involution of a group and when it is a subgroup; the inversion as the canonical involution, whose fixed set is central and generally not a subgroup. -->

<a href="articles_maths/involutive-group-actions.html">Involutive Group Actions</a>
<!-- a group acting on an involutive structure and preserving the involution; the induced involution on the fixed points and on the quotients. -->

<a href="articles_maths/free-involutions-and-the-quotient.html">Free Involutions and the Quotient</a>
<!-- a fixed-point-free involution of a group; the quotient and the double cover it defines, with the antipodal and the dihedral examples. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-commuting-algebra-of-an-involution.html">The Commuting Algebra of an Involution</a>
<!-- the elements commuting with an involutive automorphism; the centraliser, its relation to the fixed subgroup and its place in the semidirect product. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-centre-of-an-involutive-group.html">The Centre of an Involutive Group</a>
<!-- the centre of a group with an involution and the involution it inherits; the compatibility of the involution with centrality and with the commutator subgroup. -->

### Applications

<a href="articles_maths/finite-groups-and-symmetry.html">Finite Groups and Symmetry</a>
<!-- cyclic and dihedral groups, symmetric and alternating groups, cycles and parity, conjugacy classes, the quaternion group $Q_8$, the classification of groups of small order, and the finite group theory that a symmetry group draws on; the symmetry groups themselves, their realisation inside the orthogonal group and their crystallographic refinements, belong to Part IV, where a form and a distance are available. -->

## Rings and Fields

### Theory

<a href="articles_maths/rings.html">Rings</a>
<!-- definition of an associative ring with $1 \neq 0$, elementary properties, subrings, ring homomorphisms and quotients of rings; ideals, left, right and two-sided, generated ideals, the correspondence theorem, quotient rings; units, zero divisors, nilpotents and idempotents as vocabulary; prime and maximal ideals with their quotient characterisations. **This is the Ring rung of the chain that follows.** The former multi-rung article has been apportioned: the commutative law to *Commutative Rings*, nilpotent structure to *Reduced Rings and the Nilradical*, the domain to *Integral Domains*, fields to *Fields*, division rings to *Division Rings*, the factorisation rungs to *Unique Factorisation Domains*, *Principal Ideal Domains* and *Euclidean Domains*, and modules and algebras to *Modules* and *Algebras*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/commutative-rings.html">Commutative Rings</a>
<!-- the commutative law and what it adds: the binomial and multinomial theorems, the commutativity of the product of ideals, sums, products and intersections of ideals and the radical of an ideal; coprime ideals and the Chinese remainder theorem; the commutative theory of prime and maximal ideals — a quotient by a prime ideal is a domain and a quotient by a maximal ideal is a field; $\operatorname{Spec} R$ as a poset; the failure of each statement without commutativity. Ideals and quotient rings themselves are owned by *Rings*, §§6–7. -->

<a href="articles_maths/reduced-rings-and-the-nilradical.html">Reduced Rings and the Nilradical</a>
<!-- nilpotents as a class; a ring is reduced when it has no nonzero nilpotent, equivalently when its nilradical vanishes; the nilradical as the intersection of the prime ideals and as the radical of the zero ideal; reduced rings as subrings of products of domains; $\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}$ as the counterexamples that fix the rung. -->

<a href="articles_maths/integral-domains.html">Integral Domains</a>
<!-- a commutative ring with $1 \neq 0$ and no zero divisors; cancellation; associates and divisibility; irreducibles and primes; the characteristic and the embedding of the prime field; the root theorem, that a polynomial over a domain of degree $< m$ with $m$ roots is zero; $\mathbb{Z}$ and $K[x]$ as the standard examples; the fraction field once localization is available; the domain that is not a unique factorisation domain is deferred to the rung below. -->

<a href="articles_maths/gcd-domains.html">GCD Domains</a>
<!-- the greatest common divisor and the least common multiple in a domain; the gcd of two elements always existing; a GCD domain as the most general rung at which divisibility is governed by a gcd; the ideal-theoretic characterisation; UFD and Bézout domains as the two incomparable strengthenings, forward-referenced. -->

<a href="articles_maths/bezout-domains.html">Bézout Domains</a>
<!-- Bézout's identity promoted to a definition: every finitely generated ideal is principal; the relation to the gcd; a Bézout domain is a GCD domain, and the converse fails; the principal ideal domains as the Noetherian Bézout domains, forward-referenced; the ring of all algebraic integers as the standard non-Noetherian example. -->

<a href="articles_maths/unique-factorisation-domains.html">Unique Factorisation Domains</a>
<!-- irreducibles and primes; existence and uniqueness of factorisation into irreducibles; a domain is a unique factorisation domain exactly when every irreducible is prime; Euclid's lemma; the failure of unique factorisation in $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$; content and Gauss's lemma; Eisenstein's criterion; the transfer of unique factorisation to the polynomial ring and the factorisation of polynomials over a field; $c(f)$. -->

<a href="articles_maths/principal-ideal-domains.html">Principal Ideal Domains</a>
<!-- every ideal principal; a principal ideal domain is a unique factorisation domain; the ideal structure of the quotient by a prime ideal; the maximal ideals; $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ as the unique factorisation domain that is not principal. -->

<a href="articles_maths/euclidean-domains.html">Euclidean Domains</a>
<!-- the Euclidean degree function $N$, division with remainder, the Euclidean algorithm and the extended form giving Bézout coefficients; a Euclidean domain is a principal ideal domain and hence a unique factorisation domain, giving the chain Euclidean $\Rightarrow$ principal $\Rightarrow$ unique factorisation; norm-Euclidean domains; $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ and the Gaussian primes as the standard worked example; $\mathbb{Z}[(1+\sqrt{-19})/2]$ as the principal ideal domain that is not Euclidean. -->

<a href="articles_maths/localization-and-the-fraction-field.html">Localization and the Fraction Field</a>
<!-- multiplicative sets, localization, $\operatorname{Frac}(R)$, local rings, the universal property. -->

<a href="articles_maths/noetherian-and-artinian-rings.html">Noetherian and Artinian Rings</a>
<!-- the ascending and descending chain conditions; the Hilbert basis theorem; the Akizuki–Hopkins theorem; the relation to the finitely generated modules of Part I. -->

<a href="articles_maths/primary-decomposition.html">Primary Decomposition</a>
<!-- primary ideals and primary decomposition; the uniqueness of the associated primes; the relation to the Nullstellensatz and to the ideals of this part. -->

<a href="articles_maths/integral-extensions-and-krull-dimension.html">Integral Extensions and Krull Dimension</a>
<!-- integral extensions; the lying-over, going-up and going-down theorems; the Krull dimension; the dimension of a polynomial ring. -->

<a href="articles_maths/dedekind-domains-and-ideal-class-groups.html">Dedekind Domains and Ideal Class Groups</a>
<!-- Dedekind domains and the unique factorisation of ideals; fractional ideals; the ideal class group and the finiteness of the class number. -->

<a href="articles_maths/valuation-theory-and-henselian-rings.html">Valuation Theory and Henselian Rings</a>
<!-- valuations and valuation rings; the extension of valuations; the p-adic completions are treated in Part II, where a distance first appears; Hensel's lemma, Henselian rings and the lifting of factorisations. -->

<a href="articles_maths/fields.html">Fields</a>
<!-- definition, elementary properties, characteristic and the prime subfield, examples and non-examples, extensions and degree, algebraic and transcendental elements, minimal polynomials, the tower law, splitting fields, algebraic closure, separability and perfect fields, Galois groups and the fundamental theorem, straightedge-and-compass constructions. -->

<a href="articles_maths/field-extensions.html">Field Extensions</a>
<!-- degree, algebraic and transcendental elements, minimal polynomials, the tower law, simple extensions. -->

<a href="articles_maths/splitting-fields-and-algebraic-closure.html">Splitting Fields and Algebraic Closure</a>
<!-- splitting fields, algebraic closure, existence and uniqueness, separability, perfect fields. -->

<a href="articles_maths/finite-fields.html">Finite Fields</a>
<!-- structure, existence, uniqueness, subfields, the Frobenius map, explicit constructions. -->

<a href="articles_maths/galois-theory.html">Galois Theory</a>
<!-- Galois groups, the fundamental theorem, solvability by radicals, straightedge and compass constructions. -->

<a href="articles_maths/ring-and-field-automorphisms.html">Ring and Field Automorphisms</a>
<!-- the transformation group of a ring, $\operatorname{Aut}(R)$, and what it preserves: addition and multiplication, hence $0$, $1$ and the prime subfield; inner automorphisms $x\mapsto uxu^{-1}$ by a unit $u$, and the failure of commutativity in the non-commutative case; the fixed subring and the invariance of the centre; field automorphisms, the prime field as their fixed field, and complex conjugation on $\mathbb{C}$; the Frobenius $x\mapsto x^p$ in prime characteristic as an automorphism of a finite field; the Galois group $\operatorname{gal}(L/K)$ as the automorphism group of $L$ over $K$; what an automorphism of a ring does not preserve: no length, angle or norm is involved. -->

<a href="articles_maths/cyclotomic-fields.html">Cyclotomic Fields</a>
<!-- the cyclotomic polynomial and the cyclotomic field; the Galois group; the relation to the Galois theory of this part; the constructible polygons belong to Part IV. -->

<a href="articles_maths/kummer-theory.html">Kummer Theory</a>
<!-- abelian extensions of exponent $n$; the Kummer pairing. -->

<a href="articles_maths/galois-cohomology.html">Galois Cohomology</a>
<!-- the cohomology of a Galois group, over the fields met in the earlier articles. -->

<a href="articles_maths/class-field-theory.html">Class Field Theory</a>
<!-- abelian extensions of the $p$-adic fields and of the number fields; the Artin reciprocity law; the Hilbert class field; the relation to Galois cohomology and to Kummer theory; the adelic formulation is not developed here. -->

<a href="articles_maths/algebraic-number-theory.html">Algebraic Number Theory</a>
<!-- number fields and rings of integers; ideals and unique factorisation; the ideal class group and Dirichlet's unit theorem; the Minkowski theory; the decomposition of primes; the relation to Galois theory. -->

<a href="articles_maths/global-fields.html">Global Fields</a>
<!-- number fields and function fields of curves over a finite field as the two kinds of global field; places and the product formula; the arithmetic of global fields. -->

<a href="articles_maths/elliptic-curves.html">Elliptic Curves</a>
<!-- elliptic curves and the group law; the Weierstrass equation; the Mordell–Weil theorem; the algebraic theory of elliptic curves and their isogenies; the L-function and modularity are treated in Part III. -->

<a href="articles_maths/algebraic-curves.html">Algebraic Curves</a>
<!-- affine and projective plane curves; the function field of a curve; divisors and the genus; the relation to algebraic number theory and to the Riemann–Roch theorem. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-riemann-roch-theorem-for-curves.html">The Riemann–Roch Theorem for Curves</a>
<!-- divisors and linear systems on a curve; the classical Riemann–Roch theorem and Serre duality for curves; the genus as the first obstruction; the surface and Grothendieck forms require the sheaf and derived machinery of Part II. -->

<a href="articles_maths/grobner-bases-and-elimination-theory.html">Gröbner Bases and Elimination Theory</a>
<!-- monomial orders; the division algorithm; Gröbner bases and Buchberger's algorithm; the elimination theorem; the relation to polynomial rings and to ideal theory; resultants, discriminants and the elimination theorem, as the classical counterpart of Buchberger's algorithm. -->

<a href="articles_maths/invariant-theory.html">Invariant Theory</a>
<!-- the invariant ring of a group action; the Hilbert basis theorem for invariants; the nullcone. -->

<a href="articles_maths/symmetric-functions-and-schur-functions.html">Symmetric Functions and Schur Functions</a>
<!-- symmetric polynomials and symmetric functions; the elementary, complete and power-sum bases; the fundamental theorem of symmetric functions; the Schur functions and Young tableaux, the Jacobi–Trudi identity and the Littlewood–Richardson rule. -->

<a href="articles_maths/representation-theory-of-symmetric-groups.html">Representation Theory of Symmetric Groups</a>
<!-- the irreducible representations of the symmetric group; Young diagrams and Specht modules; the hook length formula. -->

<a href="articles_maths/schur-weyl-duality.html">Schur–Weyl Duality</a>
<!-- the double commutant theorem for the symmetric and general linear groups; the decomposition of tensor powers of the defining representation. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-inverse-galois-problem.html">The Inverse Galois Problem</a>
<!-- the problem and its history; the solution for solvable groups; the relation to the classification of finite simple groups and to the Galois theory of this part. -->

<a href="articles_maths/ordered-fields.html">Ordered Fields</a>
<!-- orders, compatibility with addition and multiplication, Archimedean ordered fields, orderability. -->

<a href="articles_maths/real-closed-and-complete-ordered-fields.html">Real-Closed and Complete Ordered Fields</a>
<!-- real-closed fields, the intermediate value property, Dedekind completion, completeness, uniqueness of $\mathbb{R}$ up to order-isomorphism. -->

<a href="articles_maths/algebraically-closed-fields.html">Algebraically Closed Fields</a>
<!-- algebraic closure, the fundamental theorem of algebra, Artin–Schreier, the non-orderability of $\mathbb{C}$. -->

<a href="articles_maths/semiprime-rings.html">Semiprime Rings</a>
<!-- the non-commutative analogue of a reduced ring: a ring with no nonzero nilpotent ideal; the lower nilradical as the intersection of the prime ideals; a semiprime ring as a subdirect product of prime rings; the commutative case is *Reduced Rings and the Nilradical*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/prime-rings.html">Prime Rings</a>
<!-- a ring in which a product of two nonzero ideals is nonzero; prime ideals in the non-commutative sense and the failure of the commutative correspondence with quotients; every prime ring is semiprime and the converse fails; every domain is prime and the converse fails. -->

<a href="articles_maths/non-commutative-domains.html">Non-Commutative Domains</a>
<!-- a ring with $1 \neq 0$ and no zero divisors, without the commutative hypothesis; cancellation on both sides; the asymmetry of the left and the right ideals; $\mathbb{H}$, the free algebra, the Weyl algebra and the group ring of a torsion-free group; the intersection with the commutative rung is exactly the integral domains. -->

<a href="articles_maths/ore-domains-and-division-rings-of-fractions.html">Ore Domains and Division Rings of Fractions</a>
<!-- the Ore condition and the Ore domain; the division ring of fractions of an Ore domain, the non-commutative analogue of the fraction field; Malcev–Neumann series over an ordered group; the division ring of fractions of the Weyl algebra; the free algebra as the standard non-Ore domain; no completion and no adic topology are used. -->

<a href="articles_maths/division-rings.html">Division Rings</a>
<!-- a ring with $1 \neq 0$ in which every nonzero element is a unit, without the commutative hypothesis; a skew field; the centre is a field and the division ring is an algebra over it, possibly of infinite dimension there; a commutative division ring is a field; Wedderburn's little theorem, that every finite division ring is a field; $\mathbb{H}$ and the division ring of fractions of the Weyl algebra as the two kinds of example. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-column-ideals-of-a-matrix-ring-one-idempotent-and-n-1-nilpotents.html">The Column Ideals of a Matrix Ring: One Idempotent and $n-1$ Nilpotents</a>
<!-- the column ideal $L_j=AE_{jj}$ of the matrix ring $M_n(D)$ over a division ring $D$, the matrices supported in one column, a minimal left ideal of dimension $n$; the Peirce decomposition of the algebra by the matrix units into the corners $E_{ii}AE_{kk}=DE_{ik}$, one-dimensional over $D$; the cut of the column into one diagonal corner $E_{jj}AE_{jj}=DE_{jj}$, a division ring isomorphic to $D$ whose identity $E_{jj}$ is an idempotent, and $n-1$ off-diagonal corners $E_{ii}AE_{jj}=DE_{ij}$, each square-zero, so that an off-diagonal corner has no nonzero idempotent and its nonzero elements are nilpotents; the theorem that a corner-adapted basis, one element per corner, has exactly one idempotent, $E_{jj}$, and $n-1$ nilpotents, the off-diagonal matrix units, the off-diagonal nilpotency being insensitive to the normalisation of the corner element while the diagonal idempotency requires that element to be the identity of its corner; the count $1+(n-1)=n=\dim_D L_j$ as the arithmetic of the corners, $n-1$ being the number of off-diagonal corners of a column; the nilpotents of the column as exactly the off-diagonal part $N_j$, each square-zero, $N_j$ being the kernel of the surjective ring homomorphism $\pi(x)=x_{jj}$ to $D$, so that $L_j/N_j\cong D$, that $N_j^2=0$ and that the column is a ring with right identity $E_{jj}$ but no two-sided identity for $n\geq2$; the idempotents of the column as the affine family $E_{jj}+N_j$ of dimension $n-1$, so that the count is a count of basis elements and not of idempotents, and a basis of the column can consist entirely of idempotents; the counts per column and per algebra, the $n$ diagonal corners giving the complete orthogonal family $E_{11},\dots,E_{nn}$ and the $n(n-1)$ off-diagonal corners the nilpotents $E_{ik}$; the boundary, that over a ring with a proper nonzero ideal the column is not minimal, with $M_n(I)E_{jj}$ the counterexample, so that the coefficient ring must be a division ring; the scalar-side trap for $D$ noncommutative, where $dE_{ik}\neq E_{ik}d$ and the corners are read as left multiples; and the biquaternion instance $n=2$, $D=\mathbb{C}$, where the first column is the spinor space $\mathbb{B}\tilde\Pi_1=\mathbb{C}\{\tilde\Pi_1,\vec\Pi_{\mathrm{nil},2}\}$ with one idempotent and one nilpotent and with $\tilde\Pi_1+c\vec\Pi_{\mathrm{nil},2}$ the affine family. The matrix units and the left ideals are *Matrix Algebras*; the Peirce decomposition is *Unital Algebras*, §*Idempotents and the Peirce Decomposition*; the rank and the length are *Direct Sums, Free Modules and Rank*; and the biquaternion instance is *Ideals and Peirce Decomposition of the General Plain Algebra*, with the physical reading in *The Spinor Space as a Module and as a Hilbert Space*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/von-neumann-regular-rings.html">Von Neumann Regular Rings</a>
<!-- a ring in which every principal left ideal is generated by an idempotent, equivalently every finitely generated left ideal is idempotent-generated; the commutative von Neumann regular rings as exactly the reduced rings of Krull dimension zero, equivalently those whose localization at every maximal ideal is a field; reduced von Neumann regular rings as the strongly regular rings; Boolean rings as the examples of characteristic two, and $\mathbb{Z}$, $k[x]$, $\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}$ and the local rings as the non-examples; the failure of the class to be closed under quotients, and the place of the class among the rings of *Reduced Rings and the Nilradical*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/real-algebraic-geometry.html">Real Algebraic Geometry</a>
<!-- real algebraic sets and semialgebraic sets; the Tarski–Seidenberg theorem; the relation to the real-closed fields of this part. -->

### * Theory

<a href="articles_maths/involutive-rings.html">Involutive Rings</a>
<!-- an involutive ring, that is a ring with an involution, an anti-automorphism of order two; the notion presupposes no commutativity, and it is the same datum as an order-two isomorphism $A \to A^{\mathrm{opp}}$, so every ring with an involution is isomorphic to its opposite ring, while in the commutative case the opposite ring is the ring itself and the notion degenerates to an automorphism of order dividing two. The general structure: the fixed set $A^\sigma$ and the symmetric and anti-Hermitian elements, with $A = \mathrm{sym} \oplus \mathrm{Skew}$ as abelian groups when $2$ is invertible, and the failure without commutativity of the multiplicative grading and of the closedness of $A^\sigma$ under multiplication; $\sigma$-ideals, the induced involution on a quotient and on a product, and $\sigma$-prime ideals and $\sigma$-prime rings, with the sufficient elementwise condition $aAb^{*} \neq 0$, with prime implying $\sigma$-prime and with the converse failing. The commutative case: $\sigma$ an automorphism of order two, $R = R^\sigma \oplus R^-$ with the characteristic-two failure, the conjugate product $x\sigma(x)$ and the conjugate sum $x+\sigma(x)$, the monic quadratic and the integrality of $R$ over $R^\sigma$, the affine involutions of $R[x]$ and their fixed subrings, localization and $\operatorname{Frac}(R)^\sigma = \operatorname{Frac}(R^\sigma)$, fields with involution as quadratic Galois extensions, quadratic in one characteristic and Artin–Schreier in the other, the exclusion of nontrivial order-preserving involutions of an ordered field, a table of examples, and the fixed ring $k[x^2,xy,y^2]$ of $k[x,y]$ as a ring that is not a unique factorisation domain. **An additional structure on the ring, not a rung of either chain; it stands at the seam between the commutative half and the non-commutative chain, after *Algebraically Closed Fields* and before *Semiprime Rings*.** The classification of the involutions of a central simple algebra is *Involutions of a Central Simple Algebra*, in *Algebras*; the forms attached to an involution, and everything a form or a pairing defines, are *Hilbert Algebras*, in Part II. -->

<a href="articles_maths/matrix-rings-with-an-involution.html">Matrix Rings with an Involution</a>
<!-- the transpose, the conjugate transpose and the symplectic involution on a matrix ring; the classification of the involutions of $M_n(R)$. -->

<a href="articles_maths/rings-with-a-semilinear-involution.html">Rings with a Semilinear Involution</a>
<!-- a semilinear involution with respect to a ring automorphism; the $\sigma$-semilinear case and the failure of the naive identities. -->

<a href="articles_maths/involutions-of-a-group-ring.html">Involutions of a Group Ring</a>
<!-- the involutions of a group ring induced by the inversion and by an involution of the group; the twisted group ring and the compatibility with the coefficients. -->

<a href="articles_maths/involutive-local-rings.html">Involutive Local Rings</a>
<!-- local rings with an involution; the involution on the maximal ideal and on the residue field, and the lifting of the residue involution. -->

<a href="articles_maths/involutions-of-a-polynomial-ring-and-the-symmetric-part.html">Involutions of a Polynomial Ring and the Symmetric Part</a>
<!-- the involutions of $R[x]$, chiefly $x\mapsto -x$; the symmetric part and the graded decomposition it induces. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-skew-field-of-a-ring-with-involution.html">The Skew Field of a Ring with Involution</a>
<!-- the anti-Hermitian elements $\{x : x^* = -x\}$ against the symmetric elements; their interaction with the product and with the trace. -->

## Algebras

### Theory

<a href="articles_maths/algebras-a-general-introduction.html">Algebras: A General Introduction</a>
<!-- modules over a commutative ring; what an algebra is (an $R$-module with a bilinear product); the relation to modules; associativity, unit and commutativity; ideals and quotients; constructions, including the tensor and free algebras. -->

<a href="articles_maths/associative-algebras.html">Associative Algebras</a>
<!-- the associative algebras; associativity as a polynomial identity; the associator, and the power-associativity that outlives it; the free associative algebra and the tensor algebra; the universal enveloping algebra of a Lie algebra as the associative algebra attached to a non-associative one; the algebras that fail associativity. -->

<a href="articles_maths/unital-algebras.html">Unital Algebras</a>
<!-- the algebras with an identity, and the rings with identity read as algebras; the group of invertibles and the invertible elements; the unitisation of a non-unital algebra by adjoining a unit; the homomorphisms that preserve the identity and those that do not; the idempotents, the Peirce decomposition $A=eAe\oplus eAf\oplus fAe\oplus fAf$ and the central idempotents that split the algebra as a product; the non-unital algebras of the corpus. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-algebra-generated-by-an-element-and-the-chinese-remainder-decomposition.html">The Algebra Generated by an Element and the Chinese Remainder Decomposition</a>
<!-- the evaluation map $f\mapsto f(a)$ and the subalgebra $k[a]$; the minimal polynomial $m_a$ and the isomorphism $k[a]\cong k[x]/(m_a)$; the dimension $\deg m_a$ and the power basis $1,a,\dots,a^{d-1}$; the Chinese remainder decomposition for $m_a=m_1\cdots m_r$ with the factors pairwise coprime, the canonical idempotents $\varepsilon_i=g_i(a)$, and the components $a_i=a\varepsilon_i$ with minimal polynomial $m_i$; the primary decomposition $m_a=\prod_i f_i^{e_i}$ and the two extreme cases of an irreducible polynomial and a power of a linear one; the distinction between the decomposition of $k[a]$ and the Peirce decomposition of $A$ when the idempotents are not central; the companion matrix of $x^3-x$ with its three rational idempotents, the split-complex and dual numbers, and the complex numbers as a real algebra; the commutative-ring caveat on the minimal polynomial and on the units $\lambda_i-\lambda_j$. -->

<a href="articles_maths/separable-elements-and-split-minimal-polynomials.html">Separable Elements and Split Minimal Polynomials</a>
<!-- the separable polynomials and the criterion $\gcd(f,f')=1$; the discriminant, the resultant and the Vandermonde determinant; characteristic $p$, the polynomial $x^p-t$ and perfect fields; separable elements, split elements and the split squarefree form $m_a=\prod_i(x-\lambda_i)$; the trace form $\tau(x,y)=\operatorname{Tr}(L_{xy})$ on $k[a]$, the theorem that its nondegeneracy is the separability of $a$, and the identity $\det T=\Delta(m_a)$ in the power basis; the distinction between separable elements and separable algebras, with $M_p(k)$ over an imperfect field as the warning; the independence table for the split and the separable conditions; and the roles of the two conditions in the eigenvalue and Jordan–Chevalley decompositions. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-eigenvalue-decomposition-of-an-element.html">The Eigenvalue Decomposition of an Element</a>
<!-- the eigenvalues as the roots of $m_a$, the criterion that $a-\lambda$ is not invertible, and the left and right eigenvalue equations; the multiplicity in $m_a$ against the algebraic multiplicity; the decomposition $a=\sum_i\lambda_i e_i$ with distinct $\lambda_i$, orthogonal idempotents $e_i$ and $\sum_i e_i=1$; the equivalence with $m_a$ split with distinct roots, with $L_a$ diagonalisable and with $R_a$ diagonalisable; uniqueness and the Lagrange idempotents; the eigenspaces $\ker(L_a-\lambda_i)=e_iA$ and $\ker(R_a-\lambda_i)=Ae_i$, the simultaneous eigenspaces $e_iAe_j$ and the two-sided Peirce decomposition; the matrix case and the distinction between the matrix eigenspace $e_iV$ and the algebra eigenspace $e_iA$; the generalized eigenvalue decomposition $a=\sum_i(\lambda_i\varepsilon_i+n_i)$ for a split polynomial with repeated roots; and the Jordan block and biquaternion examples. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-lagrange-sylvester-eigenprojector-formula.html">The Lagrange–Sylvester Eigenprojector Formula</a>
<!-- Lagrange interpolation at distinct eigenvalues and the eigenprojector formula $e_i=\prod_{j\ne i}(a-\lambda_j 1_A)/(\lambda_i-\lambda_j)$; the minimal-polynomial form $e_i=m_i(a)/m_i(\lambda_i)=m_i(a)/m_a'(\lambda_i)$; Sylvester's formula $f(a)=\sum_i f(\lambda_i)e_i$ for polynomials and holomorphic functions; the resolvent identity $(z-a)^{-1}=\sum_i e_i/(z-\lambda_i)$ and the contour formula $e_i=(2\pi i)^{-1}\oint(z-a)^{-1}\,dz$; Hermite interpolation in the repeated-root case, the generalized eigenprojectors $\varepsilon_i=q_i(a)u_i(a)$ with $q_i=m_a/(x-\lambda_i)^{e_i}$ and $u_i q_i\equiv1$ modulo $(x-\lambda_i)^{e_i}$, the generalized Sylvester formula, and the higher-order poles of the resolvent; and the two-by-two, companion, Jordan-block and block-with-two-eigenvalues examples. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-centraliser-and-the-diagonal-peirce-part.html">The Centraliser and the Diagonal Peirce Part</a>
<!-- the centraliser $C(a)=\{x:ax=xa\}$, the kernel of the commutator map $x\mapsto ax-xa$, equal to $C(k[a])$; the theorem $C(a)=\bigoplus_i e_iAe_i$ for a split separable element, with the proof from the two-sided Peirce decomposition and the distinct eigenvalues; the dimension $\sum_i\dim e_iAe_i$, and $\sum_i m_i^2\ge n$ in $M_n$; the double centraliser $C(C(a))=k[a]$ in a full matrix algebra and its failure in a general algebra; the diagonal part $D=\bigoplus_i e_iAe_i$ and the off-diagonal part $N=\bigoplus_{i\ne j}e_iAe_j$; the diagonal projection $\pi$, its multiplicativity criterion, and the contrast between $N=0$ and the vanishing of the diagonal part of $N^2$; the identity $C(a)=\bigcap_i C(e_i)$; and the scalar, distinct-eigenvalue, multiplicity, upper-triangular and central examples. -->

<a href="articles_maths/off-diagonal-peirce-components-and-noncentral-idempotents.html">Off-Diagonal Peirce Components and Noncentral Idempotents</a>
<!-- the Peirce decomposition $A=eAe\oplus eAf\oplus fAe\oplus fAf$ for one idempotent and the multiplication table of the four corners; the diagonal part $D=eAe\oplus fAf$ and the off-diagonal part $N=eAf\oplus fAe$, with $N^2\subseteq D$; the commutator interpretation $N=[e,A]$, the centraliser $C(e)=D$, the values of the commutator with $e$ on the four corners and the $\mathbb{Z}$-grading; the equivalence of centrality with $N=0$ and with $A\cong Ae\times Af$; the noncentral case, the ideal $AeA=eAe\oplus eAf\oplus fAe$ and the corner quotient $A/AeA\cong fAf$; the warning that $N$ measures noncentrality, not noncommutativity; the rank-$k$ matrix case with $\dim N=2k(n-k)$, $N^2=D$ and the quotient $M_{n-k}(k)$; and the biquaternion rank-one example. -->

<a href="articles_maths/nilpotent-elements-and-the-jordan-chevalley-decomposition.html">Nilpotent Elements and the Jordan–Chevalley Decomposition</a>
<!-- nilpotent elements, their index, the failure of the sum of nilpotents to be nilpotent and the closure under commuting sums and products; the radical and the nilradical; the semisimple elements as those with squarefree minimal polynomial, against the separable elements; the additive decomposition $a=s+n$ with $sn=ns$, $s$ semisimple and $n$ nilpotent, and its uniqueness; the theorem over a perfect field via the Chinese remainder decomposition and the lifting of the roots, with $s,n\in k[a]$, $m_s$ the squarefree part of $m_a$ and the index of $n$ the largest exponent; the general-field criterion and the failure of $x^p-t$ squared over $\mathbb{F}_p(t)$ and of its companion matrix; the multiplicative decomposition $a=su$ for units, with $u$ unipotent; the generalized eigenvalue decomposition $s=\sum_i\lambda_i\varepsilon_i$ and $n=\sum_i n_i$; the matrix case and the Jordan form; and the Jordan block, the block with two eigenvalues and the unipotent biquaternion examples. -->

<a href="articles_maths/ideals-and-quotients-of-algebras.html">Ideals and Quotients of Algebras</a>
<!-- subalgebras, ideals, quotient algebras, algebra homomorphisms, the isomorphism theorems. -->

<a href="articles_maths/centre-invertibles-zero-divisors-and-division-algebras.html">Centre, Invertibles, Zero Divisors and Division Algebras</a>
<!-- the centre, units, zero divisors, the regular module $A_A$; the finite-dimensional theorem that the non-units are the origin and the zero divisors, proved by rank-nullity on the left multiplication, with the infinite-dimensional counterexample $\operatorname{diag}(1/2,1/3,\dots)$. -->

<a href="articles_maths/idempotents-and-involutions-of-an-algebra.html">Idempotents and Involutions of an Algebra</a>
<!-- the idempotents $e^2=e$ and the involution $\sigma$ acting on them by $e\mapsto e^*$; the Klein four action generated by $\sigma$ and the complement $e\mapsto1-e$, with orbit contained in $\{e,e^*,1-e,1-e^*\}$; the Hermitian idempotents $e^*=e$ and the $*$-stable Peirce corners with the diagonal corners as $*$-subalgebras; the complementary idempotents $e^*=1-e$, equivalently $e+e^*=1$ and $e^*e=ee^*=0$, in bijection with the anti-Hermitian roots $u=2e-1$ of the identity when $2$ is invertible; the left isotropic idempotents $e^*e=0$, the right isotropic $ee^*=0$ and the two-sided condition $e^*e=ee^*=0$, equivalent to $e+e^*$ being idempotent when $2$ is invertible; the matrix algebras with the transpose, the conjugate transpose, the hyperbolic and the symplectic involutions, and the split algebra with the exchange involution; and the characteristic-two collapse of the halving. -->

<a href="articles_maths/complementary-idempotents-and-the-peirce-decomposition.html">Complementary Idempotents and the Peirce Decomposition</a>
<!-- the complement $1-e$, the fixed-point-free involution of the set of idempotents and the order it reverses, and the relative complement $g-e$ in a corner; the Boolean algebra $B(A)$ of central idempotents; the Peirce decomposition $A=\bigoplus_{i,j}A_{ij}$ of a complete orthogonal family with $A_{ij}=e_iAe_j$, the multiplication table $A_{ij}A_{kl}\subseteq\delta_{jk}A_{il}$, the diagonal part $D$, the off-diagonal bimodule $N$ and the diagonal projection, with its multiplicativity criterion; the generalised matrix algebra of the corners; the refinement obtained by splitting a member and the coarsening obtained by a partition, and the primitive families and local corners; the central families, the product decomposition $A\cong\prod_iA_{ii}$ and the atoms of $B(A)$; and the split-complex, upper triangular, matrix, biquaternion and noncentral $M_3$ examples. -->

<a href="articles_maths/peirce-coordinates-and-companion-nilpotents.html">Peirce Coordinates and Companion Nilpotents</a>
<!-- the one-idempotent Peirce decomposition as the joint eigenspaces of multiplication by $e$ on the left and on the right; the companion corner $fAe$ and its square-zero property; the companion nilpotents and the count $s$ as the least number of generators of $fAe$ over $eAe$; the carrier $C(e)=Ae=eAe\oplus fAe$ and its stability under left multiplication; the coordinate vector $(d_0;d_1,\dots,d_s)$ and the Peirce matrix of the left action; the count $s=\lceil N/r\rceil-1$ in $M_N(k)$, hence $s=N-1$ for a primitive idempotent; the frame root $h=2e-1_A$ and the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ grading of the carrier; and the biquaternion, matrix, triangular and dual-number examples. -->

<a href="articles_maths/spinors-as-peirce-coordinates.html">Spinors as Peirce Coordinates</a>
<!-- the spinor as an element of the Peirce carrier $C(e)=Ae=eAe\oplus fAe$ that satisfies the half-root weight condition: $h=2e-1_A$ acts with weights $+\tfrac12$ and $-\tfrac12$, each once; the coordinate vector $(d_0;d_1,\dots,d_s)$ with one coordinate on the idempotent and one on each companion nilpotent; the theorem that in $M_N(k)$ with $e=E_{11}$ the carrier is a spinor space only for $N=2$; the distinction between an irreducible Peirce carrier and a spinor carrier, with $M_3$ as the counterexample; the failure in the upper triangular algebra and the dual numbers; the coordinate count $1+s$ against the spin; the Clifford carrier as the Dirac module with the bivector action supplying the half-spin splitting; and the matrix, quaternion, biquaternion and Clifford examples. -->

<a href="articles_maths/primitive-idempotents-and-minimal-left-ideals.html">Primitive Idempotents and Minimal Left Ideals</a>
<!-- the primitive idempotents as the nonzero idempotents that do not split into two nonzero orthogonal idempotents; the equivalence with the corner $eAe$ having no nontrivial idempotent and with $Ae$ and $eA$ being indecomposable; the minimal left ideals $Ae$ and the division ring criterion, that a minimal one-sided ideal generated by $e$ forces $eAe$ to be a division ring; the failure of the converse without semisimplicity, with the upper triangular algebra $T_2$ separating the two sides and the dual numbers showing that primitivity need not give a division corner; the semisimple equivalence of primitivity, minimal left and right ideals, division corner and simple module; the index of the simple modules in the Wedderburn–Artin decomposition; and the local idempotents of the general finite-dimensional case. -->

<a href="articles_maths/roots-of-the-identity-split-algebras-and-nontrivial-idempotents.html">Roots of the Identity, Split Algebras and Nontrivial Idempotents</a>
<!-- the roots of the identity $u^2=1$, the group of roots in the commutative case and its failure to be a group in the noncommutative case; the division algebras with only $\pm1$ (or only $1$ in characteristic two); the matrix roots as the diagonalisable involutions with eigenvalues $\pm1$; the halving correspondence $e\mapsto2e-1$, $u\mapsto(1+u)/2$ when $2$ is invertible, its spectral reading and its Boolean group form $e\mapsto1-2e$; the split algebras as the algebras with a nontrivial idempotent, equivalently a nontrivial root when $2$ is invertible; the division/split dichotomy for semisimple algebras and the dual numbers as the algebra that is neither; and the characteristic-two separation, with $F\times F$ having idempotents and only the trivial root while the dual numbers have many roots and only the trivial idempotents. -->

<!-- crossed products of algebras by group actions. -->

### Operator Theory

the rule that a condition linear in the operator defines a subspace — the derivations with the Leibniz rule, the $A$-linear operators as the centralizer of the left multiplications, the infinitesimal symmetries — while a condition nonlinear in the operator defines a group — the algebra endomorphisms, their invertible part the automorphisms, and the groups preserving a pairing; the exponential as the passage from the subspace to the group, and the equality of dimensions it forces between $\operatorname{Aut}$ and $\operatorname{Der}$; the ladder inside $M_4(\mathbb{C})$ for $\mathbb{B}$: the all-operators rung of dimension $16$, the left multiplications $L(\mathbb{B})$ and the $A$-linear operators $R(\mathbb{B})$ of dimension $4$ each, the derivations of dimension $3$, the scalars of dimension $1$; the worked case of $\mathbb{C}$ as an $\mathbb{R}$-algebra, where $M_2(\mathbb{R}) = L(\mathbb{C})\oplus\{\text{conjugate-linear operators}\}$ of dimensions $2+2$, $\operatorname{Der}_{\mathbb{R}}(\mathbb{C}) = 0$ and $\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathbb{R}}(\mathbb{C}) = \mathbb{Z}/2$ generated by a reflection; the worked case of the three two-dimensional algebras, where $\dim\operatorname{Der} = n - \dim Z(A)$ and the derivation dimension is the invariant that detects the nilpotent generator of $\mathbb{C}^{\mathrm{dln}}$; the four-dimensional cases $\mathbb{H}$ over $\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{B}$ over $\mathbb{C}$ and over $\mathbb{R}$, with $\dim\operatorname{Der} = 3$, $3$ and $6$; the warning that the algebra isomorphism $\mathbb{B}\cong M_2(\mathbb{C})$ concerns the elements while the operator space is $M_4(\mathbb{C})$; and the note that an automorphism preserves no metric data, so the structure-preserving groups are strictly larger and require the form of Part II, with the rotations and boosts that the derivations generate named there and in Part IV. -->

No form, no norm, no distance: the adjoint involutions, the orthogonal and the symplectic type and the trace and the reduced norm belong to *Hilbert Algebras*, and the graded algebra to *Superalgebras and Graded Structures*. -->
