## Sesqualgebras

### Theory

<a href="articles_maths/sesqualgebras.html">Sesqualgebras</a>
<!-- an $R$-module with a product that is $R$-linear in the first slot and $\varsigma$-semilinear in the second, $(\lambda x)y=\lambda(xy)$ and $x(\lambda y)=\varsigma(\lambda)(xy)$, where $\varsigma$ is an involution of the base ring and is part of the datum; equivalently, with the conjugate module $A^{\varsigma}$ carrying the twisted action $\lambda\cdot x=\varsigma(\lambda)x$, a product that is $R$-bilinear as a map $A\times A^{\varsigma}\to A$; the collapse to an ordinary (bilinear) algebra exactly when $\varsigma=\mathrm{id}$, so the sesquilinear kind contains the bilinear one; the relation to the algebras of *Algebras* and the reason the object is not a special case of them for $\varsigma\neq\mathrm{id}$; the derived operation $x\star y=xy^{*}$ of an algebra with a $\varsigma$-semilinear involution as the standard example, its failure of associativity, its right unit without a left one, and the ternary product it forces; the standing hypotheses of the category. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-sesquilinear-product.html">The Sesquilinear Product</a>
<!-- the two-variable product $\star:A\times A\to A$; linearity in the first slot and $\varsigma$-semilinearity in the second as the two axioms; the rule of the scalars of a combination and the structure constants; the conjugate of a product and the conjugate module; the transposed product $y\star x$, of the opposite parity and bilinear on $A^{\varsigma}\times A$, against $x\star y$; the difference, which vanishes exactly when the involution on $A$ is the identity and the algebra is commutative, and for an algebra of full type only when $\varsigma=\mathrm{id}$; the one-sided products $a\star x$ and $x\star a$, conjugate-linear and linear, the module structures they give when the product is associative, and the $\varsigma$-twisted composition of two one-sided operators. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-symmetric-and-antisymmetric-parts-of-a-sesqualgebra-product.html">The Symmetric and Antisymmetric Parts of a Sesqualgebra Product</a>
<!-- the split of a $\varsigma$-sesquilinear product $\star$ into its symmetric part $f_{+}=\tfrac12(f+E(f))$ and its antisymmetric part $f_{-}=\tfrac12(f-E(f))$ by the plain exchange $E(f)(x,y)=f(y,x)$; the reconstruction $f=f_{+}+f_{-}$, the uniqueness of the pair, the vanishing of the antisymmetric part on the diagonal, and the polarisation of the square, all four independent of the scalar rules and identical to the bilinear case; the obstruction, that the exchanged product is $\varsigma$-semilinear in the first slot and $R$-linear in the second, so its two parts are only $R^{\varsigma}$-bilinear; the two projections $p$ and $q$ of the additive maps, idempotent, orthogonal and summing to the identity, so that a symmetric and an antisymmetric map are independent data, against the failure of the projections to preserve the class; the two halves named as the symmetrised sesquilinear product $x\circ y$ and half the sesquilinear commutator $[x,y]_{\varsigma}$; the Hermitian values of the symmetric part and the anti-Hermitian values of the antisymmetric part in the derived case $x\star y=xy^{*}$, and the Hermitian square on the diagonal; the split of the constants by the transposition of the two lower indices, and the reason the bilinear counts $\binom{n+1}{2}n$ and $\binom{n}{2}n$ do not transcribe; the biquaternion instance $\mathrm{sps}$, $\mathrm{aps}$, $\mathrm{sqs}$, $\mathrm{aqs}$ of the two sesqualgebra products, only $\mathbb{R}$-bilinear; the class-preserving alternative $c(y\star x)$ of *The Conjugate-Symmetric and Antisymmetric-Conjugate-Symmetric Parts of a Sesquilinear Product*; and the collapse when $\varsigma=\mathrm{id}$ and in characteristic two. -->

<a href="articles_maths/conjugate-linear-maps-and-the-conjugate-dual.html">Conjugate-Linear Maps and the Conjugate Dual</a>
<!-- the $\varsigma$-semilinear maps $f(\lambda x)=\varsigma(\lambda)f(x)$ and the reading $\operatorname{Hom}_{\varsigma}(M,N)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{R}(M^{\varsigma},N)$; their additive group and the scalar action that makes them a module; the parity rule, two semilinear maps composing to a linear one, and the $\mathbb{Z}/2$-graded ring of the linear and semilinear endomorphisms; the conjugate dual $M^{\varsigma*}=\operatorname{Hom}_{\varsigma}(M,R)\cong(M^{\varsigma})^{*}$, distinct from the conjugate module; the pairing linear in the first slot and $\varsigma$-semilinear in the second, which the ordinary dual cannot see; the transpose of a semilinear map, exchanging the two duals; the evaluation into the double conjugate dual as the evaluation of the conjugate module; the transport of a sesquilinear structure along a conjugate-linear map, which preserves the parity. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-sesquilinear-associator-and-the-ternary-product.html">The Sesquilinear Associator and the Ternary Product</a>
<!-- the associator $[x,y,z]=(x\star y)\star z-x\star(y\star z)$ of the sesquilinear product; the $\varsigma$-twisting it carries; the associator of the derived product $xy^{*}$, its value $x((zy)^{*}-zy^{*})$, and the criterion for the derived product to be associative; the theorem that an associative or a commutative product forces the trivial involution, so an algebra of full type with a nontrivial involution is neither; the ternary product that the failure forces, and the passage to it. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-conjugate-symmetric-and-anti-conjugate-symmetric-parts-of-a-sesquilinear-product.html">The Conjugate-Symmetric and Anti-Conjugate-Symmetric Parts of a Sesquilinear Product</a>
<!-- the split of a $\varsigma$-sesquilinear product into two halves by an exchange twisted by a conjugation $c$; the obstruction, that the plain transposition reverses the parity and is semilinear in the first slot, so the plain split into the symmetrised product and the difference is only $R^{\varsigma}$-bilinear and splits the scalar form into its $\varsigma$-even and $\varsigma$-odd parts; the adapted exchange $x\star^{c}y=c(y\star x)$ as an involution of the class of products, its uniqueness, the two projections $p$ and $q$, and the independence of the two halves; the scalar theorem, that a Hermitian scalar form lies wholly in the conjugate-symmetric half, and the diagonal of the anti-Hermitian half, which need not vanish in the sesquilinear case although it stays scalar-free; the constants of the exchange, conjugate-symmetry $c^{k}{}_{ij}=\varsigma(c^{k}{}_{ji})$ and the equal rank $n^{3}$ of the two halves over the fixed field; the failure of the polarisation of the square, which sees the plain symmetrisation and not the exchanged one; the standard example, the complex matrices with the entrywise conjugation, and the four general products with their two exchanges. -->

<a href="articles_maths/algebraic-j-star-algebras.html">Algebraic J*-Algebras</a>
<!-- the algebraic, norm-free $J^{*}$-algebra: an $R$-module $V$ with a ternary product that is additive in each slot, $R$-linear in the outer two and $\varsigma$-semilinear in the middle, satisfying the Jordan triple identity, and naming no binary product; the model $\{x,y,z\}=xy^{*}z$ of an associative algebra with a $\varsigma$-semilinear involution; the unital recovery of the binary product and the involution, which make the binary product the shadow of the ternary one; the witness that a $J^{*}$-algebra need not be an algebra; the outer symmetry as the axiom the $J^{*}$-algebra omits and the Jordan triple system of *The Lie–Jordan Decomposition of a Bilinear Product and the Jordan Triple System* requires. -->

<a href="articles_maths/hermitian-and-anti-hermitian-elements.html">Hermitian and Anti-Hermitian Elements</a>
<!-- the fixed and anti-fixed sets of the involution, $H(A)=\{x:x^{*}=x\}$ and $S(A)=\{x:x^{*}=-x\}$; the decomposition $A=H\oplus S$ when $2$ is invertible and its failure in characteristic two; the Hermitian part closed under the symmetrised product, hence a Jordan algebra developed in *The Hermitian Jordan Algebra*; the two halves of the sesquilinear product, with the Lie algebra formed by the anti-Hermitian part developed in *The Unitary Lie Algebra*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/hermitian-squares-and-the-algebraic-positive-cone.html">Hermitian Squares and the Algebraic Positive Cone</a>
<!-- the element $x\star x=xx^{*}$ and its Hermitian property; the sum of Hermitian squares and the positive cone $C(A)$ they generate inside the Hermitian part, the purely algebraic half of positivity; the scalar action of the square semiring and the invariance under congruence; the preorder $y-x\in C(A)$ and the properness that a genuine order requires, which the algebra alone does not supply in general; the matrix model with the conjugate transpose, which is proper, against two non-proper examples. -->

<a href="articles_maths/ideals-and-quotients-of-a-sesqualgebra.html">Ideals and Quotients of a Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- the left, right and two-sided ideals, and the $R$-submodule condition that the scalar rules put on them (automatic in the unital case); closure of the ideals under intersection and sum; the conjugate image $I^{*}$, which carries a left ideal to a right ideal, and the smallest invariant ideal $I+I^{*}$ containing a two-sided ideal $I$, equal to $I$ exactly when $I$ is an invariant ideal; the quotient by a two-sided ideal, the induced sesquilinear structure over the same datum $(R,\varsigma)$, and the exact obstruction to the descent of the algebra involution when $I\neq I^{*}$; the isomorphism theorems adapted to the conjugate-linear slot; the worked quotients $\mathbb{C}$, $\mathbb{H}$ and $\mathbb{B}$. -->

<a href="articles_maths/invertibles-and-the-unitary-elements.html">Invertibles and the Unitary Elements</a>
<!-- the unit of a sesqualgebra and its Hermitian property, and the unit as a right unit of the derived operation only; the unitary elements $U(A)=\{u:uu^{*}=u^{*}u=1\}$ as the units with $u^{*}=u^{-1}$, and the group structure under the product; the stability of $U(A)$ under the involution and the inverse, with the involution restricting to the inversion, an anti-automorphism that is an automorphism exactly when $U(A)$ is abelian; the Hermitian unitary elements $U(A)\cap H(A)=\{u:u^{2}=1, u=u^{*}\}$; the inner $*$-automorphisms $x\mapsto uxu^{*}$ that the unitaries induce, their preservation of $H(A)$ and $S(A)$, and their restriction to the group; the worked cases $M_n(\mathbb{C})$, $\mathbb{H}$, the commutative algebras and $\mathbb{B}$; the Lie algebra of the anti-Hermitian elements is *The Unitary Lie Algebra*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/subalgebras-and-the-involution.html">Subalgebras and the Involution</a>
<!-- the subalgebras of a sesqualgebra, closed under the product and under the scalars, and the $*$-subalgebras, closed under the involution; the restriction of the sesquilinear structure to a subalgebra, which keeps the datum $(R,\varsigma)$ and makes the inclusion a morphism; the conjugate image, a subalgebra, and the $*$-stability $B^{*}=B$; the closure under intersection and the failure of the sum, against the ideals of *Ideals and Quotients of a Sesqualgebra*; the subalgebra generated by a set as the span of the words in it, and the $*$-subalgebra generated by a set as the subalgebra of the set with its conjugate image; the role of the Hermitian generators and of the Hermitian and anti-Hermitian parts; the restriction of the involution to a $*$-subalgebra, with $H(B)=B\cap H(A)$; the largest $*$-subalgebra inside a subalgebra and the smallest containing it; the reading of a $*$-subalgebra through the derived operation $x\star y=xy^{*}$; the matrix and quaternion cases; the counterexample that a subalgebra need not be $*$-stable. -->

<a href="articles_maths/derivations-of-a-sesqualgebra.html">Derivations of a Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- the derivations $D(xy)=D(x)y+xD(y)$, $R$-linear and untwisted on the scalars, and the $*$-derivations with $D(x^{*})=D(x)^{*}$; the Lie algebra $\operatorname{Der}(A)$ under the commutator and its module structure; the inner derivations $D_{a}(x)=ax-xa$ and the centre as the kernel of $a\mapsto D_{a}$; the inner derivations generated by the anti-Hermitian elements and the link to *The Unitary Lie Algebra*; the failure of the Leibniz rule for the derived operation $x\star y=xy^{*}$, and the twisted derivation that it forces. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-centre-and-the-zero-divisors-of-a-sesqualgebra.html">The Centre and the Zero Divisors of a Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- the centre $Z(A)=\{z: zx = xz \text{ for all } x\}$, an $R$-submodule closed under every scalar and carried to itself by the involution; the Hermitian and the anti-Hermitian parts of the centre and their decomposition when $2$ is invertible; the centre as the kernel of the inner maps; the one-sided and the two-sided zero divisors and their annihilators, which are $R$-submodules, the involution exchanging the sides; the derived operation, whose one-sided zero divisors are the same elements with the conjugate partner; the theorem that a central element lies in the annihilator over a twisted base, so a unital or annihilator-free sesqualgebra over $(\mathbb{C},\varsigma)$ has zero centre; the comparison with *Centre, Invertibles, Zero Divisors and Division Algebras* of the bilinear layer. -->

<a href="articles_maths/hermitian-idempotents-and-the-peirce-decomposition.html">Hermitian Idempotents and the Peirce Decomposition</a>
<!-- the idempotents $e^{2}=e$ and the Hermitian ones $e=e^{*}$; the orthogonality of Hermitian idempotents, the idempotence of $e+f$ for orthogonal $e$ and $f$ when $2$ is invertible, and the partial order they carry; the Peirce spaces $eAe$, $eA(1-e)$, $(1-e)Ae$ and $(1-e)A(1-e)$, with the involution exchanging the two mixed spaces when $e$ is Hermitian; the two-sided Peirce decomposition relative to a family of orthogonal Hermitian idempotents, and the multiplication table of the spaces, transposed for the derived product; the corner algebra $eAe$ and the sesquilinear structure that it inherits; the matrix model $M_n(\mathbb{C})$, where a Hermitian idempotent is the matrix with $P^{2}=P=P^{*}$ and the four spaces are the blocks. -->

<a href="articles_maths/simple-sesqualgebras-and-minimal-ideals.html">Simple Sesqualgebras and Minimal Ideals</a>
<!-- the simple sesqualgebra, with no two-sided ideal other than $0$ and $A$ for its own product $\star$, the product being the one fixed by the two scalar rules, against the two-sided ideals of the underlying algebra for the juxtaposition product, which form a different set; the invariant-simple one, with no proper $\ast$-ideal; the theorem that in the derived model with a unit the two notions coincide, since $1\star i=i^{*}$ forces every two-sided $\star$-ideal to be stable, so the two-sided $\star$-ideals are exactly the $\ast$-ideals, the trivial direction simple $\Rightarrow$ invariant-simple being immediate from the definition; the minimal left, right and two-sided ideals, generated by the primitive idempotents of *Ideals and Peirce Decomposition of the General Plain Algebra* and *List of Rings by Their Idempotents*, with the $\ast$-stability that the Hermitian condition of *Hermitian Idempotents and the Peirce Decomposition* adds and the primitivity that makes the ideal minimal; the centre of a simple algebra and the zero divisors that it may still have; the worked cases $M_n(\mathbb{C})$ with the conjugate transpose and $\mathbb{H}$ with the quaternion conjugation. -->

<a href="articles_maths/tensor-products-of-sesqualgebras.html">Tensor Products of Sesqualgebras</a>
<!-- the sesquilinear tensor product $A\otimes_R B$ with the involution $x\otimes y\mapsto x^{*}\otimes y^{*}$; the $\varsigma$-twisting carried through the tensor product; the commuting images of $A$ and $B$; the universal property for the pairs of maps with commuting images that are compatible with the $\varsigma$-twist, the coproduct of the noncommutative case being the free product instead, as in *Tensor Products of Algebras*; the examples $\mathbb{C}\otimes_{\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{H}$ and $\mathbb{H}\otimes_{\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{H}$. -->

<a href="articles_maths/direct-products-of-sesqualgebras.html">Direct Products of Sesqualgebras</a>
<!-- the direct product $A\times B$ with the componentwise product and involution, a sesqualgebra over the same datum $(R,\varsigma)$; the component idempotents and the central Hermitian idempotents that cut a direct product; the criterion that a decomposition $A=I\oplus J$ into two-sided ideals comes exactly from a pair of orthogonal central idempotents, the central splitting being that of *Unital Algebras*, §*Idempotents and the Peirce Decomposition*, with the Hermitian condition of *Hermitian Idempotents and the Peirce Decomposition* the extra datum that makes the two ideals $\ast$-ideals, so that the involution descends to the factors; the failure of the direct product to be a coproduct, the coproduct of noncommutative algebras being the free product and the tensor product being universal only for pairs with commuting images, as in *Tensor Products of Algebras*; the worked case $R\times R$ and the exchange involution, for which the idempotent $(1,0)$ is central but not Hermitian. -->

<a href="articles_maths/real-forms-of-a-sesqualgebra.html">Real Forms of a Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- the fixed ring $R^{\varsigma}$ of the base involution and the fixed subalgebra $A^{\alpha}$ of an algebra involution $\alpha$; the descent of the sesquilinear structure to the fixed ring; the real forms of a complex sesqualgebra; the two involutions and the four subobjects they cut; the worked cases $\mathbb{C}$, $\mathbb{H}$ and $\mathbb{B}=\mathbb{C}\otimes_{\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{H}$, and the caution that $\mathbb{H}$ carries no $\mathbb{C}$-sesquilinear structure, because the centre of $\mathbb{H}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ and the quaternion conjugation is $\mathbb{C}$-antilinear, not $\mathbb{C}$-linear. -->

### Operator Theory

<a href="articles_maths/the-left-and-right-multiplication-operators-of-a-sesqualgebra.html">The Left and Right Multiplication Operators of a Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- the operators $L_a(x)=a\star x$ and $R_a(x)=x\star a$ of the sesquilinear product; $L_a$ $\varsigma$-semilinear in $\operatorname{End}_{R^{\varsigma}}(A)$ while $R_a$ is $R$-linear in $\operatorname{End}_{R}(A)$; the parameter laws $L_{\lambda a}=\lambda L_a$ and $R_{\lambda a}=\varsigma(\lambda)R_a$; the composition in the associative case and its failure in the standard example, where the residue is the two-sided multiplication $T_{a,b^{*}}$; the two regular maps, one linear and multiplicative and one conjugate-linear and anti-multiplicative, and the failure of a single faithful linear representation to carry the whole product; the comparison with *Left and Right Multiplication* and *Associative Algebras*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-sesquilinear-two-sided-operator.html">The Sesquilinear Two-Sided Operator</a>
<!-- the two-sided operator $x\mapsto ax^{*}b$ as the triple product with the middle slot variable; its conjugate-linear middle slot and its reading $\mathcal{T}_{a,b}=T_{a,b}\circ{}^{*}$; the relation to the ordinary two-sided multiplication $T_{p,q}(x)=pxq$ and to the signed two-sided operator of *The Signed Adjoint Two-Sided Operator on a Bimodule over an Algebra*; the composition table and the monoid the two families form, the composite of two such operators being linear; the invertibility $\mathcal{T}_{a,b}^{-1}=\mathcal{T}_{(b^{-1})^{*},(a^{-1})^{*}}$ with the central units as the kernel of the parametrisation; the reflections $\mathcal{T}_{u,u}$ of the unitary elements and the inner involution $\mathcal{T}_{u,u^{*}}=\sigma_u$. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-sesquilinear-adjoint-operator.html">The Sesquilinear Adjoint Operator</a>
<!-- the conjugate-transpose operator of a matrix or of an endomorphism, defined by the involution of the algebra; the anti-automorphism $T\mapsto T^{\dagger}$ of the endomorphism algebra and the involution it defines; the two adjoints that a conjugate-linear operator requires, and the relation between them. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-sesquilinear-commutator.html">The Sesquilinear Commutator</a>
<!-- the bracket $[x,y]_{\varsigma}=x\star y-y\star x$ of the sesquilinear product, the antisymmetric half of the split of the product, treated for its own sake; its antisymmetry for free and its linearity over the fixed ring $R^{\varsigma}$ alone, the correction term $(\lambda-\varsigma(\lambda))(y\star x)$ being the whole difference from the bilinear case; the failure of the Jacobi identity, with the witness $E_{11},E_{22},E_{12}$ in $M_2(\mathbb{C})$ whose Jacobi sum is $E_{21}-E_{12}$, and the observation that the failure needs the noncommutativity and not the twist, since it vanishes for the sesquilinear field; the is not a Lie bracket, its values in the anti-Hermitian part; the Lie algebra that the sesqualgebra carries instead, on the anti-Hermitian half under the commutator, being *Lie Algebras of Sesqualgebras*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-sesquilinear-symmetrised-product.html">The Sesquilinear Symmetrised Product</a>
<!-- the symmetrised product $x\circ y=\tfrac12(x\star y+y\star x)$ of a sesquilinear product, the companion of the difference bracket of *The Sesquilinear Commutator* and the symmetric half of the same split; its $R^{\varsigma}$-bilinearity, each slot taking one linear and one conjugate-linear contribution so that the two parities collapse to the fixed ring, against the $R$-bilinearity that returns only in the degenerate case; its polarisation of the square $x\star x=xx^{*}$; the Hermitian value of $x\circ y$ for arbitrary arguments in the derived case $x\star y=xy^{*}$; its agreement with the plain symmetrisation $\tfrac12(xy+yx)$ on $H(A)$ and the Jordan identity there, through the associativity of the envelope; the failure of the Jordan identity off $H(A)$, with the witness $E_{12},E_{22}$ in $M_2(\mathbb{C})$; the obstruction read as the non-associativity of the derived product against the associativity of the algebra product; the worked cases $M_n(\mathbb{C})$, the sesquilinear field, $\mathbb{H}$ and $\mathbb{B}$; the Jordan structure it generates on $H(A)$ is *Jordan Algebras of Sesqualgebras*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-ternary-product-as-an-operator.html">The Ternary Product as an Operator</a>
<!-- the operator $\Theta_{x,y}(z)=\{x,y,z\}=xy^{*}z$ attached to a pair; its linearity in $z$ and conjugate-linearity in $y$; the Lie triple system the operators form under the commutator; the quadratic representation of a Jordan algebra as the commutative case; the operators it generates in the worked algebras $M_n(\mathbb{C})$ and $\mathbb{B}$. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-graded-sesquilinear-action.html">The Graded Sesquilinear Action</a>
<!-- the action of a $\mathbb{Z}/2$-graded sesqualgebra on a graded module; the degree count that forces the involution of a graded sesqualgebra to be even, so that no Koszul sign enters the scalar rules; the two classes of order-two anti-maps, the graded involution and the superinvolution, and the condition $A^{1}A^{1}=0$ under which they coincide; the ternary product of a superinvolution and its failure of the Jordan triple identity on two odd elements; the graded $\varsigma$-compatibility, holding on the even part and obstructed on the odd part; the derived action $a\star m=a\cdot\theta(m)$ and the conjugation $\theta$; the matrix superalgebra as the nondegenerate case and $k[x]/(x^{2})$ with an odd $x$ as the degenerate one; the relation to *The Graded Action on a Module over an Algebra* and the one new datum. -->

### * Theory

<a href="articles_maths/the-involutions-of-a-sesqualgebra.html">The Involutions of a Sesqualgebra</a>
<!-- the involutions of a sesqualgebra, the $\varsigma$-semilinear anti-automorphisms $\alpha$ with $\alpha^{2}=\mathrm{id}$, and the set they form, closed under composition and inversion; the composite $\alpha\beta$ of two involutions and the criterion for it to be an involution again; the family $x\mapsto ux^{*}u$, an involution for every unitary $u$ and the composite of the datum involution with the inner $\ast$-automorphism $x\mapsto uxu^{*}$ of *Invertibles and the Unitary Elements*; the fixed subspaces $H(A,\alpha)$ and the Galois-type correspondence between involutions and the subspaces they fix; the partial order on the set of the involutions; the datum involution $*$ as one element of the set, and the distinction from the involutive algebras of *Algebras*, where $\varsigma=\mathrm{id}$ cuts the same construction down. -->

<a href="articles_maths/lie-algebras-of-sesqualgebras.html">Lie Algebras of Sesqualgebras</a>
<!-- the Lie structures a sesqualgebra carries, the sesquilinear counterpart of the Lie half of *The Lie–Jordan Decomposition of a Bilinear Product and the Jordan Triple System*; the antisymmetrisation $[x,y]_{\varsigma}=x\star y-y\star x$ is antisymmetric and $R^{\varsigma}$-bilinear but its Jacobi identity fails, with the witness $E_{11},E_{22},E_{12}$ in $M_2(\mathbb{C})$ whose Jacobi sum is $E_{21}-E_{12}$, and it is a Lie bracket exactly when the product being antisymmetrised is associative, which for an algebra of full type forces $\varsigma=\mathrm{id}$; the Lie structure that is available is the commutator $xy-yx$ of the associative product, making $A$ a $\mathbb{Z}/2$-graded Lie algebra with even part $S(A)$, odd part $H(A)$ and the involution reversing the bracket, $[x,y]^{*}=-[x^{*},y^{*}]$; $S(A)$ as a Lie algebra over $R^{\varsigma}$, the unitary Lie algebra, acting by the inner $*$-derivations with $[\mathrm{ad}_{s},\mathrm{ad}_{t}]=\mathrm{ad}_{[s,t]}$ and kernel the central anti-Hermitian elements, and the Hermitian half acting by the anti-Hermitian derivations instead; the ternary companion, the Lie triple system $[[x,y],z]$ and its three identities; the degeneration to the bilinear case, with the comparison table; the worked cases $M_n(\mathbb{C})$, $\mathbb{C}$, $\mathbb{H}$ and $\mathbb{B}$; the narrow articles feeding it are *The Sesquilinear Commutator*, *The Unitary Lie Algebra*, *Derivations of a Sesqualgebra* and *The Ternary Product as an Operator*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-unitary-lie-algebra.html">The Unitary Lie Algebra</a>
<!-- the anti-Hermitian elements $x^{*}=-x$ and the Lie algebra they form under the commutator, the concrete model of the umbrella *Lie Algebras of Sesqualgebras*; the closedness of that part under the bracket, which the Hermitian part does not have; the failure of the anti-Hermitian part to be closed under the product, where $(xy)^{*}=yx$, so $xy$ is anti-Hermitian exactly when $x$ and $y$ anticommute and Hermitian exactly when they commute, and neither in general, while $xy+yx$ is always Hermitian; the action of the unitary group on the anti-Hermitian part by the inner automorphisms; the worked cases $M_n(\mathbb{C})$, $\mathbb{H}$ and $\mathbb{B}$; the unitary group itself and its elements are *Invertibles and the Unitary Elements*, and the exponential that carries the anti-Hermitian part into it, with its convergence and its failure of surjectivity, belongs to Part II and is *The Exponential Map on a Banach Sesqualgebra*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/jordan-algebras-of-sesqualgebras.html">Jordan Algebras of Sesqualgebras</a>
<!-- the Jordan structures a sesqualgebra carries, the sesquilinear counterpart of the Jordan half of *The Lie–Jordan Decomposition of a Bilinear Product and the Jordan Triple System*; the symmetrisation $x\circ y=\tfrac12(x\star y+y\star x)$ is commutative and $R^{\varsigma}$-bilinear with image in $H(A)$, and it is a Jordan product exactly on $H(A)$, where the derived operation coincides with the associative product, the Jordan identity failing off $H(A)$ with the witness $E_{12},E_{22}$ in $M_2(\mathbb{C})$, the criterion that would repair it being associativity, which for an algebra of full type forces $\varsigma=\mathrm{id}$; $J(A)=(H(A),\circ)$ as a Jordan algebra over $R^{\varsigma}$, functorial in the involutive algebra, special with envelope $A$, and its quadratic representation $U_x(y)=xyx$ against the $\mathrm{ad}$ of the Lie twin; the ternary structure $\{x,y,z\}=xy^{*}z$ of an algebraic $J^{*}$-algebra on the whole module and the recovery of the binary product at the unit, with the exceptional algebras outside the class; the degeneration to the bilinear case, with the comparison table; the worked cases $M_n(\mathbb{C})$, $\mathbb{C}$, $\mathbb{H}$ and $\mathbb{B}$; the narrow articles feeding it are *The Sesquilinear Symmetrised Product*, *The Hermitian Jordan Algebra*, *Algebraic J\*-Algebras* and *The Self-Adjoint Part of an Algebra*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-hermitian-jordan-algebra.html">The Hermitian Jordan Algebra</a>
<!-- the Hermitian elements $H(A)$ under the symmetrised product $x\circ y=\tfrac12(xy+yx)$ as a Jordan algebra over the fixed ring $R^{\varsigma}$, the sesquilinear counterpart of *The Self-Adjoint Part of an Algebra*, the invariant being the scalars rather than the axioms, and the concrete model of the umbrella *Jordan Algebras of Sesqualgebras*; the axioms and the envelope, $J$ special with the associative algebra $A$ as envelope inside $A^{+}$; the powers $x^{\circ n}=x^{n}$ and the subalgebra generated by one Hermitian element; the trace form $\tau(x\circ y)=\tau(xy)$ and its reality on the Hermitian matrices; the Hermitian idempotents, the Jordan orthogonality $e\circ f=0$ equivalent to $ef=fe=0$, and the degree, $n$ for $M_n(\mathbb{C})$; the Peirce decomposition as the Hermitian part of the associative Peirce decomposition of $e$, with the eigenvalues $1,\tfrac12,0$ on the Hermitian parts of $eAe$, of $eAf\oplus fAe$ and of $fAf$; the quadratic representation $U_x(y)=xyx$; the worked cases $M_n(\mathbb{C})$ with the conjugate transpose, $\mathbb{C}$ with conjugation, $\mathbb{H}$, where the layer degenerates to the bilinear one, and $\mathbb{B}$, of degree two. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-eigenvalue-decomposition-of-a-hermitian-element.html">The Eigenvalue Decomposition of a Hermitian Element</a>
<!-- the Hermitian spectral resolution $a=\sum_i\lambda_i e_i$ in a Hermitian Jordan algebra; the eigenspaces $J_{ij}=H(e_iAe_j\oplus e_jAe_i)$; the diagonal and mixed Peirce components; the eigenvalue decomposition of a self-adjoint element and its comparison with the associative and the Jordan cases; the existence theorem and the uniqueness of the resolution. -->

<a href="articles_maths/anti-automorphisms-twisted-by-the-base-involution.html">Anti-Automorphisms Twisted by the Base Involution</a>
<!-- the anti-automorphisms of $A$ twisted by $\varsigma$, $f(\lambda x)=\varsigma(\lambda)f(x)$ and $f(xy)=f(y)f(x)$, of any order; the linear and the conjugate-linear kinds for a central simple algebra and the constraint the $\varsigma$-twist puts on the order; the order-two case, that is the involutions of the algebra, is *The Involutions of a Sesqualgebra*; the relation to *Opposite Algebras and Anti-Isomorphisms* and to *Involutions of a Central Simple Algebra* with the extra datum the $\varsigma$-twist adds. -->

<a href="articles_maths/involutions-of-a-sesquilinear-tensor-product.html">Involutions of a Sesquilinear Tensor Product</a>
<!-- the tensor involution $x\otimes y\mapsto x^{*}\otimes y^{*}$; its composition with the flip and the two involutions of the tensor square; the $\varsigma$-compatibility of the tensor product; the analogies with *Involutions of the Tensor Algebra* and the single new datum; the worked cases $\mathbb{C}\otimes_{\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{H}$ and $\mathbb{B}\otimes_{\mathbb{C}}\mathbb{B}$. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-hermitian-pair-in-the-biquaternion-algebra-with-hermitian-adjoint.html">The Hermitian Pair in the Biquaternion Algebra with Hermitian Adjoint</a>
<!-- the biquaternion algebra $\mathbb{B}=M_2(\mathbb{C})$ as the one algebra in which the whole Hermitian theory is written in coordinates: the operator $\mathrm{Hp}_x$, the forms, positivity, the unitary slice, the Lorentz transformation it produces and complete positivity. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-unitary-slice-and-the-compact-real-form-with-hermitian-adjoint.html">The Unitary Slice and the Compact Real Form with Hermitian Adjoint</a>
<!-- the unitary slice $U=\{x:x^{\dagger}x=1\}$ on which the dagger is the inverse and the Hermitian pair is the inner conjugation; the shape of the slice recording the signature; the compact real form, the identity involution with $U=\mathrm{Pin}$, and the definite case over $\mathbb{C}$ and $\mathbb{H}$. -->

<a href="articles_maths/positivity-and-the-hermitian-cone-of-a-hermitian-algebra-with-hermitian-adjoint.html">Positivity and the Hermitian Cone of a Hermitian Algebra with Hermitian Adjoint</a>
<!-- the positive involution of the algebra; the self-adjoint and anti-Hermitian elements and the decomposition of the algebra; the cone of the elements $x^{\dagger}x$ and the criterion that the dagger is positive; the polar decomposition and the Cartan involution of the group of invertibles. -->

<a href="articles_maths/self-adjoint-and-anti-self-adjoint-operators-with-hermitian-adjoint.html">Self-Adjoint and Anti-Self-Adjoint Operators with Hermitian Adjoint</a>
<!-- the $\ast$-algebra $\mathrm{End}_A(S)$ of operators on a Hermitian Clifford module; the adjoint, the splitting into the self-adjoint and anti-self-adjoint parts, the graded commutator rules; the anti-Hermitian part as the Lie algebra of the unitary group and the self-adjoint part as the Jordan algebra; the Hilbert–Schmidt orthogonality of the two halves; the blade sign and the regular representation. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-spectra-of-self-adjoint-operators-with-hermitian-adjoint.html">The Spectra of Self-Adjoint Operators with Hermitian Adjoint</a>
<!-- the finite-dimensional spectral theorem: real spectrum, orthogonal eigenspaces, the spectral decomposition $T=\sum_i\lambda_iP_i$ and the functional calculus; the min-max principle, the positivity criterion; the purely imaginary spectrum of the anti-self-adjoint operators; normality and unitary invariance; the two-sided spectrum and the Sylvester solvability condition; the failure of the theorem in indefinite signature. -->

<a href="articles_maths/unitary-equivalence-and-congruence-of-operators-with-hermitian-adjoint.html">Unitary Equivalence and Congruence of Operators with Hermitian Adjoint</a>
<!-- the conjugation $T\mapsto UTU^{-1}$ with its invariant the spectrum and the congruence $T\mapsto A^{\dagger}TA$ with its invariant the inertia; the two relations agreeing on the slice and the equivalence being strictly finer off it; the preservation of positivity and the cone; the Takagi invariant in the complex-symmetric case. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-hermitian-sylvester-equation-with-hermitian-adjoint.html">The Hermitian Sylvester Equation with Hermitian Adjoint</a>
<!-- the Hermitian Sylvester equation and its operator form $L_a+R_b$; the solvability exactly when no eigenvalue sum vanishes, the spectral form of the classical solvability condition; the alternating and symmetric cases and the congruence law which belongs to the unitary Witt group. -->

<a href="articles_maths/mixed-inner-conjugation-and-hermitian-adjoint.html">Mixed Inner Conjugation and Hermitian Adjoint</a>
<!-- the four two-sided operators formed by the independent choices of the left twist, identity or signed, and the right factor, inverse or dagger; the interaction of the involutive and the orthogonal structure; the two defects between the members and the signed Hermitian pair $\alpha(x)yx^{\dagger}$. -->

<a href="articles_maths/completely-positive-maps-of-a-hermitian-algebra-with-hermitian-adjoint.html">Completely Positive Maps of a Hermitian Algebra with Hermitian Adjoint</a>
<!-- the Clifford algebra with a positive involution as a finite-dimensional $C^{*}$-algebra; Choi's theorem, the Kraus form of a completely positive map and the innerness of the automorphisms of a full matrix algebra, read in the Clifford language; the biquaternion instance $d=2$, with Kraus length at most four, the diagonal projection and the null two-sided operator. -->

### * Theory, One-Sided Operator with Hermitian Adjoint

<a href="articles_maths/one-sided-operators-on-a-hermitian-algebra-with-hermitian-adjoint.html">One-Sided Operators on a Hermitian Algebra with Hermitian Adjoint</a>
<!-- the left and right multiplications and their graded and anti-involution variants; the composition laws, the commutation and the two-sided operator as their product; the adjoint $L_a^{*}=L_{a^{\dagger}}$ and $R_b^{*}=R_{b^{\dagger}}$ with respect to $\mathrm{Sc}(x^{\dagger}y)$, and the self-adjoint, anti-Hermitian and unitary criteria; the double centraliser, the images as ideals and the annihilators as kernels. -->

<a href="articles_maths/hermitian-modules-over-a-hermitian-algebra-with-hermitian-adjoint.html">Hermitian Modules over a Hermitian Algebra with Hermitian Adjoint</a>
<!-- the Clifford module carrying a form for which the action is self-adjoint, $(x\cdot s,t)=(s,x^{\dagger}\cdot t)$; the two-point function, the positivity and the self-adjointness axiom; the reducibility and the module-level form. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-adjoint-of-the-one-sided-action-with-hermitian-adjoint.html">The Adjoint of the One-Sided Action with Hermitian Adjoint</a>
<!-- the adjoint of the action $\rho(x)^{*}=\rho(x^{\dagger})$; the resulting $\ast$-structure on the operator algebra, the rule for the adjoint of a composite and the reversal of the factors; the vectors acting anti-self-adjointly; the elementary algebraic reason the Dirac operator is formally self-adjoint. -->

<a href="articles_maths/bilinear-operators-on-a-hermitian-module-with-hermitian-adjoint.html">Bilinear Operators on a Hermitian Module with Hermitian Adjoint</a>
<!-- operators built from two spinors; the completeness of the Clifford action and the Fierz identity; the bilinear covariants $(s,\Gamma^{A}t)$ spanning the bilinear forms and reconstructing every endomorphism; the adjoint of a bilinear operator. -->

<a href="articles_maths/invariant-operators-and-intertwiners-with-hermitian-adjoint.html">Invariant Operators and Intertwiners with Hermitian Adjoint</a>
<!-- the commutant of the Clifford action and its identification with the intertwiners; Schur's lemma on an irreducible module and the right multiplications on the regular module; the adjoint of an intertwiner and the self-adjoint invariant operators. -->

<a href="articles_maths/dirac-operators-with-hermitian-adjoint.html">Dirac Operators with Hermitian Adjoint</a>
<!-- the Dirac operator as a Hermitian operator: the product of the anti-self-adjoint Clifford action and a formally anti-self-adjoint first-order operator; its self-adjointness with respect to the module form, the positivity of the Hermitian square, the reality of the spectrum, the orthogonality of the eigenspinors and the splitting of the module by the kernel. -->

<a href="articles_maths/spinor-adjoints-and-the-dirac-adjoint-with-hermitian-adjoint.html">Spinor Adjoints and the Dirac Adjoint with Hermitian Adjoint</a>
<!-- the spinor adjoint $s\mapsto(s,\cdot)$ as the Clifford-equivariant identification of the module with its dual, and the Dirac adjoint $\psi^{\dagger}\gamma_0$ with the invariant $\psi^{\dagger}\gamma_0\psi$; the repair of the isotropy of the scalar form and the interaction with the self-adjointness of the Dirac operator. -->

### * Theory, Two-Sided Operator with Signed Hermitian Adjoint

<a href="articles_maths/two-sided-operators-on-a-hermitian-algebra-with-signed-hermitian-adjoint.html">Two-Sided Operators on a Hermitian Algebra with Signed Hermitian Adjoint</a>
<!-- the two-sided operator $\Theta^{\alpha}_x(y)=\alpha(x)yx^{\dagger}$, the signed Hermitian member whose left factor carries the grade involution and whose right factor carries the dagger; the parity sign $\Theta^{\alpha}_x=\varepsilon_x\Theta_x$ with $\varepsilon_x=(-1)^k$, so that it is the Hermitian pair on the even part and its negative on the odd part; bijectivity, the composition law and the parameter rule $\Theta^{\alpha}_{ax}=a\sigma(a)\Theta^{\alpha}_x$; the action on the Clifford group, $\Theta^{\alpha}_x=\varepsilon_x\sigma(N(x))\,x(\ )\sigma(x)^{-1}$, an isometry exactly when $\sigma(N(x))^2=1$ and otherwise a similarity of ratio $\sigma(N(x))^2$; the kernel of the invertible elements with central dagger, $F^{\times}\cap U$ on the slice against the kernel $F^{\times}$ of the signed inner conjugation; the reflection $\Theta^{\alpha}_u=-q(u)\rho_u$, which is $\rho_u$ exactly on the slice; the slice reduction $\Theta^{\alpha}_x=\mathrm{Ad}^{\alpha}_x$ for $x^{\dagger}=x^{-1}$; the biquaternion dictionary $\tilde{Q}x\tilde{Q}^{\dagger}$ and the Lorentz group. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-grading-of-a-hermitian-algebra-with-signed-hermitian-adjoint.html">The Grading of a Hermitian Algebra with Signed Hermitian Adjoint</a>
<!-- why the signed Hermitian member is not a second structure: the sign is the parity, $\Theta^{\alpha}_x=\varepsilon_x\Theta_x$; the dagger is even, so $\Theta^{\alpha}_x\Theta^{\alpha}_z=\varepsilon_x\varepsilon_z\Theta^{\alpha}_{xz}$ and two odd steps compose to the ordinary Hermitian pair, $\Theta^{\alpha}_x\Theta^{\alpha}_z=\Theta_{xz}$ for $x,z$ odd; the odd part of the unitary slice as a coset and $U/U^0\cong\mathbb{Z}/2$; the algebra as a free rank-two module over its even part; the even-ness of the Hermitian form, so that the two parity sectors are orthogonal; the determinants $\det\mathrm{Ad}^{\alpha}_x=\varepsilon_x$ against $\det\mathrm{Ad}_x=(\varepsilon_x)^{n+1}$, and the comparison by the scalar $\sigma(N(x))$ off the unitary slice. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-pin-and-spin-groups-with-signed-hermitian-adjoint.html">The Pin and Spin Groups with Signed Hermitian Adjoint</a>
<!-- the Hermitian formulation of the covering groups: the Clifford group $\Gamma$, the Hermitian Clifford group $\Gamma_{\dagger}=\{x\in\Gamma:\sigma(N(x))^2=1\}$ where the Hermitian pair is an isometry, and the unitary slice $U$ where the dagger is the inverse; $\Gamma_{\dagger}=\mathrm{Pin}$ and $U\cap\Gamma=\{N=1\}$ for the trivial involution, the two coinciding for a definite form in the corpus's convention; the reflections as the odd elements, $\Theta^{\alpha}_u=\rho_u$ for $q(u)=-1$; the double cover $\{\pm1\}\to\mathrm{Pin}\to O$ and $\{\pm1\}\to\mathrm{Spin}\to SO$, Cartan–Dieudonné, the low-dimensional groups, and the indefinite and degenerate cases. -->

<a href="articles_maths/versors-rotors-and-the-two-sided-action-with-signed-hermitian-adjoint.html">Versors, Rotors and the Two-Sided Action with Signed Hermitian Adjoint</a>
<!-- versors and rotors under the signed Hermitian pair: the dagger of a versor is a versor of the same length and parity, so the two-sided operator has versors on both sides; the form of the operator on the Clifford group, $\Theta^{\alpha}_x=\varepsilon_x\sigma(N(x))\,x(\ )\sigma(x)^{-1}$; the rotor as an even $\sigma$-real versor of norm with $\sigma(N)=1$, for which the Hermitian pair is the plain rotation $RvR^{-1}$; the two actions and the half angle against the full angle; the adjointness axiom $(x\cdot s,t)=(s,x^{\dagger}\cdot t)$ on a Hermitian Clifford module, with the dagger entering the module side as the adjoint and never as a rotation; the similarity of ratio $\sigma(N(x))^2$ off the slice. -->

<a href="articles_maths/reflection-groups-and-the-pin-lift-with-signed-hermitian-adjoint.html">Reflection Groups and the Pin Lift with Signed Hermitian Adjoint</a>
<!-- the reflection of a root as a signed Hermitian pair: $\Theta^{\alpha}_u=-q(u)\rho_u$, so the reflection is realised exactly on the unitary slice, by the slice-normalised root $q(u_\alpha)=-1$; the Hermitian Clifford lift $\Gamma_\Phi=\langle u_\alpha\rangle\subseteq U\cap\Gamma_{\dagger}$; its finiteness, the twofold cover $\Gamma_\Phi\to W_\Phi$, the orders $|\Gamma_\Phi|=2|W_\Phi|$ and $|\Gamma_\Phi^0|=|W_\Phi|$, and the even part covering the rotation subgroup; the cases $A_1$, $A_2$ and $A_3$, the Hurwitz units and the $24$-cell. -->

### * Theory, One-Sided Operator with Signed Hermitian Adjoint

<a href="articles_maths/one-sided-operators-on-a-hermitian-algebra-with-signed-hermitian-adjoint.html">One-Sided Operators on a Hermitian Algebra with Signed Hermitian Adjoint</a>
<!-- the signed left multiplication $\Lambda^{\alpha}_x(y)=\alpha(x)y$ and the dagger right multiplication $R_{x^{\dagger}}(y)=yx^{\dagger}$ as the two one-sided factors of the signed Hermitian pair; $\Lambda^{\alpha}_x=\varepsilon_xL_x=\alpha L_x\alpha$, the value $\alpha(x)$ at the unit and the parity; the composition laws, the commutation, and the adjoints $(\Lambda^{\alpha}_x)^{*}=\Lambda^{\alpha}_{x^{\dagger}}$ and $(R_{x^{\dagger}})^{*}=R_x$ for the form $\mathrm{Sc}(x^{\dagger}y)$; the split of linearity, the left factor linear and the right factor $\sigma$-semilinear in the parameter, giving $\Theta^{\alpha}_{ax}=a\sigma(a)\Theta^{\alpha}_x$; the reflection $\rho_u$ against $-q(u)\rho_u$; the kernels and the images, which see the involution but not the sign. -->

<a href="articles_maths/pin-representations-and-hermitian-modules-with-signed-hermitian-adjoint.html">Pin Representations and Hermitian Modules with Signed Hermitian Adjoint</a>
<!-- the pin representation on a Hermitian Clifford module: the restriction of the algebra action to the whole Pin group, one-sided by construction, with the adjoint $\rho(x)^{*}=\rho(x^{\dagger})$ and unitarity on the unitary slice; the intertwining identities $\rho(x)\rho(v)\rho(x)^{*}=\rho(\Theta_x(v))$ and $\rho(\Theta^{\alpha}_x(v))=\varepsilon_x\rho(x)\rho(v)\rho(x)^{*}$; the module form of the reflection $\rho(u)\rho(v)\rho(u)^{*}=\rho(-q(u)\rho_u(v))$, which is $\rho_u$ on the slice, with $\rho(u)^2=-\mathrm{id}$ there; the chirality, the Hermitian-orthogonal chiral halves, the kernel, the real modules and the definite case. -->

<a href="articles_maths/peirce-carriers-and-signed-hermitian-adjoint.html">Peirce Carriers and Signed Hermitian Adjoint</a>
<!-- a spinor as an element of a minimal left ideal $I=\mathrm{Cl}(V,q)\pi$ with the whole Pin group acting by left multiplication; the parity splitting $I=I^0\oplus I^1$, the even elements preserving and the odd ones interchanging the summands, with the two halves Hermitian-orthogonal; the signed Hermitian pair realised on the ideal as $\Theta^{\alpha}_x(v)\psi=\rho(\alpha(x))\rho(v)\rho(x)^{*}\psi$, the adjoint of the left multiplication playing the role of the right factor, with the defect $\rho(xx^{\dagger})$ off the slice; the reflection $\rho_u(v)\psi$ on the slice against $-q(u)\rho_u(v)\psi$; the central volume element exchanging the two summands, the unsigned Hermitian pair acting on it by $-\mathrm{id}$ and the signed one by $+\mathrm{id}$. -->

the fixed and the anti-Hermitian sets are closed, being equalizers, so a dense fixed set forces the trivial involution, and closedness is the whole gain, the fixed set of a continuous anti-automorphism being closed without being a subring; the averaging map is continuous when $2$ is invertible and makes the fixed set a retract, so that the additive group splits topologically into the fixed and the anti-Hermitian parts; the $I$-adic criterion $\sigma(I)^m\subseteq I$ gives continuity whenever the involution preserves the ideal defining the topology, and the involution then extends to a continuous involution of the $I$-adic completion, whose fixed set is the closure of the fixed set when $2$ is invertible, as in $\mathbb{Z}_p[i]=\mathbb{Z}_p[X]/(X^2+1)$ with $X\mapsto-X$ and $\mathbb{R}[[x]]$ with $f(x)\mapsto f(-x)$; a $\sigma$-stable closed ideal gives a Hausdorff quotient carrying the involution, whose fixed set can be strictly larger than the image of the fixed set, as $\mathbb{Z}[i]/(2)$ shows, while the completion introduces no such new fixed element; on a topological field the fixed field of a continuous involution is a closed subfield of index two and a topological field in the subspace topology with open group of invertibles, on an ordered field the identity is the only monotone involution and every nontrivial one is non-monotone, and $\mathbb{C}$ with the usual topology and the conjugation is the model continuous case. **An additional structure on the topological ring, not a rung of any chain; it stands immediately after *Topological Rings and Fields*, whose $I$-adic topologies, linear topologies, neighbourhoods of zero and completions it uses, and before *Absolute Values, Valuations and Completions*, which owns the $p$-adic fields and the valuation topologies that are named here and not used.** -->

<a href="articles_maths/involutive-topological-algebras.html">Involutive Topological Algebras</a>

continuity at the origin, the homeomorphism, the uniform continuity, determination on a dense subset, and the descent to the Hausdorff quotient by the closure of zero; the topological opposite algebra and the involution as the certificate of a topological isomorphism $A\to A^{\mathrm{opp}}$ of order two; the criterion for a linear topology, that for every $n$ there is $m$ with $\sigma(I_m)\subseteq I_n$, the cofinal $\sigma$-stable system $J_n=I_n\cap\sigma(I_n)$, the $I$-adic criterion $\sigma(I)^m\subseteq I$ and the automatic continuity of a linear involution with $\sigma(I)\subseteq I$; the continuous linear involutions $f(x)\mapsto f(b-x)$ of $\mathbb{R}[x]$ with the $(x)$-adic topology, continuous exactly for $b=0$ because the constant term of $(b-x)^m$ is $b^m$, with fixed algebra $\mathbb{R}[x-x^2]$ dense and not closed, and the continuous antilinear $\theta(f)(x)=\overline{f(-x)}$ of $\mathbb{C}[x]$ extending to $\mathbb{C}[[x]]$; the extension of a continuous involution to the completion $\widehat A=\varprojlim_n A/I_n$, with symmetric part the closure of the image of $A^+$ when $2$ is invertible; the symmetric and the anti-Hermitian parts as closed equalizers and closed topological modules over $R^\varsigma$, the symmetric part a closed topological Jordan algebra under the symmetrised product and the anti-Hermitian part a closed topological Lie algebra under the commutator, a dense symmetric part forcing the trivial involution; the topological direct sum $A=A^+\oplus A^-$ by the continuous averaging maps when $2$ is invertible, the projection multiplicative only for an involutive automorphism; the quotient by a closed stable ideal with the induced involution, its symmetric part the image of $A^+$ over a field of characteristic not two and strictly larger in characteristic two, as the swap on $\mathbb{F}_2[x,y]$ modulo $(x+y)$ shows with image $\mathbb{F}_2[x^2]$; the closure of a stable set and the kernel of a continuous morphism; the product algebra with the involution $\sigma\times\tau$, and the exchange involution on $A\times A^{\mathrm{opp}}$ whose symmetric part is the diagonal, a subalgebra exactly when $A$ is commutative; the $\mathrm{C}^*$-case, where the involution of a $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra is isometric and determines the norm, $\lVert a\rVert^2=\lVert a^*a\rVert=r(a^*a)$, so that a *-algebra carries at most one $\mathrm{C}^*$-norm and a unital *-homomorphism of unital $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebras is contractive; <a href="articles_maths/the-continuous-quadratic-form-and-the-polar-form.html">The Continuous Quadratic Form and the Polar Form</a>
<!-- the quadratic form of the layer as a continuous map and the continuity of its polar form; the uniform norm on the forms and the operator norm on the polar forms, equal by polarisation; the completeness of the space of continuous forms; the radical closed and its comparison with the closure of zero; the openness of the non-degenerate forms and the local constancy of the signature over $\mathbb{R}^n$; the continuous isometries and the closedness of the isometry group. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-continuous-symplectic-form-and-the-poisson-bracket.html">The Continuous Symplectic Form and the Poisson Bracket</a>
<!-- the continuous alternating form and its contraction; the topological splitting of the bilinear forms into the symmetric and the alternating parts; the rank lower semicontinuous and the symplectic forms open, with two components over the real numbers from the sign of the Pfaffian; the symplectic group closed and contained in the special linear group; the canonical form on a module and its dual; the continuous Poisson bracket, the Hamiltonian derivations and the Poisson centre. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-continuous-grade-decomposition-and-the-filtration.html">The Continuous Grade Decomposition and the Filtration</a>
<!-- the grade projections as continuous maps and the grade decomposition as a topological direct sum; the descending chain of elements of degree at least $k$ and the filtration topology it generates; the quotients as the bounded-degree parts; the separatedness and the discreteness in finite dimension; the associated graded algebra as the exterior algebra and the symbol map; the completion of the filtration. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-continuous-volume-element-duality-and-the-hodge-star.html">The Continuous Volume Element, Duality and the Hodge Star</a>
<!-- the volume element as a continuous function of the orthogonal frame, the set of volume elements open with two components over the real numbers; the complement map a homeomorphism from each grade to its complement; the duality pairing of a grade with its complement, continuous and non-degenerate; the Hodge star a continuous homeomorphism and the two topological cases of its square, the self-dual splitting and the complex structure; the cross product; the failure of the construction in infinite dimension. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-completion-of-a-clifford-algebra.html">The Completion of a Clifford Algebra</a>
<!-- the two completions of the algebra, the normed one and the one of the filtration; the comparison of the topologies; the completed algebra as a complete topological algebra with the same associated graded; the convergence of the exponential and the power series; the canonical anticommutation relations read on the completion; the Hilbert-space case and the continuous inclusion of the algebra. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-topological-orthogonal-group-and-the-spin-group.html">The Topological Orthogonal Group and the Spin Group</a>
<!-- the isometry group of a continuous form as a closed subgroup of the invertible operators, locally compact in finite dimension; the identity component and the determinant; the two-fold covering of the special orthogonal group by the spin group as a covering of topological groups; the connectedness and the local structure; the low-dimensional isomorphisms read topologically; the spinor norm; the symplectic and the Hermitian counterparts named. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-topological-witt-group-and-the-brauer-wall-group.html">The Topological Witt Group and the Brauer–Wall Group</a>
<!-- the isometry classes of non-degenerate continuous forms modulo the hyperbolic ones as a topological group of components; the Witt and the Grothendieck–Witt groups read topologically; the topological Brauer–Wall group and the periodicity; the classification of the real Clifford algebras at the layer of the topology; the relation to topological K-theory. -->

<a href="articles_maths/infinite-dimensional-clifford-algebras-and-car-with-inner-conjugation.html">Infinite-Dimensional Clifford Algebras and CAR with Inner Conjugation</a>
<!-- the Clifford algebra of a Hilbert space; the canonical anticommutation relations; the CAR algebra as a C*-algebra and the uniqueness of its representation; its relation to the finite-dimensional Clifford algebras and to the exterior algebra; the infinite-dimensional Pin and Spin groups. -->

<a href="articles_maths/operators-on-a-topological-clifford-algebra.html">Operators on a Topological Clifford Algebra</a>
<!-- the ambient space of the continuous operators on the algebra; the operator norm and the submultiplicative bound; the two one-sided multiplications as the elementary operators, with their continuity and their norms; the two-sided operators and the two-sided operator as the geometric operators, continuous in the parameter; the closure of the operator algebra and the passage to the completion. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-bounded-left-and-right-multiplication-on-a-clifford-algebra.html">The Bounded Left and Right Multiplication on a Clifford Algebra</a>
<!-- the left and the right multiplication as bounded operators for the Euclidean form; the explicit norms and the sharp constant $2^{n/2}$; the adjoint of each with respect to the form; the subalgebra of $\mathrm{End}$ they generate and its closure; the contrast with the general topological case, where the bound is a hypothesis and not a theorem. -->

### * Theory

<a href="articles_maths/hilbert-algebras.html">Hilbert Algebras</a>
<!-- the structure: an associative algebra with an involution $\dagger$ and a positive definite sesquilinear form $\langle x,y\rangle=\tau(x^\dagger y)$ satisfying the adjoint axiom $\langle xy,z\rangle=\langle y,x^\dagger z\rangle$, equivalently $\langle x^\dagger y,z\rangle=\langle y,xz\rangle$; the left regular representation as a $\ast$-representation; the positive cone $\{\sum_i x_i^\dagger x_i\}$ and the positivity of the involution; the intrinsic anti-involutions reversion $x^r$ and the conjugate $\alpha(x^r)$, their signs $(-1)^{k(k-1)/2}$ and $(-1)^{k(k+1)/2}$ on a $k$-blade, the involution of the base and the induced dagger $x^\dagger=\sigma(\alpha(x^r))$ with the conjugate reversion $x^{r,\sigma}$, the Klein four-group on the biquaternions; the trace form, its Hermitian Gram matrix $H^\dagger=\sigma(H)^T=H$, its radical and non-degeneracy, and its positivity, $\operatorname{Trd}(\tilde Q\tilde Q^\dagger)=2\sum_\mu|Q_\mu|^2$; the polar form of the reduced norm. The operators built from the dagger are in the group `- * Operator Theory`, and the completion, the GNS construction and the modular theory are later articles of this group. -->

<a href="articles_maths/indefinite-inner-product-spaces.html">Indefinite Inner Product Spaces</a>
<!-- the general theory of spaces with a non-degenerate indefinite Hermitian form; the Gram matrix, the inertia, the signature and its classification over $\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{C}$, and the radical; the finite-dimensional case; the fundamental decomposition; the existence of a fundamental symmetry. -->

<a href="articles_maths/krein-spaces.html">Krein Spaces</a>
<!-- the complete case: an indefinite Hermitian form admitting a fundamental decomposition into a positive and a negative part, both complete; the signature $(p,q)$ with $p$ or $q$ possibly infinite; the topological structure induced by the decomposition; the distinction from a Hilbert space. -->

<a href="articles_maths/pontryagin-spaces.html">Pontryagin Spaces</a>
<!-- the case of finite rank of negativity $\Pi_\kappa$; the finite-dimensional spectral theorem for self-adjoint operators on a Pontryagin space; the finite-dimensional $\mathbb{C}^{p,q}$ and its linear algebra; the role of $\kappa$. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-fundamental-symmetry.html">The Fundamental Symmetry</a>
<!-- the operator $J$ with $J^2=\mathrm{id}$ and $J^\dagger=J$ that defines the positive-definite inner product from the indefinite form; the fundamental decomposition as the eigenspaces of $J$; the non-uniqueness of $J$; $J$ as the bridge between the indefinite and the positive cases. -->

<a href="articles_maths/krein-algebras.html">Krein Algebras</a>
<!-- the indefinite analogue of a Hilbert algebra: a $\ast$-algebra with an indefinite sesquilinear form compatible with the product; the $J$-positivity condition; the relation to Hilbert algebras through $J$; the $J$-positive cone and the $J$-order structure. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-indefinite-gns-construction.html">The Indefinite GNS Construction</a>
<!-- the Krein-space representation from an indefinite state or weight; the difference from the standard GNS construction; the role of the fundamental symmetry in selecting a positive-definite inner product. -->

<a href="articles_maths/krein-von-neumann-algebras.html">Krein–von Neumann Algebras</a>
<!-- the operator algebras on Krein spaces; the $J$-representations of $\ast$-algebras; the $J$-commutant and the $J$-bicommutant theorem; the modular theory in the indefinite setting. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-indefinite-modular-operator.html">The Indefinite Modular Operator</a>
<!-- the analogue of the Tomita–Takesaki modular operator for Krein spaces; the construction from a $J$-cyclic and $J$-separating vector; the $J$-modular operator and the $J$-modular conjugation. -->

<a href="articles_maths/krein-tomita-takesaki-theory.html">Krein–Tomita–Takesaki Theory</a>
<!-- the indefinite Tomita–Takesaki theorem; the modular group and the modular flow for a Krein–von Neumann algebra; the $J$-modular automorphism group; the $J$-KMS condition. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-completion-of-a-hilbert-algebra.html">The Completion of a Hilbert Algebra</a>
<!-- the completion of a Hilbert algebra; the Hilbert space it defines and the involution it carries. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-left-and-the-right-regular-representation.html">The Left and the Right Regular Representation</a>
<!-- the left and the right regular representations of a Hilbert algebra; their commutation and the von Neumann algebra they generate. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-gns-construction.html">The GNS Construction</a>
<!-- the GNS construction from a state; the cyclic representation and the irreducibility criterion. -->

<a href="articles_maths/self-adjoint-elements-and-the-positive-cone.html">Self-Adjoint Elements and the Positive Cone</a>
<!-- the self-adjoint elements and the positive cone; the order and the square roots. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-modular-operator-and-tomita-takesaki-theory.html">The Modular Operator and Tomita-Takesaki Theory</a>
<!-- the modular operator of a von Neumann algebra; the Tomita–Takesaki theorem and the modular conjugation. -->

## Topology on Sesqualgebras with a degree-2 form

### Theory

<a href="articles_maths/topological-sesqualgebras-with-a-form.html">Topological Sesqualgebras with a Form</a>
<!-- the entry for the layer: a topological sesqualgebra with a continuous Hermitian form $h$; the compatibility of the form with the product, $h(xy,z)=h(y,x^{*}z)$; the collapse to the bilinear degree-2 form category exactly when $\varsigma=\mathrm{id}$; the relation to *Topology on Sesqualgebras* and the boundary with *Topology on Algebras with a degree-2 form*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/positivity-and-the-positive-cone-of-a-hermitian-form.html">Positivity and the Positive Cone of a Hermitian Form</a>
<!-- positive definite and positive semi-definite Hermitian forms, the diagonal in the ordered fixed ring and its scaling by squares, and the cone of the positive semi-definite forms in the module of the Hermitian forms; the tolerance $x\succeq y\iff h(x-y,x-y)\geq0$, reflexive, symmetric and translation invariant, transitive exactly for the semi-definite forms and hence not an order, the genuine order being the cone of the Hermitian squares read by the positive functionals; the positive set $P(h)$ and the null set, with $P(h)\cap(-P(h))=N(h)$ and $P(h)=A$ exactly in the semi-definite case; the null set as the radical in the semi-definite case, by Cauchy–Schwarz, and the definite quotient by the radical; the positivity of $h_{\varphi}(x,y)=\varphi(y^{*}x)$ as the positivity of $\varphi$ on the algebraic cone of the Hermitian squares of *Hermitian Squares and the Algebraic Positive Cone*, so that a definite form is a certificate of properness; the collapse at $\varsigma=\mathrm{id}$ to the positivity of a quadratic form, the companion of the bilinear layer being *Positivity and the Hermitian Cone of a Hermitian Algebra with Hermitian Adjoint*; and the absence of any order on a base of characteristic two. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-norm-defined-by-a-form.html">The Norm Defined by a Form</a>
<!-- the norm $\|x\|^{2}=h(x,x)$ on a sesqualgebra with a positive definite form; the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality; the triangle inequality and the passage to a normed and then a Banach sesqualgebra; the $C^*$-condition and its relation to the involution. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-fundamental-symmetry-of-the-form.html">The Fundamental Symmetry of the Form</a>
<!-- the symmetry $J$ that splits an indefinite form into its positive and its negative parts; the Gram operator; the equivalence of the indefinite and the definite pairings; the passage to the Krein space of the bilinear degree-2 form category, named and deferred. -->

### Operator Theory

<a href="articles_maths/the-adjoint-under-a-hermitian-form.html">The Adjoint under a Hermitian Form</a>
<!-- the adjoint of a bounded operator with respect to the Hermitian form $h$; the anti-automorphism $T\mapsto T^{\dagger}$; the two-slot adjoint of a conjugate-linear operator; the self-adjoint and the normal operators; the relation to *Hermitian Adjoints on a Hermitian Algebra* of the bilinear layer. -->

<a href="articles_maths/unitary-and-isometric-operators-of-the-form.html">Unitary and Isometric Operators of the Form</a>
<!-- the operators preserving the form, $h(Tx,Ty)=h(x,y)$; the unitary group and the isometry group; the indefinite case and the Krein isometries; the relation to the unitary group of the elements. -->

<a href="articles_maths/self-adjoint-and-anti-self-adjoint-operators-of-the-form.html">Self-Adjoint and Anti-Self-Adjoint Operators of the Form</a>
<!-- the splitting of the operator algebra into the self-adjoint and the anti-self-adjoint part of the adjoint, $T=\tfrac12(T+T^{\dagger})+\tfrac12(T-T^{\dagger})$; the sign rule and the three product relations; the anti-Hermitian part as the Lie algebra of the unitary group and the self-adjoint part as a special Jordan algebra; the exponential and the Cayley transform; the regular representation and the indefinite transport $T^{\dagger}=JT^{*}J$. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-spectra-of-self-adjoint-operators-of-the-form.html">The Spectra of Self-Adjoint Operators of the Form</a>
<!-- the finite-dimensional spectral theorem in the definite case: the $h$-orthonormal diagonalisation, the real spectrum, the spectral decomposition and the functional calculus; the min-max principle and the Rayleigh quotient; the norm identity $\|T\|=\rho(T)$; the positivity criterion $T$ positive $\iff$ the spectrum in $[0,\infty)$ and the positive square root; the imaginary spectrum of the anti-self-adjoint operators and the unit circle of the unitary ones; the invariance under the unitary group; the failure in the indefinite case with the hyperbolic witness. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-polar-decomposition-of-an-operator-of-the-form.html">The Polar Decomposition of an Operator of the Form</a>
<!-- the modulus $|T|=(T^{\dagger}T)^{1/2}$ and the phase $U$ with $U(|T|x)=Tx$; the decomposition $T=U|T|$ with the partial-isometry projections, the unitary case and the uniqueness; the obstruction in the indefinite case, the hyperbolic operator whose modulus would be $\mathrm{i}$ times the identity. -->

<a href="articles_maths/unitary-equivalence-and-congruence-of-operators-of-the-form.html">Unitary Equivalence and Congruence of Operators of the Form</a>
<!-- the conjugation $T\mapsto UTU^{\dagger}$ with its invariant the spectrum and the congruence $h\mapsto h\circ(C\times C)$ with its invariant the inertia; the Gram matrix transformation $H\mapsto C^{T}H\varsigma(C)$ and Sylvester's law; the unitary group as the stabiliser of the form; the transport $T\mapsto C^{-1}TC$ of the operator theory, and the failure of compatibility under a general congruence, preserved only by a $*$-automorphism. -->

<a href="articles_maths/completely-positive-maps-of-a-sesqualgebra-with-a-form.html">Completely Positive Maps of a Sesqualgebra with a Form</a>
<!-- the positive maps of the cone of the Hermitian squares and the amplification by the form on $M_n(A)$; the Hermitian pair $\mathrm{Hp}_a(x)=axa^{*}$ as the completely positive map of Kraus rank one; Choi's theorem and the Kraus form in the matrix model; the transpose as the positive and not completely positive witness; the unital and the unitary channels as the inner automorphisms. -->

### * Theory

<a href="articles_maths/the-completion-of-a-sesqualgebra-with-a-form.html">The Completion of a Sesqualgebra with a Form</a>
<!-- the completion with respect to the norm of the form; the extension of the product, of the involution and of the form; the universal property; the recovery of the form and the collapse at $\varsigma=\mathrm{id}$. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-euclidean-form-the-norm-and-the-completion-on-a-clifford-algebra.html">The Euclidean Form, the Norm and the Completion on a Clifford Algebra</a>

<a href="articles_maths/the-modular-structure-of-a-hermitian-algebra.html">The Modular Structure of a Hermitian Algebra</a>
<!-- the involution on the completion, bounded exactly for a tracial form and closable otherwise; the Tomita operator $S(x\xi)=x^{\dagger}\xi$ and the polar decomposition $\bar S=J\Delta^{1/2}$; the modular conjugation and the exchange $\jmath\bar L_x\jmath=\bar R_{x^{\dagger}}$; the modular operator of the two-sided operator and the modular flow; the standard form $(\mathcal{M},H,\jmath,P)$ and the self-dual cone; the commutant, the modular transpose $T\mapsto\jmath T^{*}\jmath$ and the polar decomposition of intertwiners; the completion-level companion of the Part I Hermitian-adjoint articles. -->

## Analysis on Linear Spaces

### Theory

<a href="articles_maths/banach-and-hilbert-spaces.html">Banach and Hilbert Spaces</a>
<!-- normed and Banach spaces; bounded linear operators and the operator norm; the dual space and the Hahn–Banach, open mapping and closed graph theorems; inner product spaces, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and the parallelogram law; Hilbert spaces, orthonormal bases and the Riesz representation theorem; orthogonal projection and the geometry of a Hilbert space; the adjoint; the spectral theorem for bounded self-adjoint and normal operators; compact operators, their spectral theory and the Fredholm alternative; $L^2$ and $\ell^2$ as the standard examples; the finite-dimensional case, where every operator is a matrix and the theory reduces to the spectral theorem for normal matrices. -->

<a href="articles_maths/interpolation-theory.html">Interpolation Theory</a>
<!-- interpolation of Banach and Sobolev spaces; the real and complex methods; the relation to the function spaces of this part. -->

<a href="articles_maths/differential-calculus-on-normed-spaces.html">Differential Calculus on Normed Spaces</a>
<!-- the Fréchet derivative, its uniqueness and the chain rule; continuity of the derivative and the class $C^1$; partial derivatives and the total derivative; the inverse and implicit function theorems; higher derivatives, the second derivative as a bilinear form, and Taylor's theorem with remainder; the role of completeness and of the contraction mapping principle; the finite-dimensional case, where the derivative is the Jacobian matrix. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-gradient-as-the-riesz-representative.html">The Gradient as the Riesz Representative of the Differential</a>
<!-- the differential as a covector and the absence of a canonical representative, with the objection that every finite-dimensional space carries an inner product and the answer that existence is cheap and uniqueness is not; the Riesz map of an inner product, an isomorphism in finite dimension and conjugate-linear for a Hermitian form; the gradient as the unique element with $DF(a)[h]=\langle h,\operatorname{grad}F(a)\rangle$, nondegeneracy the hypothesis of the definition and definiteness the hypothesis of the steepest-ascent theorem; the coordinate formula with the Gram matrix and its inverse, the orthonormal case, and the worked witness $1$, $1+i$ on $\mathbb{C}$ where the naive sum of partials fails; the realified Gram matrix of a complex basis as the block matrix with $A=\operatorname{Re}G$ and $B=\operatorname{Im}G$; the complex plane, $\operatorname{grad}F=F_q+iF_{q'}$, the two Wirtinger normalisations and the factor two as a normalisation and not a geometric fact; complex-valued functions as a pair of gradients, and the holomorphic case $\operatorname{grad}u=\overline{f'}$, $\operatorname{grad}v=i\overline{f'}$; the quaternion and biquaternion cases, $\operatorname{grad}\langle Q\rangle_{*}=2Q$ against the gradient $2\bar Q$ of $\operatorname{Re}(Q^{2})$, with the side carried by the conjugate; the change $v_2=G_2^{-1}G_1v_1$ under a change of form, and what the form does not touch, the differential, the critical set, the level sets and their tangent spaces; steepest ascent in the definite case and the unbounded derivative on the null cone in the indefinite one; and the derivation as an object of another kind, the vanishing of every derivation of $\mathbb{C}$ against the inner derivations of $\mathbb{H}$. -->

<a href="articles_maths/distributions-and-fundamental-solutions.html">Distributions and Fundamental Solutions</a>
<!-- test functions and the space of distributions as the topological dual; differentiation of distributions and the derivative of a locally integrable function; the delta distribution, its derivatives and the Heaviside function; multiplication and the limits of the theory; the Fourier transform of a tempered distribution; convolution and the convolution algebra; fundamental solutions of linear differential operators and the parametrix. -->

<a href="articles_maths/distributions-on-surfaces-layers-and-jump-conditions.html">Distributions on Surfaces, Layers, and Jump Conditions</a>
<!-- the surface delta and the coarea formula; the jump formula and the layer decomposition of the gradient, the divergence and the rotor; single and double layers and the structure of a distribution supported on a surface; the surface gradient, divergence and rotor; the jump conditions of first- and second-order equations and the characteristic of the principal symbol; the Rankine–Hugoniot condition of a conservation law; traces and the restriction problem. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-schwartz-kernel-theorem.html">The Schwartz Kernel Theorem</a>
<!-- the Schwartz kernel theorem and its consequences; the relation to the topological tensor products of Part II and to the distributions of this part. -->

<a href="articles_maths/fredholm-theory.html">Fredholm Theory</a>
<!-- Fredholm operators and their index; the Fredholm alternative; compact perturbations; the relation to the index theory of Part IV and to the spectral theory of operators. -->

<a href="articles_maths/unbounded-operators-and-spectral-measures.html">Unbounded Operators and Spectral Measures</a>
<!-- an unbounded linear operator, its domain, the graph and the closed graph theorem; closable operators, the adjoint of an unbounded operator, and the distinction between symmetric and self-adjoint, which no longer coincide; the deficiency indices and the self-adjoint extensions of a symmetric operator; the spectrum of a closed operator and the resolvent as a bounded operator away from it; the spectral theorem for a self-adjoint operator in its projection-valued form, with the spectral measure $E$ and the representation $A=\int\lambda\,dE(\lambda)$; the Borel functional calculus and the spectrum as the support of the spectral measure; the multiplication operator on $L^2$ of a measure space as the model case, and the diagonalisation of a self-adjoint operator as the statement that it is unitarily equivalent to one. -->

<a href="articles_maths/pseudodifferential-operators.html">Pseudodifferential Operators</a>
<!-- pseudodifferential operators and their symbols; elliptic operators. -->

<a href="articles_maths/microlocal-analysis.html">Microlocal Analysis</a>
<!-- the wavefront set and microlocal regularity; the propagation of singularities; the relation to the pseudodifferential operators of this part. -->

<a href="articles_maths/semiclassical-analysis.html">Semiclassical Analysis</a>
<!-- the semiclassical limit and its properties; the mathematical content only. -->

<a href="articles_maths/nonlinear-functional-analysis.html">Nonlinear Functional Analysis</a>
<!-- nonlinear operators and their properties; monotone and accretive operators. -->

<a href="articles_maths/fixed-point-theory-and-degree-theory.html">Fixed Point Theory and Degree Theory</a>
<!-- the fixed point theorems of analysis; the contraction mapping principle; the Schauder and Kakutani theorems; the relation to the nonlinear functional analysis of this part; the Leray–Schauder degree and its use in existence theorems. -->

<a href="articles_maths/besov-and-triebel-lizorkin-spaces.html">Besov and Triebel–Lizorkin Spaces</a>
<!-- Besov spaces and their properties; the relation to the interpolation theory and to the Sobolev spaces of this part; the Triebel–Lizorkin spaces and their relation to the Besov spaces. -->
