## Analysis on Algebras

### Theory

<a href="articles_maths/hypercomplex-analysis.html">Hypercomplex Analysis</a>
<!-- what becomes of analyticity when the ground algebra is no longer a field: the obstructions, non-commutativity, zero divisors, a one-sided module structure and the dimension; the ambiguity of the derivative defined by a difference quotient, and why it is over-determined; the two notions that survive, holomorphy inside a commutative subalgebra and regularity with respect to a first-order operator; the Cauchy–Riemann operator $D=\sum_i e_i\partial_i$ as the generalisation of $\bar\partial$, its square as the Laplacian, and the class of regular functions it defines; the general form of the Cauchy integral formula and the hypotheses that must replace the classical ones, with the failure of Morera, Liouville and the maximum principle in each setting; the parallel structure of the theory for $\mathbb{C}$, the split complex numbers, the dual numbers, $\mathbb{H}$ and the split biquaternions, with forward references to the per-system articles; the role of the Clifford algebra in the construction of the operator. -->

<a href="articles_maths/regularity-and-the-cauchy-riemann-operator.html">Regularity and the Cauchy–Riemann Operator</a>
<!-- the first-order operator $D$ assembled from a frame of the algebra, and the class of functions it annihilates; the classical Cauchy–Riemann equations in $\mathbb{C}$, their generalisation and the several distinct meanings the equation $Df=0$ takes once multiplication is one-sided; monogenic and regular functions; the relation between regularity and holomorphy inside a commutative subalgebra; the square of the operator as the Laplacian, and the harmonicity of regular functions; the Cauchy integral formula and the hypotheses that replace the classical ones; the mean value property, the maximum principle and Liouville's theorem, with the systems in which each fails; the Fischer and Stokes decompositions; forward references to the per-system analysis articles. -->

<a href="articles_maths/clifford-analysis.html">Clifford Analysis</a>
<!-- the analysis of functions with values in a Clifford algebra; the Dirac operator and monogenic functions; the Cauchy integral formula; the relation to the Clifford algebras of Part II; the monogenic, polymonogenic and shifted theories; the Hermitean refinement, with the four Hermitean Dirac operators, the simultaneous null solutions and the circulant matrix of Cauchy kernels; the measure-theoretic boundary theory, with the Federer normal, the Cauchy and Hilbert transforms on Ahlfors–David regular surfaces, the Plemelj calculus and the complementary projections, the removable singularities, and the $d$-summable fractal boundaries on which the transform is rebuilt from the Teodorescu transform and a Whitney extension, with the approximate dimension in the solvability condition. -->

<a href="articles_maths/geometric-calculus-and-the-vector-derivative.html">Geometric Calculus and the Vector Derivative</a>
<!-- the vector derivative $\partial=\sum_ie^i\partial_i$ and the reciprocal basis; $\partial x=n$; the split $\partial F=\partial\cdot F+\partial\wedge F$ into divergence and curl; the Leibniz rule with the bracket convention; the fundamental theorem $\int_M\underline{\partial}F\,dV=\int_{\partial M}dS\,F$ and its grades, Gauss, Stokes and the fundamental theorem of calculus; $\partial^2=\Delta$ and the monogenic functions; the Green's function and the Cauchy integral formula; the exterior derivative and the codifferential; the Dirac-type and Maxwell-type equations. -->

<a href="articles_maths/clifford-modules-and-the-twisted-cauchy-riemann-operator.html">Clifford Modules and the Twisted Cauchy–Riemann Operator</a>
<!-- Clifford modules and their structure; the spinor module; the twisted Cauchy–Riemann operator acting on a Clifford module; the resulting elliptic complex and the computation of its index. -->

<a href="articles_maths/fueter-theory.html">Fueter Theory</a>
<!-- Fueter's theory of regular functions of a quaternionic variable; the Cauchy–Fueter integral formula; the relation to the hypercomplex analysis of this part. -->

<a href="articles_maths/hypercomplex-integration.html">Hypercomplex Integration</a>
<!-- integration of functions with values in a hypercomplex algebra; the contour integral and the obstruction to a Cauchy theorem when the algebra is not a field; the splitting into idempotent or characteristic coordinates, which reduces the integral to two ordinary integrals; the residue theory that survives and the systems where it degenerates; path independence and the role of the zero divisors; the relation to the measure-theoretic integral, which supplies the underlying integration of an algebra-valued function and is treated in the general theory; the Cauchy integral formula as the boundary form of the theory; forward references to the per-system integration articles for $\mathbb{C}$, the split complex numbers, the dual numbers, $\mathbb{H}$, $\mathbb{B}$ and the split biquaternions. -->

<a href="articles_maths/riemann-boundary-value-problems-and-singular-integral-equations.html">Riemann Boundary Value Problems and Singular Integral Equations</a>
<!-- the boundary value problem with a jump that the Cauchy transform and the Plemelj formulas lead to; sectionally regular functions and the classes by order at infinity; the Riemann problem $f^+=f^-B+h$ and the Plemelj projectors $P_\pm=\tfrac12(I\pm S)$; the canonical factor for a constant coefficient, the reduction to the trivial jump and the explicit solution in the classes $\mathcal{R}_{-1}$ and $\mathcal{R}_0$; the order of the factors when the algebra is not commutative; the singular integral equation of Cauchy type, its factorisation through the projectors and its split equivalence with the Riemann problem, with the closed-form solution and the degenerate coefficients; the index of a variable coefficient, the canonical function and the counting of solutions in the classical complex case; the complex, quaternion and Clifford instances, with the conventions of the Clifford source; the corpus's boundary-value criterion as the case $B=1$. -->

<a href="articles_maths/harmonic-analysis-over-hypercomplex-systems.html">Harmonic Analysis over Hypercomplex Systems</a>
<!-- the transform theory a hypercomplex algebra supports, and why it depends on the underlying additive group rather than on the multiplication; the Fourier transform on $\mathbb{C}$, on the split complex numbers, on the dual numbers and on the quaternion groups; the discrete and continuous cases; convolution and the algebra it defines; the Plancherel and Paley–Wiener theorems; the Laplace, Hilbert, Mellin and Radon transforms; the Calderón–Zygmund theory of singular integrals; the obstruction in the non-commutative and zero-divisor cases, and the reduction to the factor algebra; forward references to the per-system harmonic analysis articles. -->

<a href="articles_maths/dirac-differential-operators.html">Dirac Differential Operators</a>
<!-- the differential theory of Dirac operators: the analysis of the family of Dirac-type operators; self-adjointness, the domain and the closure, the spectrum and the compact resolvent, and the index of the chiral part; the relation to the algebraic and topological operator of Part II and to the spin geometry and index theory of Part IV. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-dirac-kahler-equation.html">The Dirac–Kähler Equation</a>
<!-- the multivector Dirac equation $(d-\delta+m)\Phi=0$; the exterior derivative, the codifferential $\delta=-\star d\star$ and the Laplace–de Rham operator, $(d-\delta)^2=\square$; the Clifford product $dx_\mu\vee dx_\nu=dx_\mu\wedge dx_\nu+\delta_{\mu\nu}$; the decomposition into four Dirac equations through the basis change $Z$ and the internal $\mathrm{SO}(2,4)$ symmetry; minimal coupling; the simplicial discretization and the equivalence to staggered fermions; the harmonic-form zero modes; the curved-spacetime failure of the fourfold split; the relation to the biquaternion algebra, the even part $\mathrm{Cl}_{1,3}^+=\mathbb{B}$ contained in the multivector and the oddness of $d-\delta$ that prevents a restriction to it. -->

## Geometry on Groups

### Theory

<a href="articles_maths/the-three-two-dimensional-algebras-and-the-three-kinds-of-rotation.html">The Three Two-Dimensional Algebras and the Three Kinds of Rotation</a>
<!-- the same vector space $\mathbb{R}^2$ carries three distinct algebra structures, and the relation of the generator to $1$ selects the geometry: $\mathbb{C}$ with $i^2=-1$ gives the elliptic rotation and the compact group $U(1)\cong SO(2)$; the split complex numbers with $j^2=+1$ give the hyperbolic rotation and $SO(1,1)$; the dual numbers with $\epsilon^2=0$ give the parabolic rotation and the shear. For each: the units, the norm preserved, the parametrisation, the orbit of a point, and the fixed lines. Why a rotation implemented by multiplication needs exactly two dimensions and a multiplicative norm, why dimension three forces a non-commutative algebra, and how the sign of the square of the generator selects a definite, an indefinite or a degenerate geometry. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-rotation-group-and-orientation.html">The Rotation Group and Orientation</a>
<!-- the rotation group $SO(V,Q)$ as the kernel of the determinant on $O(V,Q)$; orientation of a space and of a form; rotations versus reflections and the Cartan–Dieudonné parity; the definite case and the notion of angle; the plane case $SO(2)$ as the unit circle; the rotation group of $\mathbb{R}^3$ and its axis; the normal form as a sequence of planar rotation blocks, quoted up to conjugation in $O(V,Q)$ with the finer classes in $SO(V,Q)$ named. -->

## Fractal Geometry

### Theory

<a href="articles_maths/fractal-geometry.html">Fractal Geometry</a>
<!-- fractals and their properties; the Hausdorff dimension; the relation to the metric geometry of this part and to the dynamical systems of Part III. -->

<a href="articles_maths/rectifiability-and-the-geometry-of-fractal-curves.html">Rectifiability and the Geometry of Fractal Curves</a>
<!-- rectifiable sets and curves; the arc length against the Hausdorff measure, and the dimension of a rectifiable set is one; the non-rectifiable curves, the variation and the finite-length case; the Koch curve and the snowflake as the computed examples; the relation to *Geometric Measure Theory* of this part. -->

<a href="articles_maths/fractal-trees-and-dendrites.html">Fractal Trees and Dendrites</a>
<!-- tree-like fractals and dendrites; the local cut points, the branching points and the ends; the self-similar trees and their tilings; the dendrite of the Fabrykowski–Gupta group and the tree-like Julia sets as the examples, with their limit spaces cited to *Limit Spaces and Schreier Graphs*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-geometry-of-the-julia-sets.html">The Geometry of the Julia Sets</a>
<!-- the Julia set and the Fatou set; the local connectivity and the case of a connected filled Julia set, with the external rays and the landing theorem; the dimension and the measure of the Julia sets, and the hyperbolic and parabolic cases; the Mandelbrot set as parameter space, its connectedness and the open local-connectivity question; the dynamics itself is Part III's and the ergodic theory of the Julia set too; the relation to the limit space of the iterated monodromy group of Part II. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-dimension-of-the-boundary-of-a-hyperbolic-group.html">The Dimension of the Boundary of a Hyperbolic Group</a>
<!-- the Gromov boundary of a hyperbolic group as a fractal, with the visual metric and the Hausdorff dimension of the boundary; the Patterson–Sullivan measure and the critical exponent, their equality in the cocompact case; the dimension as a quasi-isometry invariant and its behaviour under the Kleinian and the free case; the boundary of a surface group and of a free group; the group theory is Part II's, cited to *Hyperbolic Groups* and *Geometric Group Theory*. -->

### Operator Theory

<a href="articles_maths/projections-of-a-fractal-and-the-dimension.html">Projections of a Fractal and the Dimension</a>
<!-- the orthogonal projection of a fractal onto a line as an operator and the Marstrand–Mattila theorem, that for almost every direction the dimension of the projection is the minimum of the dimension and one; the exceptional set of directions, of dimension zero, and the sharpness; the slicing theorem for the section of the set by a line; the application to the distance set below. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-distance-set-of-a-fractal.html">The Distance Set of a Fractal</a>
<!-- the set of distances realised by the pairs of a fractal; the Falconer distance problem, that a set of dimension exceeding one half has a distance set of positive measure, with the dimension thresholds and the partial resolutions; the arithmetic nature of the distance set; the relation to the projection theorem above. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-hutchinson-operator-and-its-adjoint.html">The Hutchinson Operator and Its Adjoint</a>
<!-- the Hutchinson operator on the complete metric space of compact sets, its contraction and its unique fixed point, the attractor; the adjoint action on the space of probability measures, the pushforward under the contractions, and the fixed point as the self-similar measure; the duality between the attractor and the measure; the operator form of the iterated function systems of *Fractal Analysis*. -->

### * Theory

<a href="articles_maths/symmetric-fractals-and-the-involution.html">Symmetric Fractals and the Involution</a>
<!-- a fractal carrying an involutive isometry; the fixed set, which is again a fractal, and the exchanged pairs of points; the quotient by the involution and its dimension; the symmetric self-similar sets, the segment, the symmetric Cantor set and the symmetric gasket, and their tilings; the comparison with the reversible iterated function systems of *Fractal Analysis*. -->

### * Operator Theory

<a href="articles_maths/the-involution-on-the-space-of-compact-sets-and-the-symmetric-attractor.html">The Involution on the Space of Compact Sets and the Symmetric Attractor</a>
<!-- the space of nonempty compact sets with the Hausdorff metric, and the involutive isometry it acquires from a symmetry of the ambient space; the fixed compact sets and the symmetric attractor as a fixed point of the involution; the commutation of the involution with the Hutchinson operator and the existence of a symmetric fixed point; the adjoint action on the measures and the symmetric self-similar measure. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-specificities-of-the-complex-algebra.html">The Specificities of the Complex Algebra</a>

<!-- the left multiplication by $Q=q+iq'$ in the basis $(1,i)$, as the Cayley matrix $qI_2+q'J$ displayed entrywise; the image as the two-dimensional algebra of conformal matrices, characterised by $MJ=JM$ and by being the real matrices of the complex-linear maps; the left and right multiplications equal by commutativity, and the centraliser equal to the image; the trace $2q$ and the traceless imaginary line; the determinant equal to the norm $q^2+q'^2$, positive definite and with zero set a point; the absence of an idempotent but $0$ and $I_2$, and the two idempotents $\tfrac12(I_2\mp iJ)$ of the complexification, whose real and imaginary parts are the frame; the eigenvalues $q\pm iq'$ and the isotropic eigenlines; the adjugate, the transpose and the conjugate all one matrix; the trace form of inertia $(1,1)$ against the definite determinant; the two distinguished subspaces against the six of the biquaternion algebra. -->

<!-- the carrier of dimension two against the ambient $M_2(\mathbb{R})$ of dimension four; the one-sided families equal, and the two-sided operator $X\mapsto QXP$ equal to the multiplication by $QP$, so that four parameters fall to two; the plain adjoint equal to the operator itself and the Frobenius adjoint equal to the operator of the conjugate; the Kronecker display $\mathsf{M}_2(P)^{\mathsf T}\otimes\mathsf{M}_2(Q)$ of rank four, of trace $4\operatorname{Re}Q\operatorname{Re}P$ and determinant $N(Q)^2N(P)^2$; the inner automorphisms trivial on the carrier and a rotation by $2\theta$ on the traceless symmetric plane, the smallest double cover $\mathrm{SO}(2)\to SO(3)$; the linear membership test $MJ=JM$; the span closed at the family itself, because $\mathbb{C}$ is simple but not central; the operator rank two against the coefficient rank one; the transpose as the one operator outside the family. -->

## Split-Complex Numbers

### Algebra

#### The Algebra and Its Vector Spaces

<a href="articles_maths/split-complex-algebra.html">Split-Complex Algebra</a>
<!-- $\mathbb{C}^{\mathrm{spl}}=\mathbb{R}[x]/(x^2-1)$; the two fixed-point subspaces; the split complex and idempotent decompositions; zero divisors. The norm, the Hermitian form and the inner product are a form and a distance and belong to *Norm and Invertibility in the General Split-Complex Algebra*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/worked-examples-in-the-split-complex-algebra.html">Worked Examples in the Split-Complex Algebra</a>
<!-- the computed case: the two involutions and their fixed-point subspaces; the idempotents and the two minimal ideals; explicit zero-divisor pairs $Q_1Q_2=0$ with $Q_1,Q_2\neq0$; worked hyperbolic and parabolic elements. The norm criterion is a form and a distance and belongs to *Norm and Invertibility in the General Split-Complex Algebra*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-involutions-the-subspaces-and-the-idempotent-lines-of-the-split-complex-space.html">The Involutions, the Subspaces and the Idempotent Lines of the Split-Complex Space</a>
<!-- the involution group of the split-complex ring, the identity and the conjugation $j\mapsto-j$, which coincides here with the idempotent conjugation, of order two; the two decompositions, the degenerate one of the identity and $\mathbb{C}^{\mathrm{spl}}=\mathbb{R}_{\mathbb{C}^{\mathrm{spl}}}\oplus j\mathbb{R}_{\mathbb{C}^{\mathrm{spl}}}$ of the conjugation; the finer idempotent split $\mathbb{R}\Pi_+\oplus\mathbb{R}\Pi_-$, the finest of all; the one non-zero intersection, the real line; the closure of the real line and the failure of closure of the split imaginary line; and the two isotropic idempotent lines, which have no counterpart in the complex algebra. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-spectrum-and-the-two-point-structure-of-the-split-complex-numbers-over-r.html">The Spectrum and the Two-Point Structure of $\mathbb{C}^{\mathrm{spl}}$ over $\mathbb{R}$</a>
<!-- $\mathbb{C}^{\mathrm{spl}}$ over $\mathbb{R}$ read through its spectrum: the algebra $\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}$, its two characters, which are the evaluation at the two idempotents $Q\mapsto Q_\pm$, and the two points of the spectrum; the etale structure, the algebra being a product of two copies of the base and not a field; the exchange $j\mapsto-j$ acting on the two points as the only automorphism; the form the Galois correspondence takes here, a discrete two-point space instead of a degree-two extension; and the comparison with *Galois Theory of $\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{R}$, of which this is the split counterpart with the opposite conclusion. -->

#### The Products and the Classes

<a href="articles_maths/the-specificities-of-the-split-complex-algebra.html">The Specificities of the Split-Complex Algebra</a>
<!-- the properties that single out the ring: commutative, associative, dimension two, reduced but not a field, the two idempotents and the null cone, isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}\oplus\mathbb{R}$, semisimple and not simple, the split analogue of the complex field, the consequences for the classes and the degeneracy of the matrix models. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-two-products-of-the-split-complex-space.html">The Two Products of the Split-Complex Space</a>
<!-- the two products the split-complex space carries, $AC$ and $A\bar C$, and no third, the bar being the only nontrivial involution of the ring and the reading with the bar in the first slot being the conjugate of the sesquilinear product; each fixed by its own exchange, so that no antisymmetric part exists; the two on the coordinates and on the idempotent coordinates, $A\bar C=(ac-bd)+(bc-ad)j$; the laws, associativity and the two-sided unit for $AC$ against the right unit alone for $A\bar C$; the two pairings $P$ and $H$; and the point that separates the split case from the complex one, the values and not the count, the idempotent coordinates making the second product componentwise. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-ternary-product-and-the-associator-of-the-split-complex-space.html">The Ternary Product and the Associator of the Split-Complex Space</a>
<!-- the ternary product $\{A,B,C\}=A\bar BC$ in the idempotent coordinates, where it is componentwise; the outer and Hermitian symmetries; the contractions to the two binary products; the Jordan triple identity, which holds; the algebraic $J^{*}$-structure over the involutive ring; the associator $[A,B,C]=A\bar B(\bar C-C)$, confined to the sesquilinear shape and vanishing exactly when the third slot is real, its value a hyperbolic vector when it does not vanish; and the comparison with the complex case, where the two components coincide. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-classes-of-element-of-the-split-complex-algebra.html">The Classes of Element of the Split-Complex Algebra</a>
<!-- the hub of the classes: the table of the classes and their articles; the partition into units, zero and zero divisors; the inclusions and disjointness among the classes; the roots of the central values and their cardinalities $4,1,0$; the order cone of squares $q\ge|q'|$ and its order; the two algebraic norms and the classes; the three central values compared. -->

<a href="articles_maths/square-roots-of-one-and-the-idempotents-of-the-split-complex-algebra.html">Square Roots of One and the Idempotents of the Split-Complex Algebra</a>
<!-- the roots of $+1$: exactly $\pm1,\pm j$, four elements, forming $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^2$; no roots of $-1$; the halving map $\Xi\mapsto\frac12(1+\Xi)$, a bijection from roots to idempotents with inverse $2\Pi-1$; the two idempotents $\Pi_\pm(\Xi)$ of a root, complete orthogonal, with the root as their difference; the four idempotents $0,1,\Pi_+,\Pi_-$; the standard pair, central, primitive, the projectors and the minimal ideals; the correspondence with the roots and the zero divisors. -->

<a href="articles_maths/square-roots-of-zero-and-the-nilpotents-of-the-split-complex-algebra.html">Square Roots of Zero and the Nilpotents of the Split-Complex Algebra</a>
<!-- the roots of $0$: only $0$; no nonzero nilpotent, the algebra reduced; the nilpotent cone $\{0\}$ of dimension $0$; the zero element of index one and no element of index two or higher; the nilpotents and the zero divisors, disjoint; the nilpotents and the idempotents; the conjugation; the matrix model, square-zero only at the zero matrix; no nonzero nilpotent ideal and zero radical; the distinguished subspaces. -->

<a href="articles_maths/square-roots-of-a-general-element-in-the-split-complex-algebra.html">Square Roots of a General Element in the Split-Complex Algebra</a>
<!-- the reduction to $\Xi_\pm^2=Q_\pm$; four roots when both coordinates are positive, two on the boundary minus the origin, one at the origin, none outside; the roots of a real scalar, of units and of zero divisors; the three central values recovered; the worked examples; the image of the square and the forward cone $q\ge|q'|$; the fibres of the square map. The order cone is *The Classes of Element of the Split-Complex Algebra*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-square-map-of-the-split-complex-space.html">The Square Map of the Split-Complex Space</a>
<!-- the square map $Q\mapsto Q^{2}$: its image, the forward cone $\{q\ge\lvert q\rvert\}$ of the coordinate $q\ge\lvert q^{\prime}\rvert$; its Jacobian $4(q^{2}-q^{\prime 2})$, the determinant of the multiplication by $2Q$, vanishing exactly on the null pair of lines, so that the null cone is the branch locus and the map is a local diffeomorphism off it; the two sheets over the interior of the cone, one over its boundary minus the origin, and none outside; the identification of the four inverse branches with the four roots of *Square Roots of a General Element in the Split-Complex Algebra*; and the contrast with $\mathbb{C}$, where the square is onto and the only critical point is the origin. -->

<a href="articles_maths/ideals-and-peirce-decomposition-of-the-split-complex-algebra.html">Ideals and Peirce Decomposition of the Split-Complex Algebra</a>
<!-- the ideals of the commutative algebra: the four ideals, the two minimal and maximal lines, the failure of simplicity and the reason; Artinian, semisimple, reduced and length two; the idempotents and the Peirce decomposition with its multiplication table, the Peirce coordinates, the collapse for the standard idempotent, the involutions and the real structure; the lattice of ideals, Boolean of four elements; the radical. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-peirce-decomposition-of-the-split-complex-algebra.html">The Peirce Decomposition of the Split-Complex Algebra</a>
<!-- the family $\Pi_\pm=\tfrac12(1\pm j)$ of $\mathbb{C}^{\mathrm{spl}}=\mathbb{R}[j]$, $j^2=1$; the idempotents central, so the mixed components vanish; the two lines $\mathbb{R}\Pi_+$ and $\mathbb{R}\Pi_-$ and the componentwise product; the roots $\pm1,\pm j$ and the family from $\pm j$; the product decomposition $\mathbb{C}^{\mathrm{spl}}\cong\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}$; the degenerate case of the general construction. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-peirce-basis-of-the-split-complex-algebra.html">The Peirce Basis of the Split-Complex Algebra</a>
<!-- the pair $\{\Pi_+,\Pi_-\}$ as the Peirce basis, forced because the mixed lines are zero; no frame freedom, the replacement $t_\sigma t_\sigma^{-1}$ acting trivially; the coordinates $Q_\pm=q\pm q'$ and the diagonal array; the dimension count $0=0+0$; the automorphism $j\mapsto-j$ swapping the two lines. -->

<a href="articles_maths/spinors-as-peirce-coordinates-in-the-split-complex-algebra.html">Spinors as Peirce Coordinates in the Split-Complex Algebra</a>
<!-- the rows $(Q_+,0)$ and $(0,Q_-)$; a spinor as a single real scalar; no frame freedom because the basis is canonical; no chiral split, the two rows being the two factors; no half-angle, the family having no continuous parameter. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-two-forms-and-the-two-algebraic-norms-of-the-split-complex-space.html">The Two Forms and the Two Algebraic Norms of the Split-Complex Space</a>
<!-- $P(A,C)=AC$ and $H(A,C)=A\bar C$, one for each product and no third; $P$ symmetric and definite of inertia $(2,0)$, positive on the whole plane; $H$ conjugate-symmetric and indefinite of inertia $(1,1)$, with the null pair of lines as its isotropic set; the two algebraic norms $A^{2}$, $\mathbb{C}^{\mathrm{spl}}$-valued and anisotropic, and $N(A)=a^{2}-b^{2}$, real and indefinite; and the reversal of the complex case, where the definite form is the sesquilinear one and the isotropic set is a point. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-hermitian-form-the-double-cone-and-the-reversed-cauchy-schwarz-inequality.html">The Hermitian Form, the Double Cone and the Reversed Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality</a>
<!-- the indefinite positivity of $H$: the cone of $H$-positivity, the double cone $a^{2}\ge b^{2}$ with its two components, its interior of units and its boundary of zero divisors; the vanishing of $H$ on both idempotent lines, so that the form is totally isotropic there and the algebra is not a Hilbert algebra; the reversed Cauchy-Schwarz and triangle inequalities the indefiniteness forces; the order the cone defines, partial and not total; the unitary group of the module of rank one, which is the group of norm-one elements, the two branches of the hyperbola; and the comparison with the ray of the complex case. -->

#### The Forms and the Split Norm

<a href="articles_maths/norm-and-invertibility-in-the-general-split-complex-algebra.html">Norm and Invertibility in the General Split-Complex Algebra</a>
<!-- the algebraic norm of the general plain sesquilinear product, $\langle Q\rangle_*=Q\bar Q=q^2-q'^2$, real and indefinite of inertia $(1,1)$; multiplicativity, polarisation and the split bilinear form $g$; the semi-norm, the modulus and the Euclidean norm; the right unit $1$ and the absence of a left unit, so no inverse of the product and no group of invertibles of $\star$, while the plain group of invertibles survives; the one-sided inverse equations with the common solution $Q/\langle Q\rangle_*$; the criterion $\langle Q\rangle_*\neq0$; the three-way classification, the group of invertibles $\mathbb{R}^\times\times\mathbb{R}^\times$, its four components, and the norm on the distinguished subspaces. -->

<a href="articles_maths/zero-divisors-of-the-split-complex-algebra.html">Zero Divisors of the Split-Complex Algebra</a>
<!-- the definition for a general product; the criterion in idempotent coordinates, $Q_+Q_-=0$ or $q^2=q'^2$; the three-way classification; the algebra not a division algebra; the two families $\mathbb{R}^\times\Pi_\pm$, the primitive zero divisors and the annihilators; the structure of the zero-divisor set, four components, its closure closed under multiplication, not an ideal; the distribution on the distinguished subspaces; the relation to the idempotents and to the matrix model. -->

<a href="articles_maths/annihilators-of-the-split-complex-algebra.html">Annihilators of the Split-Complex Algebra</a>
<!-- the annihilator of a general product and the coincidence of the two sides in the commutative case; the annihilator as an ideal and as the kernel of $L_Q$; the matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}q&q'\\q'&q\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, trace $2q$, determinant $Q\bar Q$, rank $2/1/0$; the annihilator $\{0\}$ off the cone, the opposite null line on the cone, the whole algebra at the origin; the annihilator of an ideal, the double annihilator and the two extremes; the distribution on the distinguished subspaces and the matrix model. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-level-sets-of-the-split-norm-and-the-hyperbolic-structure.html">The Level Sets of the Split Norm and the Hyperbolic Structure</a>
<!-- the level sets of the split norm, the families of hyperbolas $a^{2}-b^{2}=c$, one for each sign of $c$, and the null pair of lines at $c=0$; the four components of a level set of non-zero value and the two branches of each; the action of the hyperbolic rotations, transitive on each branch, so that the level set of norm one is the orbit of $1$ under $O(1,1)$; the quotient of the plane by the group and the invariant it leaves; the null cone as the common boundary where the level sets meet; and the comparison with the circles of the complex plane, which are compact level sets of a definite form. -->

#### Algebra with the Split Norm

<a href="articles_maths/modulus-unit-polar-decomposition-of-split-complex-numbers.html">Modulus–Unit Polar Decomposition of Split-Complex Numbers</a>
<!-- the algebraic member: the writing $Q=ru$ with modulus $r=\sqrt{|N(Q)|}>0$ and unit factor $u=Q/r$ of norm $\pm1$; the indefinite norm of inertia $(1,1)$, the three regions and the null cone as the zero-divisor set; existence and uniqueness of the pair, with the sign of the norm forced and no ambiguity in the pair; the unit set as two hyperbolas, four components and the hyperbolic angle without period; the group of invertibles $\mathbb{R}_{>0}\times\mathbb{R}\times(\mathbb{Z}/2)^2$, the maximal compact subgroup $\{\pm1,\pm j\}$ and the deformation retract; the two axes, the real Hermitian one and the split-imaginary anti-Hermitian one, and why no continuous compact factor exists; the matrix picture $M_Q=qI+q'K$ with $K^2=I$, symmetric and generally not orthogonal, and the matrix polar decomposition $(M_Q,I)$, $(-M_Q,-I)$, $(|M_Q|,\text{reflection})$; worked examples and the comparison of the unit sets of the family. -->

<a href="articles_maths/rational-chart-polar-decomposition-of-split-complex-numbers.html">Rational-Chart Polar Decomposition of Split-Complex Numbers</a>
<!-- the rational member, opened on the modulus–unit form $Q=ru$ of the companion article so that $r$ and $u$ are the same objects throughout: the unit factor named by the Cayley chart $u(s)=(1-sj)/(1+sj)$ of the hyperbola $N=1$, rational in both directions, with inverse $s=-j(u-1)/(u+1)=-q'/(r+q)$; the two poles $s=\pm1$ as the null directions, the missing point $-1$, the negative real axis as the cut, and the domain $\{N\neq0\}\setminus\mathbb{R}_{<0}$; the four components and the discrete factor $\epsilon\in\{\pm1,\pm j\}$; the second chart $v(s)=-u(s)=u(1/s)$ and the projective conic; the group law $s_1*s_2=(s_1+s_2)/(1+s_1s_2)$, the pole at $s_1s_2=-1$ and the group-chunk structure; the matrix Cayley transform $M(s)=(I-sK)(I+sK)^{-1}$ onto $SO(1,1)\setminus\{-I\}$, symmetric and generally not orthogonal; worked examples and the price of rationality. -->

#### Spectral Algebra with the Split Norm

## Quaternions

### Algebra

#### The Algebra and Its Vector Spaces

<a href="articles_maths/quaternion-algebra.html">Quaternion Algebra</a>
<!-- $\mathbb{H}$ on $\mathbb{R}^4$; the three fixed-point subspaces; the quaternion and conjugate decompositions; the Lie algebra structure; the tensor product decomposition. The quadratic form and the inner product are a form and a distance and belong to *Quaternion Norm and Invertibility*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-axis-free-construction-of-the-quaternion-algebra.html">The Axis-Free Construction of the Quaternion Algebra</a>
<!-- the algebra declared from the four units alone, without a base field and without a doubling step: the units $e_t=1,\vec e_x,\vec e_y,\vec e_z$, the inner product and the orientation of the vector part as the only two data on it, and the rule $(\lambda e_t+\vec u)(\mu e_t+\vec v)=(\lambda\mu-\vec u\cdot\vec v)e_t+\lambda\vec v+\mu\vec u+\vec u\times\vec v$; its value on the units, that is the ten statements, of which the seven symmetric ones are invariant under every permutation of the three vector units and the three cyclic ones carry the orientation; the sixteen-product table and the three identities $\vec e_x^2=\vec e_y^2=\vec e_z^2=\vec e_x\vec e_y\vec e_z=-e_t$; associativity proved inside the coefficient display, from $L_x^2=L_y^2=L_z^2=-\mathrm I_4$ and $L_xL_y=L_z$ cyclically, the four generators being signed permutations of determinant one and zero diagonal; the unit and the centre $\mathbb{R}e_t$, the conjugation and the two fixed subspaces, the norm $q_t^2+q_x^2+q_y^2+q_z^2$ and its multiplicativity, the inverse $\tilde q^{\natural}/\langle\tilde q\rangle_{\natural}$, the division property, the classes of element with the unit sphere of roots of $-e_t$ and the absence of a distinguished root, the commutator $[\vec u,\vec v]=2\vec u\times\vec v$ and simplicity; the automorphisms $SO(3)$, a reflection as an anti-automorphism, and the other cyclic order as the opposite algebra identified by the conjugation; and the comparison with the doubling, which spends one unit on the base field and a second on the step and computes the third. This article is the reference construction of the algebra; the doubling is kept beside it for the ladder, for the exclusion of the plain rule and for the proof that the twist is forced. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-cayley-dickson-construction-of-the-quaternion-algebra.html">The Cayley–Dickson Construction of the Quaternion Algebra</a>
<!-- the double $\mathbb{H}=\mathbb{C}\oplus\mathbb{C}\vec e_x$ of the complex algebra $\mathbb{C}=\mathbb{R}[\vec e_z]$, built without arrays and without a second triple of units: the base units $e_t,\vec e_x,\vec e_y,\vec e_z$, with $\vec e_z$ the only imaginary unit and the base element $w=u+v\vec e_z$ with its bar; the product rule $(a+b\vec e_x)(c+d\vec e_x)=(ac-b\bar d)+(ad+b\bar c)\vec e_x$ and its two generating rules, the square $\vec e_x^2=-e_t$ and the twist $\vec e_xw=\bar w\vec e_x$; the twist proved to be the whole content, since the untwisted variant squares $\vec e_z\vec e_x$ to $+e_t$ and carries the two idempotents $\tfrac12(e_t\pm\vec e_z\vec e_x)$, hence zero divisors; the third unit computed and not assumed, $\vec e_y:=\vec e_z\vec e_x$, the order fixed by $\vec e_z\vec e_x\vec e_y=-e_t$ against $\vec e_x\vec e_z\vec e_y=+e_t$; the nine derivations giving the three squares, the sign flip and the six ordered products, the sixteen-product table, the cyclic form and the identity $\vec e_z^2=\vec e_x^2=\vec e_y^2=\vec e_z\vec e_x\vec e_y=-e_t$; associativity from the trilinearity of the associator and from the doubling criterion, the loss of commutativity, and the ladder $\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{H}\to\mathbb{O}$ with $\mathbb{H}$ its last associative division algebra; the conjugation $(a+b\vec e_x)^{\natural}=\bar a-b\vec e_x$, which restricts to the bar and reverses the order, the norm $N'=N(a)+N(b)=q_t^2+q_x^2+q_y^2+q_z^2$ and the inverse $\tilde q^{\natural}/N(\tilde q)$; the doubling order $(t,z,x,y)$ against the display order; and the choice of the doubling collected in one table. -->

#### The Two Products and Their Two Halves

<!-- the two general products of the real quaternion space and their four halves: the plain bilinear product and the quaternionic product, the only two that exist over $\mathbb{R}$, since the base field carries no second involution; the symmetrisation and the antisymmetrisation of each, taken under the bare exchange of the arguments because both slots are linear; the four halves named and the two reconstructions; the count $2\times3=6$ against the $4\times3=12$ of the biquaternion space, the six sesquilinear pairings having collapsed with the coefficient conjugation. The products themselves, with their coordinate rules and their six multiplication tables, are named here and read in the section below; this section owns the structures the halves define. -->

##### The Two Products

<a href="articles_maths/the-general-plain-bilinear-product-of-the-quaternions.html">The General Plain Bilinear Product of the Quaternions</a>
<!-- the first of the two general products read alone, the product $\tilde q_1\tilde q_2$ of the slot pairing $(\mathrm{id},\mathrm{id})$: the coordinate rule and the scalar–vector form $q_{1t}q_{2t}-(\vec q_1,\vec q_2)+q_{1t}\vec q_2+q_{2t}\vec q_1+\vec q_1\times\vec q_2$; the class of the product, $\mathbb{R}$-bilinear in both slots; the laws, associativity, the two-sided unit $e_t$, and the division property read as the absence of zero divisors; the image, the whole algebra, and the diagonal, the square $\tilde q^2$; the two halves and the reconstruction $\tilde q_1\tilde q_2=\tilde q_1\bullet\tilde q_2+\tilde q_1\wedge\tilde q_2$; the four composites of the product with its two halves; the trace form $\mathrm{Sc}(\tilde q_1\tilde q_2)$, of inertia $(1,3)$; and the place of this product among the two, the one that is associative and carries the unit. The algebra it makes of the space is the subject of the *Quaternions* category, entered at *Introduction to the Quaternion Algebra*; the products of the two halves are *The Jordan Structure of the Symmetric Plain Product of the Quaternions* and *The Lie Structure of the Antisymmetric Plain Product of the Quaternions*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-general-quaternionic-bilinear-product-of-the-quaternions.html">The General Quaternionic Bilinear Product of the Quaternions</a>
<!-- the second of the two general products read alone, the product $\tilde q_1^{\natural}\tilde q_2$ of the slot pairing $({}^{\natural},\mathrm{id})$: the coordinate rule and the scalar–vector form $q_{1t}q_{2t}+(\vec q_1,\vec q_2)+q_{1t}\vec q_2-q_{2t}\vec q_1-\vec q_1\times\vec q_2$; the class of the product, $\mathbb{R}$-bilinear in both slots; the laws, the failure of associativity, of flexibility and of power-associativity, with witnesses, and the left unit $e_t$ alone, since $e_t^{\natural}\tilde q=\tilde q$ while $\tilde q^{\natural}e_t=\tilde q^{\natural}$; the image, the whole algebra, and the diagonal $\tilde q^{\natural}\tilde q=N(\tilde q)e_t$, the quaternion norm read as a product; the two halves and the reconstruction $\tilde q_1^{\natural}\tilde q_2=\langle\tilde q_1,\tilde q_2\rangle_{\natural}e_t+\tilde q_1\wedge^{\natural}\tilde q_2$; the four composites; the trace form $\mathrm{Sc}(\tilde q_1^{\natural}\tilde q_2)$, the quaternion form, positive definite; and the place of this product among the two, the one that is neither associative nor unital and the only one that carries a definite form. The general quaternionic algebra it defines is the companion structure of the same space; its two halves are *The Jordan Structure of the Symmetric Quaternionic Product of the Quaternions* and *The Lie Structure of the Antisymmetric Quaternionic Product of the Quaternions*. -->

##### The Jordan Structures

<a href="articles_maths/the-jordan-structure-of-the-symmetric-plain-product-of-the-quaternions.html">The Jordan Structure of the Symmetric Plain Product of the Quaternions</a>

<a href="articles_maths/the-jordan-structure-of-the-symmetric-quaternionic-product-of-the-quaternions.html">The Jordan Structure of the Symmetric Quaternionic Product of the Quaternions</a>

<a href="articles_maths/the-lie-structure-of-the-antisymmetric-quaternionic-product-of-the-quaternions.html">The Lie Structure of the Antisymmetric Quaternionic Product of the Quaternions</a>

#### The Idempotents, the Ideals and the Peirce Decomposition

<a href="articles_maths/ideals-and-simplicity-of-the-quaternion-algebra.html">Ideals and Simplicity of the Quaternion Algebra</a>

## Biquaternions

### Algebra

#### The Algebra of Biquaternions

<a href="articles_maths/introduction-to-the-algebra-of-biquaternions.html">Introduction to the Algebra of Biquaternions</a>
<!-- the construction $\mathbb{B}=\mathbb{C}\otimes_{\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{H}$ and the basis; the multiplication, its table and its coordinate rule; the algebra axioms, left alternativity and the isolation among the twelve products; the multiplication as a scalar extension; the structure map, the centre and central simplicity; the two-generator presentation; the absence of division, proved by $(e_t+i\vec e_x)(e_t-i\vec e_x)=0$. No form and no norm are used; the element, the coordinates, the conjugations and the matrix model are the companion articles. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-axis-free-construction-of-the-biquaternion-algebra.html">The Axis-Free Construction of the Biquaternion Algebra</a>
<!-- the same route on the complex algebra: the four units and the central $i$, $i^2=-e_t$, declared in one act, with no base field inside the vector part and no stack of layers; the complex-bilinear form $(\vec Q_1,\vec Q_2)$ and the orientation as the only two data on the vector part; the rule and the proof that complex bilinearity is the whole of the difference from the quaternion algebra, the sixteen products unchanged and the table real; the tensor product $\mathbb{C}\otimes_{\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{H}$ derived as a theorem and not taken as a definition; associativity from the same four integer generators; the centre $\mathbb{C}e_t$; the four conjugations and their Klein group, two linear and two antilinear, two reversing the order, with ${}^{\ast}={}^{\natural}\bar{\cdot}$; the two sectors $\mathbb{B}_{\Psi}$ and $\mathbb{B}_{\Phi}$ as the real halves of the Hermitian conjugation; the complex norm $Q_t^2+Q_x^2+Q_y^2+Q_z^2$, multiplicative, central and vanishing on a cone; the zero divisors $(e_t+i\vec u)(e_t-i\vec u)=0$ over the whole sphere of real unit vectors, with no member distinguished, and the unit criterion read from the norm; the Hermitian idempotents $\tfrac12(e_t\pm i\vec u)$ on the same sphere, with the fuller classification deferred; the roots of $\pm e_t$ as a central pair and a complex quadric each; the commutator as twice the complex cross product; and the two bits, the orientation absorbed by ${}^{\natural}$ and the sign of $i$ by the bar, set against the stack of three layers that spends two units on fields and adds the central scalar last. This article is the reference construction of the algebra; the doubling is kept beside it for the forced twist and for the proof that the third layer is a scalar extension and not a rung. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-cayley-dickson-construction-of-the-biquaternion-algebra.html">The Cayley–Dickson Construction of the Biquaternion Algebra</a>
<!-- the ladder read to its end in three layers: rung one, the unit $\vec e_z$ and $\mathbb{C}=\mathbb{R}[\vec e_z]$; rung two, the unit $\vec e_x$ under the twist, with the nine derivations of the table and $\vec e_y=\vec e_z\vec e_x$ computed rather than adjoined; the third layer, the central scalar $i$ with $i^2=-e_t$, giving $\mathbb{B}=\mathbb{H}\oplus i\mathbb{H}$ of real dimension eight; the product rule of the layer and the invariance of the quaternion table; the proof that the third layer is not a Cayley–Dickson rung, the double of an associative algebra being associative only when the algebra is commutative, with the doubling by $\natural$ and by the identity compared through two commutators, and with a rung at the third step shown to lose associativity; what the layer keeps, the table, the associativity, the non-commutativity and the centre $\mathbb{C}e_t$, read against the centre of the three lower layers; what it loses, $(i\vec u)^2=+e_t$, the idempotents $\tfrac12(e_t\pm i\vec u)$ and $(e_t+i\vec e_x)(e_t-i\vec e_x)=0$; the three two-dimensional subalgebras, $\mathbb{R}[\vec e_z]$, the central $\mathbb{R}[i]$ and the split line $\mathbb{R}[i\vec e_z]$; the three conjugations, which of them reverse the order, the norm $Q_t^2+Q_x^2+Q_y^2+Q_z^2$ and the inverse; and the place of the layer, with the theorem of Frobenius delimiting the associative division algebras. No form is used beyond the norm, and there is no matrix. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-element-the-coordinates-and-the-conjugations-in-the-biquaternion-algebra.html">The Element, the Coordinates and the Conjugations in the Biquaternion Algebra</a>
<!-- the element $\tilde Q=Q_te_t+\vec Q$, its coefficients and its scalar-vector split; the real, complex and quaternionic coordinate systems; the complex structure $J$ and the linear and antilinear maps; the four conjugations, their definitions and the split by commutation with $J$; and the real reading of the algebra. No form is used. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-group-of-involutions-of-the-biquaternion-algebra.html">The Group of Involutions of the Biquaternion Algebra</a>
<!-- the two conjugations of the algebra, the quaternion conjugation ${}^{\natural}$, $\mathbb{C}$-linear, and the Hermitian conjugation ${}^{*}$, conjugate-linear, both involutions and both reversing the order of the product, with the coefficientwise conjugation $\bar{\cdot}={}^{\natural}{}^{*}$; the Klein four-group $G=\{\mathrm{id},{}^{\natural},{}^{*},{}^{\natural}{}^{*}\}\cong V_4$, its Cayley table and its abelian character; the four maps as the four combinations of the two factor conjugations of $\mathbb{C}\otimes_{\mathbb{R}}\mathbb{H}$, one per tensor factor; the three order-two subgroups and the three splittings into fixed and anti-fixed spaces, the six subspaces of the next articles; the orbits of size one, two or four by the orbit-stabilizer count; and the sign-twisted adjoint $\flat=-{}^{*}$, outside the group because it reverses the product only up to the central sign, with the order-eight group $\{\pm1\}\times G$. -->

<a href="articles_maths/subspaces-and-decompositions-of-the-biquaternion-algebra.html">Subspaces and Decompositions of the Biquaternion Algebra</a>
<!-- the six remarkable subspaces of $\mathbb{B}$, one to a section: the centre, the vector subspace, the quaternion and anti-quaternion subspaces, the Hermitian and anti-Hermitian subspaces, each with its defining condition, its coordinate condition, its real basis, its real dimension and its role, and the table at a glance; the four coordinate blocks $A_1=\mathbb{R}e_t$, $A_2=\mathbb{R}(ie_t)$, $B_1=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{R}}\{\vec e_x,\vec e_y,\vec e_z\}$, $B_2=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb{R}}\{i\vec e_x,i\vec e_y,i\vec e_z\}$, each the intersection of the three subspaces that contain it, every remarkable subspace a sum of two of them, and the three decompositions as the three pairings of the four blocks; the three direct-sum decompositions of $\mathbb{B}$ cut out by the conjugations, $\mathbb{B}=\mathbb{B}_{C}\oplus\mathbb{B}_{V}$ of dimensions $2+6$, $\mathbb{B}=\mathbb{B}_{H}\oplus \mathbb{B}_{iH}$ and $\mathbb{B}=\mathbb{B}_{\Psi}\oplus\mathbb{B}_{\Phi}$ of dimensions $4+4$, with the projection formulas $\tilde{Q}_{\mathrm{c}}=\frac12(\tilde{Q}+\tilde{Q}^{\natural})$, $\tilde{Q}_{\mathrm{v}}=\frac12(\tilde{Q}-\tilde{Q}^{\natural})$, $\tilde{Q}_r=\frac12(\tilde{Q}+\bar{\tilde{Q}})$, $\tilde{Q}_i=\frac{1}{2i}(\tilde{Q}-\bar{\tilde{Q}})$ and $\tilde{Q}_\pm=\frac12(\tilde{Q}\pm\tilde{Q}^{*})$; the proof that the reversal $\flat=-{}^{*}$ adds no fourth; the fifteen pairwise intersections, of dimension $0$, $1$ or $3$, with the full $6\times6$ table; the $6\times6$ table of the sums, exactly the three decomposition pairs summing to $\mathbb{B}$; the $4\times6$ table of the multiplicities of $-1$ of each conjugation on each subspace, whose composition is the symmetric difference ${}^{*}=\bar{\cdot}\circ{}^{\natural}$; the lattice of the fixed spaces, which is not a chain and not closed under sum; the complex structure $J:\tilde{Q}\mapsto i\tilde{Q}$, stable on the centre and the vector subspace and exchanging the two four-dimensional pairs; and the worked examples, including the element $(2+i)e_t+3\vec e_x+i\vec e_y-4\vec e_z$ read in the three decompositions. No form and no topology appear. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-square-of-an-element-in-the-biquaternion-algebra.html">The Square of an Element in the Biquaternion Algebra</a>
<!-- the square $\tilde Q^2=(Q_t^2-B^2)e_t+2Q_t\vec Q$ in the coordinates of the element, with the complex length $B^2=Q_x^2+Q_y^2+Q_z^2$; its two parts, the scalar $Q_t^2-B^2$ and the vector $2Q_t\vec Q$; the central square; the vanishing square $Q_t=0$, $B^2=0$; the square equal to the element, $\tilde Q\in\{0,e_t\}$ or $Q_t=\tfrac12$, $B^2=-\tfrac14$; and the isotropic cone of real dimension four. No form is used. -->

<a href="articles_maths/zero-divisors-and-invertibles-in-the-biquaternion-algebra.html">Zero Divisors and Invertibles in the Biquaternion Algebra</a>
<!-- the annihilators of an element as the kernels of left and right multiplication; the explicit bases, of dimension 0 for a unit and 2 for a zero divisor; the two-sided annihilator as the common line $\mathbb{C}\tilde Q^{\natural}$; the zero divisors as the non-zero solutions of $Q_t^2+B_1^2=0$, split into the pure isotropic family and the non-pure family, with the cone of complex dimension 3; the closure under products; and the unit criterion, a trivial annihilator. No form is used. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-square-roots-of-a-general-element-in-the-biquaternion-algebra.html">The Square Roots of a General Element in the Biquaternion Algebra</a>
<!-- the problem $\tilde\Xi^2=\tilde Q$ for an arbitrary $\tilde Q$; the method free of Clifford algebras, norms and forms, by the same vector–scalar split that solves the central values; the two equations $2\Xi_t\tilde\Xi=\vec Q$ and $\Xi_t^2-(\tilde\Xi,\tilde\Xi)=Q_t$; the two cases according to whether the vector part $\vec Q$ vanishes; the reduced quadratic $4x^2-4Q_tx-(\vec Q,\vec Q)=0$ for $x=\Xi_t^2$, of discriminant $16n$ with the conjugate scalar $n=Q_t^2+Q_x^2+Q_y^2+Q_z^2$, the scalar of $\tilde Q\tilde Q^{\natural}=ne_t$, and the pair $\pm(\sqrt{x}\,e_t+\vec Q/(2\sqrt{x}))$ from each nonzero solution; the complex-scalar case, with the elements $\pm\sqrt{Q_t}e_t$ and the four-real-parameter family of pure $\tilde\Xi$ of complex square $-Q_t$, the nilpotent cone at $\tilde Q=0$; the classification of no root, two roots, four roots and continuum, with the roots stated in each case; the specialisation to the three central values, cited to the two companion articles, the roots of $+1$ and of $-1$ in the first and the roots of $0$ in the second and used as a consistency check; the worked examples, verified by squaring. This article owns the classification of $\tilde\Xi^2=\tilde Q$. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-tensor-product-of-two-biquaternion-algebras.html">The Tensor Product of Two Biquaternion Algebras</a>
<!-- the two tensor products and the quotient relation that separates them; the complex tensor product $\mathbb{B}\otimes_{\mathbb{C}}\mathbb{B}\cong M_4(\mathbb{C})$, central simple of degree four, with no non-trivial two-sided ideal and hence no sector decomposition; the partial star ${}^{*}\otimes\mathrm{id}$ and the failure of descent, with the two-line proof, and the total star ${}^{*}\otimes{}^{*}$ that descends and is the Hermitian adjoint with fixed space of real dimension sixteen; the corner identity $(i\vec e_\mu)\otimes(i\vec e_\mu)=-\vec e_\mu\otimes\vec e_\mu$ and the parity rule, by which the $2^{n}$ corners collapse onto the Hermitian and anti-Hermitian parts of $M_{2^{n}}(\mathbb{C})$; the real tensor product $M_4(\mathbb{C})\oplus M_4(\mathbb{C})$, its centre of real dimension four, the central involution $\mathsf J=i\otimes i$ and the idempotents $u,v$; the identification of the physical summand, the one with $\mathsf J=-1$, with $\mathbb{B}\otimes_{\mathbb{C}}\mathbb{B}$; the star on each summand as an involution of the second kind; the count $2^{n-1}$; and what the tensor product is not. The companion articles are *Introduction to the Algebra of Biquaternions*, *The Group of Involutions of the Biquaternion Algebra*, *Subspaces and Decompositions of the Biquaternion Algebra* and *The Category of Modules in the Biquaternion Algebra*. -->

#### Matrix Representations

<a href="articles_maths/families-of-matrix-representations.html">Families of Matrix Representations</a>
<!-- the left and the right matrix of an element in a general frame $\mathcal{F}=(f_1,f_2,f_3,f_4)$, with $L_{\mathcal{F}}(\tilde Q)_{\mu\nu}=[\tilde Qf_\nu]_{\mu}$ and $R_{\mathcal{F}}(\tilde Q)_{\mu\nu}=[f_\nu\tilde Q]_{\mu}$, and the relations the algebra forces between the two families: the three laws $L(\tilde Q_2\tilde Q)=L(\tilde Q_2)L(\tilde Q)$, $R(\tilde Q_2\tilde Q)=R(\tilde Q)R(\tilde Q_2)$ and $L(\tilde Q_2)R(\tilde Q)=R(\tilde Q)L(\tilde Q_2)$, which need no coordinates and survive every change of frame; the two families as a copy of the algebra and a copy of its opposite, each faithful and of dimension four, with every left matrix commuting with every right matrix; the coincidence $L(\tilde Q)=R(\tilde Q)$ exactly on the centre, the intersection $\mathbb{B}_L\cap\mathbb{B}_R=\mathbb{C}\mathrm I_4$, the seven-dimensional joint span, and the central matrices scalar, $L(\lambda e_t)=R(\lambda e_t)=\lambda\mathrm I_4$; the shared invariants, the trace $4Q_t$, the determinant $\langle\tilde Q\rangle_{\natural}^2$, the characteristic polynomial $((X-Q_t)^2+B^2)^2$, the spectrum $Q_t\pm iB$ twice, the rank twice the rank of $A(\tilde Q)$ and hence $0$, $2$ or $4$, and the two annihilators, different subspaces of the same dimension; the trace pairing, which is $4\operatorname{Sc}(\tilde Q_2\tilde Q)$ inside a family and $4P_tQ_t$ across the two sides, so that only the centre couples them; the switch $\mathsf W$, the Gram matrix $\mathsf W_{\mu\nu}=\beta(f_\mu,f_\nu)$ of the symmetric and cyclic form $\beta(\tilde X,\tilde Y)=\operatorname{Sc}(\tilde X\tilde Y)$, which satisfies $\mathsf W R(\tilde Q)=L(\tilde Q)^{\mathsf T}\mathsf W$ and hence $R(\tilde Q)=\mathsf W^{-1}L(\tilde Q)^{\mathsf T}\mathsf W$, symmetric and nondegenerate, an involution, unique up to a nonzero scalar among symmetric solutions while the solutions without symmetry are the four-dimensional family $\mathsf W L(\tilde Q_2)$, and different from the Hermitian dictionary, which keeps the side, $L(\tilde Q)^{\dagger}=L(\tilde Q^{*})$; the reason no conjugation can carry the left family onto the right, because a conjugation preserves products and the right side reverses them, witnessed by $\vec e_x\vec e_y=\vec e_z$ against $\vec e_y\vec e_x=-\vec e_z$, and the reason a transposition alone cannot cross the divide either; the change of frame, a conjugation by an invertible $\mathsf C$ applied to both sides at once, $L_{\mathcal{F}'}=\mathsf C^{-1}L_{\mathcal{F}}\mathsf C$ and $R_{\mathcal{F}'}=\mathsf C^{-1}R_{\mathcal{F}}\mathsf C$, because the frame belongs to the carrier and the side to the action, with each frame carrying its own switch, the Gram matrix of $\beta$ on its own vectors, and the switch of the new frame given by the congruence $\mathsf W_{\mathcal{F}'}=\mathsf C^{\mathsf T}\mathsf W_{\mathcal{F}}\mathsf C$ and the compatibility $\mathsf W_{\mathcal{F}'}^{-1}L_{\mathcal{F}'}^{\mathsf T}\mathsf W_{\mathcal{F}'}=R_{\mathcal{F}'}$; the table of the two moves, change of side and change of frame, which generate every passage between the families with no further matrix; and the $2\times2$ family without a frame, with the trace $2Q_t$, the determinant $\langle\tilde Q\rangle_{\natural}$, the spectrum $Q_t\pm iB$ and the rank in $\{0,1,2\}$, the absence of a second side at the element size, and the same mechanism producing the conjugate through $\varepsilon=i\sigma_2$. -->

<a href="articles_maths/m4c-axis-free-representation.html">$M_4(\mathbb{C})$ Axis-Free Representation</a>
<!-- the axis-free basis $(e_t,\vec e_x,\vec e_y,\vec e_z)$, which is the coefficient basis of the conventions and the basis of the structure constants $\varepsilon_{\mu\nu}^{\ \ \rho}\in\{0,\pm1\}$, and why no direction is privileged; the left family built first from the multiplication alone, $L^{\mathrm{axf}}(\tilde Q)_{\mu\nu}=[\tilde Qe_\nu]_\mu$, whose columns are the products $\tilde Qe_\nu$, with multiplicativity read off associativity, faithfulness from the first column, the four matrices of the units as signed permutations, the quaternion group $Q_8$ inside $O(4)$, and the transpose identity $L(\tilde Q)^{\mathsf T}=L(\tilde Q^{\natural})$; the right family built second by the same rule on the other side, $R^{\mathrm{axf}}(\tilde Q)_{\mu\nu}=[\vec e_\nu\tilde Q]_\mu$, anti-multiplicative and commuting with the left family, the two families meeting in the scalar matrices; the switch $R^{\mathrm{axf}}=D\,(L^{\mathrm{axf}})^{\mathsf T}D$ with $D=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)$, which is the Gram matrix of $\beta(\tilde X,\tilde Y)=\operatorname{Sc}(\tilde X\tilde Y)$ on the four units, real, of square $\mathrm I_4$, of determinant $-1$, and at once the matrix of the conjugation, with the entry rule $R_{\mu\nu}=s_\mu s_\nu L_{\nu\mu}$; every frame as a conjugate of this one, $L'=\mathsf C^{-1}L\mathsf C$ and $R'=\mathsf C^{-1}R\mathsf C$ with the switch moved by the congruence $\mathsf W'=\mathsf C^{\mathsf T}D\mathsf C$, and the invariants common to all frames; the ten properties this frame has at once, integer entries, signed permutations, orthogonality, the structure constants as entries, transpose as conjugation, real diagonal switch, $Q_8$, cyclic symmetry, the real slice, determinant one and trace $4\delta_{\mu t}$, as ten readings of the one fact that the basis is multiplicative; the real-coefficient question, the ladder $\mathbb{Z}\subset\mathbb{Z}[i]\subset\mathbb{C}$, and the reading of the sparsity as the transpose identity; the uniqueness among signed-permutation frames, the basis forced to be $f_t=\pm e_t$ and $f_k=\pm e_{\sigma(k)}$, with the count $3!\cdot2^4=96$ with the scalar unit first and $48$ with $f_t=e_t$, and the failure of uniqueness among real frames and among all frames; the operator as unique and the matrix as a conjugacy class, with this frame the canonical representative of the class; the product, the trace $4Q_t$ and the determinant $\langle\tilde Q\rangle_{\natural}^2$; and the six subspaces as scalar, traceless, real, purely imaginary, Hermitian and anti-Hermitian matrices, with their real dimensions, traces and $2\times2$ determinants. -->

<a href="articles_maths/m4c-pauli-representation.html">$M_4(\mathbb{C})$ Pauli Representation</a>
<!-- the Peirce frame generated by the root $\vec\Xi=i\vec e_z$ with $\vec\Xi^2=e_t$: the idempotents $\tilde\Pi_\pm=\tfrac12(e_t\pm i\vec e_z)$ and the mixed units $\vec\Pi_{\mathrm{nil},\pm}=\tfrac12(i\vec e_x\pm\vec e_y)$ in the order $(\tilde\Pi_+,\vec\Pi_{\mathrm{nil},+},\vec\Pi_{\mathrm{nil},-},\tilde\Pi_-)$, the multiplication table of the frame, and the four Peirce coordinates as the entries of the $2\times2$ block; the roots of $e_t$ as the solutions of $a_x^2+a_y^2+a_z^2=-1$, the six coordinate roots as the only ones with the monomial display, and every frame carrying two idempotent vectors as a root frame; the Peirce change $C_{\Pi}$ with its two $2\times2$ blocks, the dictionary $e_t=\tilde\Pi_++\tilde\Pi_-$, $\vec e_x=-i(\vec\Pi_{\mathrm{nil},+}+\vec\Pi_{\mathrm{nil},-})$, $\vec e_y=\vec\Pi_{\mathrm{nil},+}-\vec\Pi_{\mathrm{nil},-}$, $\vec e_z=i(\tilde\Pi_--\tilde\Pi_+)$, the conjugation $L=C_{\Pi}^{-1}L^{\mathrm{axf}}C_{\Pi}$ read entry by entry, and the sixteen coefficients that the switch leaves unchanged; the product, the trace $4Q_t$, the determinant $\langle\tilde Q\rangle_{\natural}^2$ and the eigenvalues $Q_t\pm iB$, each twice; the six subspaces as scalar, traceless, quaternion-shaped, anti-quaternion-shaped, Hermitian and anti-Hermitian matrices, with their real dimensions, traces and $2\times2$ determinants; and, at the end, the comparison table of the Peirce, axis-free and generic frames over entries, sparsity, realness, orthogonality, unitarity, tensor display, idempotents, cyclic symmetry, the switch and the transpose. -->

#### The Idempotents, the Ideals and the Peirce Decomposition

<a href="articles_maths/the-square-roots-of-zero-and-the-nilpotents-of-the-biquaternion-algebra.html">The Square Roots of Zero and the Nilpotents of the Biquaternion Algebra</a>
<!-- the square roots of the central value $0$ in the general plain bilinear product of two biquaternions $\tilde Q_1\tilde Q_2$, the multiplication of the algebra $\mathbb{B}=\mathbb{C}\otimes_\mathbb{R}\mathbb{H}$; the problem and its reduction by the same vector–scalar decomposition, giving $\Xi_t=0$ or $\tilde\Xi=0$; the roots of $0$ as the element $0$ together with the pure elements of vanishing complex square $\Xi_x^2+\Xi_y^2+\Xi_z^2=0$, a four-real-parameter family written in the two real parts $\vec\xi+i\vec\xi'$, with $\vec e_x+i\vec e_y$ as the worked instance; the nonzero roots of $0$ as the nilpotents of the algebra; the roots of $+1$, the roots of $-1$ and the idempotents as the companion article *Square Roots of One and the Idempotents of the Biquaternion Algebra*; the nilpotents: the definition $\tilde\Pi_{\mathrm{nil}}^2=0$, with $0$ the trivial one and the nonzero ones the subject; the criterion, $\tilde\Pi_{\mathrm{nil}}^2=[\Pi_{\mathrm{nil},t}^2-(\vec\Pi_{\mathrm{nil}},\vec\Pi_{\mathrm{nil}})]e_t+2\Pi_{\mathrm{nil},t}\vec\Pi_{\mathrm{nil}}$, so that a nilpotent is pure with isotropic vector part, $\Pi_{\mathrm{nil},t}=0$ and $(\vec\Pi_{\mathrm{nil}},\vec\Pi_{\mathrm{nil}})=0$; the nilpotent cone, a complex cone of complex dimension two and real dimension four, the two real equations $\vec p\cdot\vec p=\vec p'\cdot\vec p'$ and $\vec p\cdot\vec p'=0$ on the two real vector parts $\Pi_{\mathrm{nil},k}=p_k+ip'_k$, parametrised as $r(\hat{\vec p}+i\hat{\vec p}')$ over orthogonal real unit pairs; index two, $\tilde\Pi_{\mathrm{nil}}^3=0$ exactly when $\tilde\Pi_{\mathrm{nil}}^2=0$, with the cube $\tilde\Pi_{\mathrm{nil}}^3=\Pi_{\mathrm{nil},t}[\Pi_{\mathrm{nil},t}^2-3(\vec\Pi_{\mathrm{nil}},\vec\Pi_{\mathrm{nil}})]e_t+[3\Pi_{\mathrm{nil},t}^2-(\vec\Pi_{\mathrm{nil}},\vec\Pi_{\mathrm{nil}})]\vec\Pi_{\mathrm{nil}}$; the self-annihilation $\tilde\Pi_{\mathrm{nil}}\tilde\Pi_{\mathrm{nil}}=0$, so that a nonzero nilpotent is a two-sided zero divisor and its own annihilating partner, and the nilpotents are the pure family of the zero-divisor set; the action of the conjugations, the star pairing the class and fixing none of it; the model $M_2(\mathbb{C})$, where a nilpotent is a nonzero trace-free singular matrix, $\mathrm{tr}\,\mathsf M_2(\tilde\Pi_{\mathrm{nil}})=2\Pi_{\mathrm{nil},t}$ and $\det\mathsf M_2(\tilde\Pi_{\mathrm{nil}})=C(\tilde\Pi_{\mathrm{nil}})$, with the off-diagonal Peirce units $\vec\Pi_{\mathrm{nil},x},\vec\Pi_{\mathrm{nil},y}$; the coincidence $\mathbb{B}\tilde\Pi_{\mathrm{nil}}=I_{\tilde\Pi_{\mathrm{nil}}}$ of the ideal generated and the annihilator; the position in the remarkable subspaces, the vector subspace being the only one containing a nilpotent; and the free real parameters of the root family. The zero-divisor set and the two families are *N-Regularity and N-Degeneracy in the Biquaternion Algebra*, §*The Zero Divisors*; the roots of the general quadratic are *Square Roots of a General Element in the Biquaternion Algebra*; the minimal ideals are *The Minimal Left Ideals*; and the same class read against the four products is the zero-divisor article of the derived-structures category. -->

the roots of $+1$ as units and the nonzero roots of $0$ as zero divisors; the free real parameters of the root families; the roots read in the general plain bilinear product, the other three products having different squares and different roots; the two idempotents a root carries, $\tilde\Pi_+(\tilde\Xi)=\tfrac12(e_t+\tilde\Xi)$ and $\tilde\Pi_-(\tilde\Xi)=\tfrac12(e_t-\tilde\Xi)=e_t-\tilde\Pi_+(\tilde\Xi)$, a complete orthogonal pair summing to $e_t$, multiplying to $0$ and differing by the root, with multiplication by the root acting by $+1$ on the first and $-1$ on the second, the pair splitting the algebra into the eigenspaces, and the pair map a bijection from the roots onto the ordered complete orthogonal pairs; the idempotents of the general plain bilinear product, the equation $\tilde\Pi^2=\tilde\Pi$ being relative to the product: idempotents and the direct sum decompositions they carry; orthogonal, complete and primitive idempotents and the primitivity criterion; the standard idempotents $\tilde\Pi_+(i\vec e_z)$ and $\tilde\Pi_-(i\vec e_z)$ as the diagonal matrix units; the families of idempotents through the halving map, the trivial $0$ and $e_t$ from the central roots, the Hermitian idempotents from the family $\pm i\vec u$, and a four-real-parameter family from the non-trivial roots; the complementary pair carried by $\{\tilde\Xi,-\tilde\Xi\}$; idempotents as projections and the Hermitian idempotents as orthogonal projections; the non-pure zero divisors as complex multiples of idempotents; the disjointness of the idempotents and the nilpotents, meeting only at $0$; the complex-dimension reading of the idempotent set; the other three products carrying idempotents of their own. <a href="articles_maths/the-regular-module-in-the-biquaternion-algebra.html">The Regular Module in the Biquaternion Algebra</a>

<a href="articles_maths/the-polarized-module-of-the-biquaternion-algebra.html">The Polarized Module of the Biquaternion Algebra</a>

<a href="articles_maths/the-pauli-module-of-the-biquaternion-algebra.html">The Pauli Module of the Biquaternion Algebra</a>

<a href="articles_maths/the-category-of-modules-in-the-biquaternion-algebra.html">The Category of Modules in the Biquaternion Algebra</a>
<!-- the dictionary between representations and left modules, with dimension, subobjects, quotients, direct sums and equivalences; the modules over $\mathbb{B}\cong M_2(\mathbb{C})$, the algebra acting on its own additive group and the category of all its modules: the left regular module ${}_\mathbb{B}\mathbb{B}$, the right regular module $\mathbb{B}_\mathbb{B}$ and the regular bimodule ${}_\mathbb{B}\mathbb{B}_\mathbb{B}$; the submodules are the left, the right and the two-sided ideals, so the ideal theory of *The Regular Module in the Biquaternion Algebra* is the submodule theory of the regular object; cyclic on the unit, faithful, free of rank one on $\{e_t\}$, a generator and the identity of the tensor product, $M\otimes_\mathbb{B}{}_\mathbb{B}\mathbb{B}\cong M$ and ${}_\mathbb{B}\mathbb{B}\otimes_\mathbb{B}N\cong N$; the endomorphism rings $\operatorname{End}_\mathbb{B}(\mathbb{B}_\mathbb{B})\cong\mathbb{B}$, $\operatorname{End}_\mathbb{B}({}_\mathbb{B}\mathbb{B})\cong\mathbb{B}^{\mathrm{opp}}$ and $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb{B}\text{-}\mathbb{B}}(\mathbb{B})\cong Z(\mathbb{B})=\mathbb{C}e_t$; the defining module $S=\mathbb{B}\tilde\Pi_+=\mathbb{C}\{\tilde\Pi_+,\vec\Pi_{\mathrm{nil},y}\}$ as the unique simple left module, with the left action in the idempotent basis and the isomorphism $\mathsf{M}_2(\vec e_k)=-i\sigma_k$; the classification, every left module a direct sum $S^{\oplus k}$ and every module projective; ${}_\mathbb{B}\mathbb{B}\cong S\oplus S$, so that $S\cong\mathbb{C}^2$ and the minimal left ideals $L_\ell$ are indexed by the lines of $\mathbb{C}^2$; the standard bimodule ${}_\mathbb{B}S_\mathbb{C}$ with its commuting actions, the dual $S^*\cong S$ and quaternion conjugation as the adjugate $\mathsf{M}_2(\tilde Q^{\natural})=\varepsilon\mathsf{M}_2(\tilde Q)^{\mathrm T}\varepsilon^{-1}$; the Morita equivalence $\operatorname{Mod}(\mathbb{B})\cong\operatorname{Mod}(\mathbb{C})$ and the doubling of every complex dimension; the degeneration of the naive torsion and the torsion-freeness of the category; the real structures of the modules obtained from $\mathbb{H}$ by extension of scalars, exactly the free ones; and $\mathbb{B}$ von Neumann regular and self-injective, so that ${}_\mathbb{B}\mathbb{B}$ is a projective generator and an injective cogenerator. The group of invertibles is in *N-Regularity and N-Degeneracy in the Biquaternion Algebra*, §*The Group of Units*; the group-theoretic representations are in *Biquaternion Rotations and Lorentz Transformations*; the $4\times4$ regular matrices are in *$M_4(\mathbb{C})_{\mathbb{B}_L}$ Representation : The Matrix Product and the Algebra Structure*; and the involution, the twist and the canonical form are in *The Canonical Hermitian Form on the Regular Module of the Biquaternion Algebra*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-unpolarized-module-of-the-biquaternion-algebra.html">The Unpolarized Module of the Biquaternion Algebra</a>

#### The Spectral Theory in the Biquaternion Algebra

<a href="articles_maths/the-spectrum-of-a-biquaternion.html">The Spectrum of a Biquaternion</a>
<!-- the eigenvalue problem of an element: the intrinsic formulation (proper left ideal, left annihilator, spectral idempotent); the spectral criterion $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue iff $\tilde Q-\lambda e_t$ is a non-unit iff $(\lambda-Q_t)^2+B^2=0$, with $aa^{\natural}=(a_t^2+B^2)e_t$ as the intrinsic invertibility test and the determinant of $\mathsf M_2$ only as a check; the characteristic polynomial $(X-Q_t)^2+B^2$ with discriminant $-4B^2$ and eigenvalues $Q_t\pm iB$; the two cases of the discriminant, the regular case of distinct eigenvalues with the Lagrange idempotents $(\tilde Q-\lambda_\mp e_t)/(\lambda_\pm-\lambda_\mp)$, the unique two-term decomposition and the eigenbasis of left multiplication, and the degeneracy case of the spectral-degenerate cone $B^2=0$ as the discriminant locus, the scalar line times the isotropic cone of the vector subspace, complex dimension $3$ and real dimension $6$, singular along the scalar vertex; the three strata of the spectral-degenerate cone, the scalar stratum at the vertex, and the nilpotent and unipotent strata of the Jordan part, with their classification and spectral data in *The Jordan Basis of a Spectrally Degenerate Biquaternion*; the operator form of the criterion, $L_{\vec Q}^2=R_{\vec Q}^2=-B^2$ and the minimal-polynomial trichotomy $X^2+B^2$, $X^2$, $X$; the isotropic line with no canonical complement and the canonical flag of the algebra; the idempotent witness that the two cones are independent; the similarity classification, determined by the unordered spectrum off the cone and split into the central and non-semisimple classes on it; and the restriction of the condition to the remarkable subspaces, identically zero on the centre. The comparison with the invertibility problem is *Relations between the N Norm and Spectral Regularity and Degeneracy*. -->

<a href="articles_maths/the-centraliser-in-the-biquaternion-algebra.html">The Centraliser in the Biquaternion Algebra</a>

<a href="articles_maths/the-semisimple-nilpotent-split-of-a-biquaternion.html">The Semisimple–Nilpotent Split of a Biquaternion</a>

the Peirce corners, the lemma that one generator $u\in\mathbb{B}_{-+}$ determines the other by $uv=\tilde\Pi_-$, the theorem that the nilpotent pair is determined up to the reciprocal rescaling, and the residual $\mathbb{C}^{\times}$; the transverse-vector construction $u_\pm=\tilde\Pi_\mp V\tilde\Pi_\pm$ with $u_+u_-=V_\perp^2\tilde\Pi_-$, the symmetric and axis closed forms and the exceptional cone $\Sigma^2=3B^2$; the chart that selects one pair, the frame group $n=i\Omega/|\Omega|$ as a second normalisation up to sign from the antisymmetric part $\Omega=\tfrac12(\tilde Q^*\tilde Q-\tilde Q\tilde Q^*)=\vec Q\times\overline{\vec Q}$, which exists exactly on the complement of the normal locus and gives $\vec\Pi_{\mathrm{nil},\pm}=-i\tilde\Pi_\mp n\tilde\Pi_\pm$, with the theorem that the normal locus admits no frame freedom built from the element; the basis $\mathcal{B}(\tilde Q)=(\tilde\Pi_+,\vec\Pi_{\mathrm{nil},-},\vec\Pi_{\mathrm{nil},+},\tilde\Pi_-)$, its multiplication table, the diagonal left and right actions $(\lambda_+,\lambda_+,\lambda_-,\lambda_-)$ and $(\lambda_+,\lambda_-,\lambda_+,\lambda_-)$, the four labels and the matrix model $\mathsf M_2^{\tilde Q}$ with $\det=\langle\tilde Q_2\rangle_{\natural}$ and $\operatorname{tr}=2Q_{2,t}$, and the trace pairing with its self-dual basis; the unique expansion of every biquaternion and the coordinate algebra isomorphism, the diagonal subalgebra $\operatorname{span}\{e_t,\tilde Q\}$, the worked example $\vec e_x+\vec e_y$, and the change of basis with its cocycle; the dependence of the basis class on the direction $[\vec Q]\in\mathbb{P}^2$ alone with the affine action on the spectrum, the equivariance under inner automorphisms up to scale, and the boundary at the spectral cone with its three strata, the canonical flag, the affine family $e_b=e+b\vec Q$ of Peirce idempotents, the obstruction to a simultaneous eigenbasis of the two actions and the frame group of two complex parameters; and the spinor spaces $S_\pm=\mathbb{B}\tilde\Pi_\pm$ as the minimal left ideals, the two chiralities, the grid of the four corners, the same diagonal left action on both chiralities against the scalar right action, the general element as a pair of elementary spinors, that is a Dirac spinor, the left-versus-right reading of the mixing, and the adjoint as a map from left to right ideals. The spectral criterion and the cone are *Spectral Regularity and Degeneracy in the Biquaternion Algebra*, the sectors are *The N-Regular, Spectrally Regular Sector* and *The N-Degenerate, Spectrally Regular Sector*, the matrix image is *The Spectrally Regular Sector and Eigenbasis of a Biquaternion in Matrix Element Representations*, and the spinor theory is *Peirce Carriers and Inner Conjugation*. #### Algebra with the H Norm

<a href="articles_maths/the-polar-decomposition-of-a-biquaternion.html">The Polar Decomposition of a Biquaternion</a>
<!-- the two-factor decomposition $\tilde Q=\tilde Q_H\tilde Q_0$ of the whole biquaternion algebra: the Hermitian positive semidefinite factor $\tilde Q_H=(\tilde Q\tilde Q^{*})^{1/2}=a e_t+i\vec W/(2a)$ with $a=\sqrt{(\langle\tilde Q\rangle_{*}+\lvert\langle\tilde Q\rangle_{\natural}\rvert)/2}$, its square $\tilde Q\tilde Q^{*}=\langle\tilde Q\rangle_{*}e_t+i\vec W$ and its quadratic identity $\tilde Q_H^{2}-2a\tilde Q_H+\lvert\langle\tilde Q\rangle_{\natural}\rvert e_t=0$; the Moore–Penrose inverse in the algebra with the four Penrose conditions and its uniqueness; the inverse of the Hermitian factor in the three cases $\langle\tilde Q\rangle_{\natural}\neq0$, $\langle\tilde Q\rangle_{\natural}=0$ with $\tilde Q\neq0$, and $\tilde Q=0$, with $\tilde Q_H^{+}=(2a e_t-\tilde Q_H)/\lvert\langle\tilde Q\rangle_{\natural}\rvert$ and $\tilde Q_H^{+}=\tilde Q_H/(4a^{2})$; the isometry factor $\tilde Q_0=\tilde Q_H^{+}\tilde Q$, the two projections $\tilde\Pi_{\mathrm f}$ and $\tilde\Pi_{\mathrm i}$, the partial-isometry identity $\tilde Q_0\tilde Q_0^{*}\tilde Q_0=\tilde Q_0$; uniqueness by the two ideals, the invariants carried by the positive factor, the continuity of $\tilde Q_H$ and the discontinuity of $\tilde Q_0$ at the null cone and at the origin; and six worked elements. the boost family as a symmetric space and the spin group, the product of two boosts as a boost times a rotor with the classical rapidity and the Thomas-Wigner angle; the half-turn proposition for the vector subspace, with the proof through the scalar part of the word and the corollary that the normalised piece of a pure vector is a root of $-1$; the domain read on the subspaces, a point on the centre and the two halves and the isotropic and null cones on the other three; and the four conjugations on the polar data, with the complex conjugation the one that preserves the shape of the word; and the action of the word by the two-sided operator on the two halves, the factorisation $r^{2}\Theta_{\tilde U_{\mathrm b}}\circ\Theta_{\tilde u_{\mathrm r}}$, the Lorentz action on $\mathbb{B}_{\Phi}$, the congruence on $\mathbb{B}_{\Psi}$, the intertwining by $i$, the kernels and the image $CO^{+}(1,3)$; the table of the subspaces the two-sided operator preserves, with the theorem that the elements whose two-sided operator preserves all six are the central multiples of the real unit quaternions, the multiplicative criterion, and the operator groups $SO(3)$ and $\mathbb{R}_{>0}\times SO(3)$; the word is that of *The Complete Polar Decomposition of an N-Regular Biquaternion*, and the boundary is the two-factor pair of *The Polar Decomposition of a Biquaternion* and *The Polar Decomposition of an N-Degenerate Biquaternion*. -->
